$comment: Content for Money & Independence (node g48, ages 18-22, Chapter 6): NEW v2 build to GDD 48 (mechanic-
embodying), the College node for standing on your own feet (Thread C · Feelings & Life Skills, Work & Money).
Reworks the old ModesEngine build onto the shared v2 engine. "Money isn't just money; it's independence, safety
and choices." 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across budget-it → save-and-traps → earn-and-ask →
money-and-love → money-is-freedom → tools-and-help, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (branch /
sort / strike-rewrite / reflect / match / role-play / spot): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: branch
(your move), sort, strike-rewrite (bust the myth). Five themes: budget it (a light sim), save & avoid traps
(debt, EMIs, BNPL, scams), earn & ask (payslips, the pay gap, negotiating), money & love (fair money in
relationships, FINANCIAL CONTROL as abuse; UN&RE), tools & help. Money = freedom; economic autonomy is
foundational to equality, especially for the young women this work exists for. Financial control in a
relationship is named as a recognised form of abuse under India's Domestic Violence Act, routed to help
(181/1091). EDUCATIONAL, NOT financial advice; no products promoted; no real financial data collected. India
realities: UPI, EMIs, first-job payslips, family expectations, low women's workforce participation and a real
pay gap. Builds on g42 (Life Ready); pairs g49 and g52; continues into g58 (Money, Together). gameId
title: Money & Independence
greet: Hey, it's Lensy. Money is independence, safety and choices. Let's get the basics school skips: budget, dodge debt traps, earn and ask, keep it fair.

badge.title: Money & Independence 🕊️
badge.blurb: You can budget, spot the debt traps, earn and ask for your worth, and keep money fair in love, because money is independence, safety and choices. 💼

helpLine: Money is freedom. Controlling your money, blocking you from earning, or taking your earnings is abuse under the Domestic Violence Act. Call 181 or 1091.
reassure: Wanting your own money isn’t selfish: it’s independence and safety. If someone controls or takes it, that’s abuse, not your fault: reach 181 or 1091. 🕊️

scenarios.hook: "Budgeting just means depriving yourself."

myth.un: Budgeting means depriving yourself.
myth.re: A budget gives you control and choices over your money, it's a plan, not a punishment.
myth.why: Knowing where your money goes is freedom, not restriction.

scenarios.relearn: A budget gives you control and choices, not deprivation.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a need, or a want?
scenarios.relearn: Rent, basic food, transport and medicine are needs; upgrades and convenience are wants.

scenarios.hook: Match the budget slice to its share (a rough starting guide).
scenarios.relearn: A rough needs/wants/savings split, around 50/30/20, is a useful starting guide.

pairs.right: What to do if it doesn't fit

scenarios.hook: Your first stipend lands and it feels like a lot.

steps.prompt: The credit alert pings on your phone. What do you do first?

options.text: Spend freely now and sort it out later
options.then: The first week is great. By the third week you are counting every coin.

options.text: Send a big chunk home and wing the rest
options.then: Home is pleased. You can't say what is left for your own month.

options.text: Copy what a senior says he does
options.then: His numbers sound neat. His rent is different from yours, so nothing fits.

options.text: Split it into needs, savings and some fun
options.then: It takes ten minutes. The amount feels smaller, but every rupee has a job.

steps.why: Giving every rupee a job first makes the money last.

steps.prompt: A week later, you spot something you want that costs a fair bit. What do you do?

options.text: Buy it now and cover rent from the next stipend
options.then: It arrives in two days. The rent date comes around with a gap.

options.text: Check what is left after needs and savings, then decide
options.then: Half of it fits. You wait for the rest, and the wait doesn't hurt much.

options.text: Cut out every want from now on
options.then: You feel strict for a week. Then you splurge on something bigger.

options.text: Put it on an easy EMI
options.then: Approval takes a minute. Now two payments are due every month.

steps.why: What is left after needs and savings is yours to enjoy.

steps.prompt: The next stipend lands tomorrow. How will you handle it this time?

options.text: Set needs and savings first, then enjoy what's left
options.then: You write three lines in a note. Fun is on it, so the plan feels doable.

options.text: Do the same as last time and see what happens
options.then: The month starts well and ends thin, much like before.

options.text: Promise to save almost everything and skip all fun
options.then: It feels disciplined for ten days. Then one big splurge breaks it.

options.text: Wait until you earn more to bother planning
options.then: The wait has no end date, and the stipend disappears again.

steps.why: A plan with fun built in is one you will actually follow.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding where money goes before spending it is the heart of budgeting.
scenarios.relearn: Plan your income across needs, savings and fun before spending it.

scenarios.hook: "You can only budget once you earn a lot."

myth.un: You can only budget once you earn a lot.
myth.re: Budgeting matters most when money is tight; it's a skill for any income.
myth.why: A plan stretches a small income further.

scenarios.relearn: Budgeting matters at any income, most of all when money is tight.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps your budget, or quietly breaks it?
scenarios.relearn: Tracking, saving first and a monthly review help; invisible buys, creep and avoidance break a budget.

scenarios.hook: You keep wondering where your money disappears each month.

steps.prompt: Another month ends with your wallet nearly empty. What do you do?

options.text: Decide you simply don't earn enough
options.then: The thought sits heavy. Nothing changes and the money vanishes again.

options.text: Cut everything fun from next month
options.then: You skip outings and feel tight. You still don't know what drained it.

options.text: Track every expense for a month
options.then: You start noting each chai, ride and order on your phone. A pattern shows.

options.text: Ask a friend where you might be overspending
options.then: She guesses food delivery. She can't see your account, so it's a guess.

steps.why: Tracking shows where money really goes before you blame income.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, you open your UPI history and see many small payments. What do you do?

options.text: Group them by type and find the biggest leaks
options.then: Food orders and small top-ups add up to more than you guessed.

options.text: Ignore them since each one is tiny
options.then: Each one is small. You still can't say where the month went.

options.text: Delete the UPI app so you can't spend
options.then: Paying gets harder, and you reinstall it within days.

options.text: Blame the friend who always asks you to pay
options.then: It feels good to pin it on someone. The total barely moves.

steps.why: Grouping turns a pile of small payments into a clear picture.

steps.prompt: At month-end, your bank app shows food orders as your biggest spend. What do you do about it?

options.text: Cut it to zero from tomorrow
options.then: It lasts four days. Then you overspend on it to make up.

options.text: Put it on a list to fix later
options.then: It sits on the list, and the leak carries on into next month.

options.text: Tell yourself everyone orders in
options.then: It stays as it is, and next month it's a little bigger.

options.text: Set a small weekly limit and track it
options.then: The limit is easy to see. The next week ends with money left over.

steps.why: A small limit you can see is easier to keep than a harsh ban.

scenarios.debrief: You can't manage what you don't measure; tracking reveals where money really goes.
scenarios.relearn: Track your spending for a month to see where money really goes.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: paying yourself first, saving before you spend, quietly builds a cushion. Like that idea?
scenarios.affirm: Saving a slice before anything else is how the cushion actually gets built.
scenarios.relearn: Pay yourself first: save a slice before you spend the rest.

scenarios.hook: Match the budget category to an example.
scenarios.relearn: Needs, wants and savings each have clear, everyday examples.

scenarios.hook: A big one-off cost, like a course fee, is due in a few months.

steps.prompt: You know the amount roughly. What do you do now?

options.text: Split the cost over the months and set it aside
options.then: The monthly amount looks manageable. You move it on payday.

options.text: Wait and handle it when it arrives
options.then: The date is far, so it fades from your mind for weeks.

options.text: Plan to borrow from a friend when it's due
options.then: A friend says she'll probably help. Nothing is fixed, only a hope.

options.text: Save whatever is left at the end of each month
options.then: Some months leave nothing. The pot grows slowly and unevenly.

steps.why: Splitting a known cost over the months leaves no scramble.

steps.prompt: A few weeks in, a friend invites you on a trip that costs a bit. What do you do?

options.text: Go, and find the fee money later
options.then: You go, and the fee plan slips back another month.

options.text: Say no to every outing until the fee is paid
options.then: You stay home for weeks and feel left out. Saving starts to feel like punishment.

options.text: Check what's spare after the fee, then decide
options.then: A smaller version of the trip fits without touching what the fee needs.

options.text: Put the trip on an easy EMI
options.then: It's approved in minutes. Now two payments are due each month.

steps.why: Checking what you can spare protects the plan without cutting all fun.

steps.prompt: A month before the due date, the fee goes up a little and you're short. What do you do?

options.text: Take a quick loan from an app
options.then: Approval is instant. The interest makes the cost bigger than it was.

options.text: Trim wants for a month to close the gap
options.then: You skip treats and extras for a month. The gap closes before the date.

options.text: Ask family for the gap with no repayment plan
options.then: They help, but it feels uneasy. Nobody has said when you'll pay back.

options.text: Hope the deadline gets extended
options.then: You check the website each week. The date stays the same.

steps.why: Trimming wants for a month closes a small gap without debt.

scenarios.debrief: Sinking a little aside for known future costs avoids debt later.
scenarios.relearn: Save a little each month toward known future costs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fixed cost, or a flexible one you can trim?
scenarios.relearn: Rent, EMIs and your recharge are fixed; eating out, subscriptions and extra clothes you can trim.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget is just you telling your money where to go, instead of wondering where it went. Click?
scenarios.affirm: Directing your money on purpose is exactly what taking charge of it feels like.
scenarios.relearn: A budget is you directing your money, instead of wondering where it went.

scenarios.hook: Friends are spending freely and you feel pressure to match them.

steps.prompt: Your friends plan a big Saturday outing. What do you do?

options.text: Go along and spend what everyone spends
options.then: It's a fun night. Your month's plan now has a dent in it.

options.text: Make up an excuse and skip it
options.then: They miss you. You feel relieved and a little lonely.

options.text: Put your share on credit and pay later
options.then: The bill doesn't hit today. A reminder for it arrives two weeks later.

options.text: Join for part of it, within your budget
options.then: They say okay. You leave a little early and your budget is intact.

steps.why: You can join on your own terms without spending to match anyone.

steps.prompt: Next week, a friend jokes that real friends don't count rupees. How do you respond?

options.text: Laugh it off and spend more to prove a point
options.then: The group cheers. Your wallet feels it on the way home.

options.text: Say you have a plan and you like sticking to it
options.then: She shrugs. "Fair enough." The teasing fades by the next outing.

options.text: Snap back that they are wasteful
options.then: The mood sours and the group goes quiet for a while.

options.text: Explain your whole budget figure by figure
options.then: They look bored. You share more than you meant to about your money.

steps.why: A calm, short answer holds your plan without a fight.

steps.prompt: Another friend is stressed about money after matching others for months. She asks what you do. What do you say?

options.text: Share your method and offer to help her plan
options.then: She relaxes. "Can you show me how you track it?"

options.text: Tell her she should have known better
options.then: She goes quiet and stops asking.

options.text: Lend her money without asking about the rest
options.then: She's grateful. The same problem is back next month.

options.text: Say everyone struggles and change the topic
options.then: She nods. The talk moves on and nothing changes.

steps.why: Sharing a simple method helps more than lecturing or lending.

scenarios.debrief: Spending to keep up with others is a fast route to money stress; your plan is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Stick to your budget; you don't have to match others' spending.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a healthy money habit, or not?

items.text: Keeping some fun money in the plan
Saving a slice before you spend

scenarios.relearn: Reviewing, budgeting fun and saving first are healthy; avoidance, never counting and borrowing for wants aren't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget with a little room for joy is one you'll actually keep. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: A realistic budget that includes some fun is the kind that actually lasts.
scenarios.relearn: A budget with room for some joy is one you'll actually keep.

scenarios.hook: "I'll start saving once I earn more."

myth.un: I'll start saving once I earn more.
myth.re: Building the saving habit now, even with small amounts, matters more than the size.
myth.why: The habit, not the amount, is what compounds.

scenarios.relearn: Build the saving habit now, even small; the habit matters more than the amount.

scenarios.hook: You have a little spare money this month and no plan for it.

steps.prompt: A few thousand rupees sit in your account after rent. What do you do with it?

options.text: Start building an emergency fund
options.then: You set aside a first chunk and name the account. It feels oddly steady.

options.text: Spend it before it disappears
options.then: A good dinner and a new top. By month-end you're watching your balance again.

options.text: Lend it all to a friend who needs it
options.then: Your friend is relieved. You have no cushion and no date for repayment.

options.text: Keep it in your wallet for whatever comes up
options.then: Some goes on chai and small buys. The rest feels thin by the week's end.

steps.why: A fund set apart from daily spending is the first cushion.

steps.prompt: A week later, you sit down to set a target for an emergency fund. How much do you aim for?

options.text: Aim for about three months of essentials
options.then: You add up rent, food and travel. The number is big, but it gives you a target.

options.text: One month of rent is enough
options.then: That covers one bad month. A longer gap in income would run past it.

options.text: Wait to pick a number until you earn more
options.then: Without a target, saving comes in fits and starts.

options.text: Aim for a round lakh, untouchable
options.then: A lakh feels grand and far away. Each small step feels like nothing.

steps.why: Three months of essentials is a clear, realistic target.

steps.prompt: Two months on, your emergency fund has a little in it. Then your phone breaks, and the repair costs a real chunk. What do you do?

options.text: Put it on an easy EMI and keep the fund
options.then: The repair goes through in a minute. Now an instalment hangs over each month.

options.text: Use the fund, then rebuild it slowly
options.then: The repair is paid without stress. You start topping the fund up again.

options.text: Borrow from a friend and leave the fund
options.then: Your friend pays. Now you owe someone, with the fund sitting unused.

options.text: Ignore the crack and keep using it
options.then: It works for a week. Then the screen dies while you fill an exam form.

steps.why: An emergency fund exists for moments like this, and you can rebuild it.

scenarios.debrief: An emergency fund, aiming for around three months of essentials, is the first thing to build.
scenarios.relearn: Build an emergency fund (aim for around three months of essentials) first.

scenarios.hook: "Buy now, pay later is basically free money."

myth.un: Buy now, pay later is free money.
myth.re: BNPL and easy EMIs are debt; they often lead to overspending and missed payments.
myth.why: Delaying payment isn't the same as affording it.

scenarios.relearn: Buy-now-pay-later and EMIs are debt, not free money.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a debt trap, or a sensible money move?

items.text: Paying only the minimum on a card
Borrowing only what you can repay
Rolling one loan into a new loan

scenarios.relearn: Minimum-only, EMIs on wants and rolling loans are traps; clearing high-interest debt, borrowing within means and saving first are sensible.

scenarios.hook: "Paying just the minimum on a loan or card is fine."

myth.un: Paying just the minimum is fine.
myth.re: High-interest debt grows fast; paying only the minimum keeps you stuck for years.
myth.why: Interest piles up on what you don't clear.

scenarios.relearn: Paying only the minimum keeps you stuck; high-interest debt grows fast.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two scam lines among the genuine ones.

scene.text: "Double your money in a week, guaranteed"
A normal salary credited to your account
"Share your OTP to claim your prize"
Your statement is ready in the app
A slow-growing recurring deposit

scenarios.why: Guaranteed-doubling and OTP-asks are the scams; a salary, a statement and a slow deposit are genuine.
scenarios.relearn: Guaranteed returns and OTP requests are the scam lines.

scenarios.hook: An SMS says you've won a cash prize, and asks for a small fee or an OTP.

steps.prompt: It says to claim within ten minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Ignore it and report the message
options.then: You delete the thread and report the number. The ten-minute countdown vanishes.

options.text: Pay the small fee to claim the prize
options.then: The fee goes through. A second message asks for a bigger 'tax' payment.

options.text: Reply and ask if the offer is real
options.then: They answer within seconds, very sure. Now they know your number is active.

options.text: Forward it to friends so they can win too
options.then: Two friends nearly click. One asks why you'd pass it on.

steps.why: A prize that asks for a fee or an OTP is a scam.

steps.prompt: A call comes from a number saying it's the prize office. What do you do?

options.text: Stay on and give only your name
options.then: They use your name to sound official and ask for one bank detail.

options.text: Ask them to send a written notice first
options.then: A neat PDF arrives in minutes. It looks real, which makes hanging up harder.

options.text: Share the OTP, since they know your name
options.then: The OTP goes through. A debit alert arrives a minute later.

options.text: Hang up without giving anything
options.then: The line goes dead. A minute later they try again from another number.

steps.why: Hanging up without sharing anything closes the door.

steps.prompt: A friend says she paid a 'fee' for a prize and got nothing. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her she should have known better
options.then: She looks down. She stops telling anyone, including her bank.

options.text: Tell her to pay again to get it back
options.then: She almost does. A second fee would only be a second loss.

options.text: Tell her it's not her fault, and to report it on 1930
options.then: She exhales. "I thought I was the only one. I'll call today."

options.text: Tell her to forget it. It's a small amount
options.then: She nods. The scammer keeps her number and tries again later.

steps.why: Scams fool many people, so blame helps no one and reporting does.

scenarios.debrief: Legitimate winnings never require a fee or your OTP; that's always fraud.
scenarios.relearn: Never share OTPs or pay fees to 'claim' a prize; it's fraud.

scenarios.hook: "A get-rich-quick offer is a real opportunity."

myth.un: A get-rich-quick offer is a real opportunity.
myth.re: If it sounds too good to be true, it's a scam, real wealth is built slowly.
myth.why: Guaranteed quick riches don't exist.

scenarios.relearn: Too good to be true means a scam; real wealth builds slowly.

scenarios.hook: A gaming console you want is just out of reach, and the shop offers a 12-month EMI.

steps.prompt: The salesperson says it's only a small amount a month. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and save for it instead
options.then: You set a monthly target and a date. The console stays in the shop for now.

options.text: Take the EMI. It's only a bit a month
options.then: The forms take ten minutes. Your income now has a 12-month claim on it.

options.text: Haggle for a discount, then take the EMI
options.then: They cut a little. The EMI still runs for twelve months.

options.text: Take a cheaper model on the EMI
options.then: It's cheaper, and so is the instalment. It's still a year of debt for a want.

steps.why: Saving first costs less and keeps your future income free.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a new want pops up and your budget feels tight. What do you do?

options.text: Pay a smaller down payment now and EMI the rest
options.then: The down payment hurts. The EMI is still there for a year.

options.text: Give up saving. You'll never get there anyway
options.then: Saving stops, and so does the progress. The want stays.

options.text: Check your plan and set a target for it
options.then: You see what you can set aside monthly. The want gets a date instead of a loan.

options.text: Ask a friend to lend you the money
options.then: She says yes. Now you owe her, with no fixed date.

steps.why: Checking your plan keeps a want on a schedule instead of on credit.

steps.prompt: A friend shows off her new EMI phone and says 'no pain'. What do you say?

options.text: Ask which shop gives the best EMI deal this week
options.then: She lists three. You're now comparing EMIs, not savings plans.

options.text: Say EMI is debt and share what you've learned
options.then: She listens. "Maybe I should have waited."

options.text: Say nothing and admire the phone
options.then: She keeps talking. A second EMI is already on her mind.

options.text: Tell her she's wasting money
options.then: She bristles. "Who asked you?" She stops sharing anything.

steps.why: Sharing your own experience helps more than judging hers.

scenarios.debrief: Putting wants on EMIs mortgages your future income; saving first is the cheaper path.
scenarios.relearn: Save for wants rather than putting them on EMIs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds financial safety, or risk?
scenarios.relearn: An emergency fund, living below your means and steady saving build safety; maxed credit, borrowing for wants and 'guaranteed' doubles are risk.

scenarios.hook: Match the small habit to what it builds.
scenarios.relearn: Small, regular money habits compound into real results.

scenarios.hook: A friend pushes you to join a scheme that pays you for recruiting others.

steps.prompt: He says his friends are already earning. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, and ask where the money comes from
options.then: He stumbles. "From new members. That's how it grows."

options.text: Join, since your friend is in
options.then: You pay a joining fee. Your first task is to bring in three friends.

options.text: Say maybe and ask for the paperwork
options.then: He sends a glossy deck full of earnings and no real product.

options.text: Join with a small amount just to test it
options.then: The amount is taken. You're told to recruit to get it back.

steps.why: If the money mostly comes from recruiting, it is not real earning.

steps.prompt: Two days later he adds you to a group chat full of 'earnings' posts and countdown timers. What do you do?

options.text: Stay in the group and watch for now
options.then: The countdowns keep pinging, and the pressure builds.

options.text: Leave the group, and tell him why you're out
options.then: He reads it and goes quiet for a day. He doesn't drop the topic.

options.text: Pay now so you don't miss out
options.then: You pay and pitch a friend. The next day, the countdown starts again.

options.text: Argue with everyone in the group chat
options.then: Others pile on with their 'earnings'. He tells friends you made a scene.

steps.why: Leaving clearly, with a reason, is fair to both of you.

steps.prompt: A classmate posts a screenshot of big 'earnings' from it. What do you do?

options.text: Believe the screenshot. Numbers don't lie
options.then: It looks so convincing that you start to believe it works.

options.text: Comment 'wow' and leave it
options.then: He replies with a fire emoji. Others in the comments ask how to join.

options.text: Ask what he paid in and what he withdrew
options.then: He goes quiet. The screenshot shows a balance, not cash in his account.

options.text: Ask how much you could make like that
options.then: He sends a figure and a link before you can blink.

steps.why: Asking what he put in and took out shows what a screenshot hides.

steps.prompt: Another friend asks if she should join. What do you tell her?

options.text: Tell her it's her choice and stay out of it
options.then: She nods, and joins the next day with only the recruiter's version.

options.text: Tell her to try with a tiny amount
options.then: She pays a tiny fee and is pushed to recruit.

options.text: Laugh it off and change the subject
options.then: She's left to decide alone, with only the recruiter's story.

options.text: Share what you found, and suggest she skip it
options.then: She thanks you and asks how to spot the next one.

steps.why: Telling a friend what you know, and leaving the choice to her, is fair.

scenarios.debrief: Recruit-to-earn schemes typically collapse and cost the latecomers; steer clear.
scenarios.relearn: Decline pay-to-recruit schemes; they're usually scams.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a smart borrowing reason, or a warning sign?

items.text: An asset or education that pays off
Borrowing to repay other debt repeatedly
A big unavoidable cost you can repay
A want you could just save for

scenarios.relearn: Borrowing for an asset, brief emergency or a repayable need can make sense; lifestyle, debt-on-debt and saveable wants are warnings.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two early signs of a debt spiral.

scene.text: Using new debt to pay old debt
Clearing a card in full each month
Only ever making minimum payments
Saving a little every payday
Spending less than you earn

scenarios.why: Debt-to-pay-debt and minimum-only payments are the spiral signs; clearing in full and saving aren't.
scenarios.relearn: Borrowing to repay debt and minimum-only payments are debt-spiral signs.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a cushion of savings is what turns an emergency into an inconvenience. Worth building?
scenarios.affirm: A savings cushion is exactly what keeps a bad week from becoming a crisis.
scenarios.relearn: A savings cushion turns an emergency into a mere inconvenience.

scenarios.hook: You notice small monthly charges quietly draining your account.

steps.prompt: You count eight recurring charges on your statement. What do you do?

options.text: Leave them. They're only small
options.then: Next month the same eight go through. The total keeps adding up.

options.text: Cancel all eight to be safe
options.then: Your music, storage and study app stop at once. You miss one in a week.

options.text: List them all and cancel the ones you don't use
options.then: You cancel four. Part of next month's money stays with you.

options.text: Ask a friend which ones she'd keep
options.then: Her list differs from yours, so it doesn't help you decide.

steps.why: Listing every charge shows which ones earn their place.

steps.prompt: Next month a charge shows up for a service you forgot you ever signed up for. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it, since this month is already paid
options.then: It renews again next month, quietly.

options.text: Pause it and promise to use it more
options.then: You don't. The pause ends after two months, and it restarts.

options.text: Switch to the yearly plan to save
options.then: The yearly bill is big, and you still don't use it.

options.text: Cancel it and ask about a refund
options.then: It confirms the end date. The refund request is pending.

steps.why: Cancelling what you forgot stops the leak at once.

steps.prompt: A free trial pops up for something that looks useful. What do you do?

options.text: Start it and trust yourself to remember
options.then: On day eight you see a charge. Memory didn't hold.

options.text: Skip free trials forever
options.then: Safe, but you miss a tool that would have helped your course.

options.text: Start it and set a reminder to cancel
options.then: The reminder pings on day six. You decide calmly.

options.text: Start it and let it renew once to decide

scenarios.hook: You're offered a role and the pay is a bit low for the work.
scenarios.setup: The hiring manager calls with the offer.

steps.prompt: The hiring manager says: "We'd love to have you. The offer is at this figure."

options.text: "Thank you so much. I accept. I'll sign whenever you like."
options.then: "Wonderful. I'll draft the letter." He pauses. "Anything before I do?"

options.text: "Let me think. I'll get back to you sometime."
options.then: "Sure, but we need an answer this week."

options.text: "Is that really the best you can possibly do for me?"
options.then: "It's a fair offer for this level." He sounds a little cooler.

options.text: "Thanks, I'm excited. Could we discuss the figure?"
options.then: "Of course," he says, sounding open.

steps.why: Thanking first and then asking to discuss the figure is polite and clear.

steps.prompt: He says: "The letter will state this figure. Anything to check before I send it?"

options.text: "No, it's all fine. Whatever you think is fair."
options.then: "Okay. We'll keep it as offered, then."

options.text: "Yes, the figure. My research puts this role higher."
options.then: "Thanks for being clear. Let me see what's possible."

options.text: "Just make it much higher. I need more than this."
options.then: "I hear you. But I need a reason to go higher."

options.text: "Let me ask my family first before I say anything."
options.then: "Of course. Can you let us know by Friday?"

steps.why: Pointing to your research gives them a real reason to move the figure.

steps.prompt: He adds: "Budgets are tight this year, so the figure may stay. Does anything besides pay matter to you?"

options.text: "Yes. Could we agree a pay review in six months?"
options.then: "That I can do. I'll run it past my manager."

options.text: "No, only the figure matters. Nothing else."
options.then: "Then I'm afraid I can't promise more."

options.text: "Nothing. I'll take it as it is now."
options.then: "Great." The figure stays as offered.

options.text: "Give me a bigger title instead. That's enough."

steps.why: A review date gives the pay a path to grow when the figure can't move now.

steps.prompt: He says: "I'll confirm it all over a quick call next week. Does that work?"

options.text: "Just email the figure. The rest we can sort later."
options.then: "Sure." Nothing else you discussed is written down.

options.text: "Yes. I'll trust your word on all of it."
options.then: "Thank you." There is nothing on paper to refer to later.

options.text: "Please put the figure and any terms in writing."
options.then: "Of course. You'll have it by evening."

options.text: "Not yet. I'll wait and see what other offers come."
options.then: "Understood. The offer stands until Friday."

steps.why: Putting the final terms in writing protects what was agreed.

steps.prompt: The thought keeps nagging at you. What do you do first?

steps.prompt: Your next review is a month away. How do you prepare?

options.text: Plan to mention pay only if they raise it first
options.then: You go in with no plan to bring it up yourself.

options.text: Prepare a demand far above a fair number
options.then: The number sounds good to you, but it's far above what the role pays.

options.then: People like you, but nobody has a number in mind.

options.text: List your work and results beside the market range
options.then: Your list shows three projects you led. It gives you something solid.

steps.why: Results next to the market range make a clear, calm case.

steps.prompt: In the review, your manager says she values you and asks what you need. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'd like to be paid fairly but give no number
options.then: She nods warmly. No number leaves the room.

options.text: Hint that you might leave if nothing changes
options.then: She tenses. The talk turns to whether you're loyal.

options.text: Share your results and the range, and ask for a fair figure

options.text: Say you're happy and leave pay for later

steps.prompt: Two weeks after the review, your pay hasn't changed. What do you do next?

options.text: Email her your case and ask for a time
options.then: She replies with a date in two weeks. You note it.

options.text: Message her every day until she answers
options.then: She replies twice, then grows visibly impatient.

options.text: Wait quietly and hope she brings it up
options.then: Weeks go by. The silence leaves you unsure.

options.text: Ask colleagues to lean on her for you

scenarios.hook: In your review, you want to make the case for a raise.
scenarios.setup: She finishes going through the year's work.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "That's the review done. Anything to add?"

options.text: "No, that's everything. Thank you for the feedback."
options.then: She closes her notebook. "Sure? Reviews are when people raise pay."

options.text: "Only that I hope my work gets noticed soon."
options.then: "We do notice it." She waits, as if expecting more.

options.text: "I'd like a raise. I've been here for quite a long time."
options.then: "Time here isn't the only thing we look at."

options.text: "Here's what I added this year. I'd like to discuss a raise."
options.then: She sits forward. "All right. Tell me about it."

steps.why: Making the case yourself beats waiting to be noticed.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Which results from this year are you proudest of?"

options.text: "I work very hard and I'm always here on time."
options.then: "I see that. What has it led to, though?"

options.text: "I led two launches and cut delays. Here are the details."
options.then: She reads them. "That's solid work."

options.text: "I think my work speaks for itself, honestly."
options.then: "I'd still like to hear it from you."

options.text: "Honestly, others on the team did a lot less than me."
options.then: "I'd rather we talk about your work only."

steps.prompt: She says: "Budgets are tight this year. Raises will be hard to promise."

options.text: "Understood. What would make it possible by next review?"

options.text: "Okay. Then forget pay. It isn't a big deal."
options.then: She nods. "Still, your results are worth noting."

options.text: "Then I'll start looking for a job that pays more."
options.then: She looks taken aback. "I'd hate to lose you. Let's talk."

options.text: "A raise is my right. You must find the money."
options.then: She stiffens. "That's not how it works here."

steps.why: Asking what would make it possible keeps the door open in a tight year.

steps.prompt: She says: "I'll share your results with the team. What do you need from me?"

options.text: "Nothing more. Whatever you decide is fine with me."
options.then: "Thanks." Nothing has a date on it.

options.text: "Please decide on my pay quickly. I can't wait long."
options.then: "I can't promise quickly. I'll do my best."

options.text: "Could you email me when we'll talk about my pay?"
options.then: "Yes. I'll send you a note by Friday."

options.text: "I'll ask my colleagues to speak up for me too."
options.then: "Please don't. I'd rather handle it with you directly."

steps.why: A dated follow-up by email keeps your ask moving.

scenarios.hook: A friend has a job offer, and the pay feels a little low to her.
scenarios.setup: She messages you before her offer call.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I'm too nervous to negotiate. Maybe I'll just accept."

options.text: "Yeah, better not rock the boat. Just say thank you."
options.then: "Right. Safer." She sounds relieved and a bit small.

options.text: "Just demand more. They'll give it if they want you."
options.then: She sounds nervous. "What if they say no?"

options.text: "Asking isn't rude. It's normal. Know your worth and ask."
options.then: She breathes out. "Okay. That does sound less scary."

options.text: "Give me their number and I'll negotiate for you."
options.then: "I don't think they'd like that."

steps.why: Negotiating is normal, and saying so calmly helps a nervous friend.

steps.prompt: She asks: "If I did ask, what would I actually say?"

options.text: "Thank them, name the market rate, and ask for it."
options.then: "That's simple enough. I can do that."

options.text: "Just say you need more for your expenses."
options.then: "That's true, but it's not about the job."

options.text: "Say another company offered more, even if it didn't."
options.then: "That feels like lying. I can't."

options.text: "Copy what I said in my last job. It worked."
options.then: "Your job was different. Mine won't fit that."

steps.why: A simple script of thanks, the market rate and the ask is easy to use.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What if they get annoyed and take the offer back?"

options.text: "It can happen, so maybe don't risk it at all."
options.then: "Yeah. That does worry me." She takes the call anyway, hoping they just say yes.

options.text: "They won't. Companies never do that to anyone."
options.then: "Never? That's hard to believe."

options.text: "If they do, you can tell everyone online."
options.then: "That would make things worse."

options.text: "A polite, prepared ask is normal. The worst is usually a no."
options.then: "A no I can handle. Okay."

steps.why: A polite, prepared ask is a normal part of hiring.

steps.prompt: After the call, she messages: "They said they'd get back to me. Now what?"

options.text: "Now wait. Don't contact them until they do."
options.then: "Okay. I'll just sit by the phone, then."

options.text: "Send a thank-you and ask when you'll hear back."
options.then: "Good idea. I'll send it now."

options.text: "Message them daily until you get an answer."
options.then: "That sounds too pushy."

options.text: "Accept whatever comes. There's nothing more to do."
options.then: "Even if it's low? I suppose."

steps.why: A thank-you with a date keeps things polite and moving.

scenarios.relearn: Encourage a friend that negotiating is normal and worth doing.

scenarios.hook: A "job" asks you to pay an upfront fee for training or a deposit.

steps.prompt: The message says the role is yours once you pay a small fee today. What do you do?

options.text: Pay the small fee to secure the role
options.then: The payment goes through. Then a second fee is asked for.

options.text: Pay half now and half after you get the job
options.then: They take the first half. The job details never come.

options.text: Ask them to send the joining letter before you pay
options.then: They send a polished letter with a logo. It proves nothing.

options.text: Decline to pay and check the company first
options.then: A quick search turns up no proper address and a few warnings.

steps.why: Real employers pay you, so a fee for a job is a warning sign.

steps.prompt: They call and say the offer expires in one hour. What do you do?

options.text: Pay quickly so you don't lose it
options.then: The payment goes through. The contact becomes harder to reach.

options.text: Stay calm and refuse to be rushed
options.then: They get pushy, then cut the call. An hour later, they message again.

options.text: Ask a friend to lend you the fee quickly
options.then: Your friend sends it. Now both of you are out of pocket.

options.text: Ask for a discount on the fee
options.then: They cut the fee. It's still an upfront fee for a job.

steps.why: Scammers rush you, so staying calm keeps you safe.

steps.prompt: A new message asks for your ID copies and bank details "for the salary account". What do you do?

options.text: Share nothing and end the conversation
options.then: They stop replying. Your details stay with you.

options.text: Send a photo of your ID but not the bank details
options.then: They thank you. Your ID can now be misused.

options.text: Send the bank details but keep the OTP to yourself
options.then: They use your details to try logins. An OTP request arrives.

options.text: Send everything, since it's probably a real company
options.then: You send it all. Hours later, odd messages start arriving.

steps.why: Sharing ID and bank details with a stranger risks real harm.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, the whole thing leaves you shaken. What do you do?

options.text: Keep quiet because you feel foolish
options.then: The worry stays with you, and nobody helps you check what's at risk.

options.text: Message the scammer and scold them
options.then: They block you. It changes nothing and leaves you more rattled.

options.text: Tell someone you trust and report it
options.then: They help you report it on the cybercrime helpline, 1930. You feel steadier.

options.text: Look for another quick job right away
options.then: You find an ad with big pay for little work. It looks the same.

steps.why: Being targeted isn't your fault. Telling someone and reporting it protects you and others.

scenarios.debrief: Upfront 'fees' to get a job are a classic scam; real employers pay you, not the reverse.

scenarios.hook: Your partner says your salary should sit in their account 'for safekeeping'.

steps.prompt: They bring it up again on payday. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself most couples pool everything, so it's normal
options.then: You nod along inside. A small knot stays in your stomach.

options.text: Ask a cousin to explain why that's unfair to them

options.text: Ask a colleague, who says to wait and it will pass

options.text: Decide it's your fault for making money a big issue

scenarios.hook: A partner has started pushing for all your money to be merged.

steps.prompt: Your partner says: "Let's put all our money in one account. I'll manage it."

options.text: "I'm not good with money, so maybe you should manage it."

options.text: "My friend says all couples pool everything. Maybe I should."

options.text: "That's such an old-fashioned way to think."

scenarios.hook: You and your partner have shared costs for months, with nothing agreed.
scenarios.setup: It's a quiet weekend afternoon.

steps.prompt: Your partner says: "We should sort out who pays for what."

options.text: "Let's set a fair split, and keep our own accounts."
options.then: "A fair split. Okay. Let's look at the numbers together."

options.text: "You decide it all. I'm easy either way, honestly."
options.then: "Okay. I'll work it out and tell you."

options.text: "Let's put everything in one pot and not keep track."
options.then: "If you like. We'll see what's left at month end."

options.text: "Let's just pay whoever is free each time."
options.then: "That's fine for now. It could get messy."

steps.why: Setting a fair split openly, with each keeping an account, starts the talk well.

steps.prompt: A week later, your partner says: "I earn more than you. Should I pay more?"

options.text: "Yes. You pay more, so you decide what we spend on."
options.then: "All right. I'll decide then."

options.text: "Maybe we split by income, and both see the numbers."
options.then: "Split by income. That seems fair. Let's try it."

options.text: "No. Exactly half, even if it stretches me."
options.then: "Are you sure? That sounds tough for you."

options.text: "Let's not bring income into it at all."
options.then: "Okay. But it does make a difference."

steps.why: Splitting by income with open numbers keeps the arrangement fair to both.

steps.prompt: Your partner says: "What if one of us loses a job?"

options.text: "Then the other one takes over everything for us."
options.then: "Everything? That's a lot to carry alone."

options.text: "Let's not think about that yet."
options.then: "We won't. But it could catch us off guard."

options.text: "We talk early, adjust, and keep our own savings."
options.then: "That's sensible. I'd feel safer knowing we have a plan."

options.text: "Then the one with the job decides."
options.then: "Decides what? That doesn't sound fair."

steps.why: Talking early and keeping your own savings keeps both partners steady.

scenarios.relearn: Agree a fair split openly, and both keep your own accounts.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign of financial control, or normal shared finances?
scenarios.relearn: Joint decisions, mutual freedom and shared knowledge are normal; hiding finances, forbidding work or seizing pay is control.

scenarios.hook: "Being financially dependent on a partner is fine if you trust them."

myth.un: Financial dependence is fine if you trust them.
myth.re: Financial independence is your safety net and freedom, regardless of how much you trust someone.
myth.why: Trust can't replace your own safety net.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your financial independence as a safety net, regardless of trust.

scenarios.hook: Your partner says they'd 'prefer' it if you gave up your job.

steps.prompt: They raise it again over dinner, and you feel pulled. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want to keep working, and ask what worries them
options.then: They look surprised. "I just thought you'd be less tired." It isn't settled.

options.text: Tell yourself a good partner's wishes come first
options.then: You stay quiet. Your job starts to feel like a favour they allow.

options.text: Wonder if you're selfish for wanting to keep working
options.then: You spend the evening feeling guilty for a plain wish.

options.text: Ask your mother what to do, and follow her answer
options.then: She says to keep the peace. You feel unheard by both of them.

steps.why: Saying plainly that you want your job opens an honest talk on your own terms.

steps.prompt: They say it would only be for a year, then you can work again. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself a year at home is a small thing to give
options.then: You turn the year over in your mind. It doesn't feel as small as it sounded.

options.text: Say you'll keep your income, since plans can change
options.then: They go quiet. "You don't trust my plan?" You say it's about security.

options.text: Ask a colleague, who says to wait and see
options.then: She says plans like this sort themselves out. The subject comes back the week after.

options.text: Tell yourself a fight now would cost more than a year
options.then: The thought is persuasive. The subject comes back the week after anyway.

steps.why: A promise to return later can't replace an income you already have.

steps.prompt: Their family says you should stay home and leave money matters to them. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you've ruined things by being stubborn
options.then: You replay every word. The guilt grows, but the facts don't change.

options.text: Think that doing even more at home would settle it
options.then: You picture it working, then doubt it would ever feel like enough to them.

options.text: Keep your job, and tell someone you trust what's happening
options.then: A friend listens. "A partner wanting you dependent is a warning sign."

options.text: Wonder if saving a little first would make quitting safe
options.then: It sounds like a plan. You can't tell whether the pressure would stop at a new date.

steps.why: Your income is your safety net, and wanting to keep it was never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: A partner who wants you financially dependent is a warning sign, not a romantic one.
scenarios.relearn: Protect your own income and autonomy; pressure to depend is a warning.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your own bank account and income are quietly some of the most powerful things you can have. Feel it?
scenarios.affirm: Your own account and income are real power, and a real safety net.
scenarios.relearn: Your own bank account and income are real power and safety.

scenarios.relearn: Your own account, fund and knowledge protect independence; blank signatures, hidden debts and giving away access erode it.

scenarios.hook: Your partner asks you to take a loan in your name for them.

steps.prompt: They say it's only for a few months and they'll repay it. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself saying no would mean you don't love them
options.then: You feel a tight worry you can't name. The question hasn't gone away.

options.text: Say you won't take a loan in your name
options.then: They look hurt. "After everything?" You hold your ground, politely.

options.text: Ask a friend what they'd do and copy it
options.then: Your friend says she'd never. You still haven't said anything to them.

options.text: Think a texted promise to repay would make it safe
options.then: You picture the text arriving. A message doesn't change whose name is on the loan.

steps.why: A loan in your name is your debt, so a clear no protects you from the risk.

steps.prompt: A few days later, they bring papers and say only your signature is left. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself they've handled it, so it must be fine
options.then: Trusting the unread papers is tempting. A small worry stays.

options.text: Wonder if reading it would show you don't trust them
options.then: You feel rude for even thinking of it, and the papers stay on the table.

options.text: Don't sign, and ask who repays and why your name is on it
options.then: They sigh. "Why so careful?" You say the papers carry your name, and leave them unsigned.

options.text: Ask a relative, who says the paperwork is a formality
options.then: He says it's only a formality. You still haven't seen what the papers say.

steps.why: Not signing keeps the debt out of your name, and asking shows who is really meant to repay.

steps.prompt: They say that if you really loved them, you'd have signed already. What do you do?

options.text: Think offering your own savings would end the argument
options.then: You imagine it ending. You also imagine the asking starting again with a new amount.

options.text: Take their promise never to ask again as enough
options.then: It sounds like peace. But a promise can be broken, and you'd have nothing to hold.

options.text: Blame yourself and wonder if you're just too cautious
options.then: You feel guilty, but the loan is still their need, not yours.

options.text: Say love isn't a loan test, and tell someone you trust
options.then: Your friend says you can call 181 or 1091 for support.

steps.why: Love is never proved by taking on debt. It isn't your fault, and help exists.

scenarios.debrief: Debt in your name should never be about proving love; that's how coerced debt traps people.
scenarios.relearn: Don't take debt in your name under pressure; that's coerced debt.

scenarios.hook: You want to set a money-as-fairness tone with a new partner early.
scenarios.setup: You're at a small restaurant after a long walk.

steps.prompt: Your partner says: "Shall we split this bill, or should I just pay?"

options.text: "You pay it this time. It's easier that way, honestly."
options.then: "Sure. I don't mind."

options.text: "Let's split it. I like money open and fair between us."
options.then: "Split it, then. I like that you said so."

options.text: "Let's not talk about money on dates."
options.then: "Fair enough. I was only asking about the bill."

options.text: "I'll always pay every time, so you never have to worry."
options.then: "Every time? That's sweet. Are you sure?"

steps.why: Saying you like money open and fair sets the tone without making it heavy.

steps.prompt: A few dates later, your partner asks: "Do you usually tell people what you earn?"

options.text: "Never. It's private."
options.then: "All right. I didn't mean to pry."

options.text: "Sure. I'll tell you everything, right now, no problem."
options.then: "Oh. That's a lot, all at once."

options.text: "I share with people I trust, once we're both ready."
options.then: "Okay. I'd like that. No rush."

options.text: "Why? Are you after my money?"
options.then: "What? No. I was only curious."

steps.why: Sharing at a pace you both choose keeps money open without pressure.

steps.prompt: Your partner says: "Money can get awkward. Any rules for us?"

options.text: "No rules. We'll figure it out."
options.then: "Okay. Though I'd like a clearer idea."

options.text: "Whoever earns more should make the rules, simple."
options.then: "Hmm. I'm not sure that feels equal."

options.text: "Keep money apart and never discuss it."
options.then: "Never? That sounds lonely."

options.text: "Open and fair, never a way to control each other."
options.then: "I like that. Open and fair. Let's shake on it."

steps.why: A simple shared rule of openness and fairness keeps money from becoming control.

scenarios.relearn: Money should add fairness to love, never become a means of control.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: money isn't just money, it's choices, safety, and the power to walk away. Feel the weight of that?
scenarios.affirm: Money as choices, safety and the power to walk away is exactly why this matters.
scenarios.relearn: Money is choices, safety and the power to walk away.

scenarios.hook: "Money and finance are too complicated for someone like me."

myth.un: Finance is too complicated for someone like me.
myth.re: The basics, budgeting, saving, avoiding debt, are learnable by anyone; you don't need to be an expert.
myth.why: You only need the basics to take control.

scenarios.relearn: The money basics are learnable by anyone; you don't need to be an expert.

scenarios.hook: You don't have your own bank account yet.

steps.prompt: A friend says she opened hers in a single afternoon. What do you do?

options.text: Plan to open one in your own name this week
options.then: You list what you need: ID, address proof, a photo. It takes an afternoon.

options.text: Keep using a family member's account for now
options.then: Nothing changes. The account still has someone else's name on it.

options.text: Wait until you earn more to bother with one
options.then: The wait has no end date. Small amounts pass through other hands.

options.text: Open a joint account with a relative to start
options.then: It's quick to set up. Your name sits second, and they can see and move the money too.

steps.why: Your own account in your own name is the first step to financial independence.

steps.prompt: A relative offers to handle the paperwork and keep the passbook for you. What do you do?

options.text: Let them keep everything for you, since it's easier
options.then: They smile and file it away. You don't see the passbook again.

options.text: Thank them, and keep your own passbook, PIN and cards
options.then: They look a little put out. "I was only trying to help."

options.text: Put their phone number on it so they can help
options.then: They get every alert. You find out little about your own money.

options.text: Wait for them to do it whenever they have time
options.then: Weeks pass. No account appears, and nobody mentions it.

steps.why: Your own account only works for your independence if the access is yours.

steps.prompt: A month later, you have a small amount left over. What do you do with it?

options.text: Keep it in cash at home
options.then: It feels safe. It also gets spent on small things by the weekend.

options.text: Give it to a relative to keep safe for you
options.then: They take it kindly. You have no record of what they hold.

options.text: Put it in your own account, opening one first if needed
options.then: You open the account if you haven't yet, and note the amount. It's the start of a habit.

options.text: Spend it now and save later, when you earn more
options.then: It goes on small treats. The saving never begins.

steps.why: A small amount in your own account builds the habit and the independence.

scenarios.debrief: Your own bank account is the literal foundation of financial independence.
scenarios.relearn: Open your own bank account; it's the foundation of independence.

scenarios.hook: Your younger sister has never had an account of her own.
scenarios.setup: She's scrolling her phone on the sofa.

steps.prompt: Your sister says: "Money isn't my concern. Someone else will handle it."

options.text: "Yeah, leave it to the men."
options.then: She grins. "Exactly. That's what I thought."

options.text: "Your money is your freedom. Let's get you an account."
options.then: She looks up. "An account? I wouldn't know how."

options.text: "Fine. Just don't ask me for money later."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "I won't. Not that I'd know how."

options.text: "You'll learn when you actually need it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then I'll learn then."

steps.why: Money is freedom, and an account of her own is the first step.

steps.prompt: Later, your sister asks: "What would I even do with an account, if I had one?"

options.text: "Whatever you want. It doesn't matter."
options.then: "Then why bother?" She looks away.

options.text: "Maybe just hold your salary there for a while."
options.then: "Only for a while? Then what?"

options.text: "Keep your own money in it, even small amounts."
options.then: "Small amounts? I can do that."

options.text: "Keep it with Papa for now, and ask later."
options.then: "Papa will keep it. Then I never see it."

steps.why: Even a small amount in an account of her own is the start of independence.

steps.prompt: Your sister asks: "What if I get it wrong?"

options.text: "Then leave it to someone else, honestly."
options.then: She nods. She drops the subject, relieved and stuck.

options.text: "Don't worry. You'll never get it wrong."
options.then: She laughs. "That's not true. You know it isn't."

options.text: "Then ask the men at home to check."
options.then: She hesitates. "I'd rather do it myself."

options.text: "Start small and learn one thing at a time."
options.then: She smiles. "One thing at a time. I can manage that."

steps.why: Learning one small thing at a time makes money basics doable for anyone.

scenarios.relearn: Economic independence is a foundation of equality, especially for women.
Your own income, savings and account build independence; having no money of your own chips at it.
scenarios.hook: Sort: builds your independence, or chips at it?

items.text: Having no money of your own
An account in your own name
Letting someone else hold it all

scenarios.hook: You could rely on family money or build your own, and relying feels easier.

steps.prompt: Your uncle offers to keep sending money each month. What do you do?

options.text: Accept it, and stop worrying about earning
options.then: The money keeps arriving. Your plans fade into the background.

options.text: Accept it for now, and start building your own income
options.then: He's happy to help. Your own small plan starts to take shape.

options.text: Refuse it angrily, to prove you're independent
options.then: He's hurt. You're on your own, with no plan for it.

options.text: Wait for one big opportunity instead of small ones
options.then: You wait. Nothing big arrives, and the small ones pass by.

steps.why: Help can carry you while you start building something of your own.

steps.prompt: A weekend tutoring gig pays very little. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since the money is so small
options.then: You spend the weekend relaxing. Your own income stays at zero.

options.text: Hold out for something better paid
options.then: A month passes, and the better job doesn't show up.

options.text: Take it, and keep the money in your own account
options.then: The pay is small. It's the first money that's truly yours.

options.text: Take it, and spend it all on something you want
options.then: You enjoy it, and nothing is left of it by Monday.

steps.why: Small, steady earnings in your own account are where independence starts.

steps.prompt: Two months on, an unexpected cost lands in the middle of the month. What do you do?

options.text: Wait and hope it sorts itself out
options.then: The week is tense. You've nothing to fall back on.

options.text: Borrow from a friend with no plan to repay
options.then: Your friend says yes. The debt now hangs over you both.

options.text: Ask a relative to cover it, and change nothing
options.then: They help, once. The same gap is likely to come back.

options.text: Trim extras this month, and start a small cushion
options.then: It stretches. You see why even a small cushion of your own helps.

steps.why: Even a little of your own gives you room when something unexpected hits.

scenarios.debrief: Even slow progress toward your own income is worth more than indefinite reliance.
scenarios.relearn: Build your own income, even slowly; it's real independence.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Imran has big news about his freelancing and his partner Sana.
scenarios.setup: Over chai.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Sana earns well. I'll stop freelancing and we'll run on her pay."

options.text: "Keep some income of your own. It's a safety net."
options.then: He goes quiet. "I hadn't thought of it that way. I just wanted to be fair."

options.text: "If you trust her, it's completely fine. Go for it."
options.then: He grins. "Exactly. I knew you'd get it."

options.text: "Your life, your call. I won't say a word about it."
options.then: He nods, relieved. "Thanks. Everyone else keeps lecturing me."

options.text: "You'll be stuck with nothing if she ever changes."
options.then: He bristles. "Sana isn't like that. Why so negative?"

steps.why: Income of your own keeps your choices open, however strong the trust.

steps.prompt: A few days later Imran says: "I keep going back and forth. How should Sana and I set up the money side?"

options.text: "Put everything in a joint account. That's fair."
options.then: "That sounds fair. We'd both see everything." Nothing in it is only his.

options.text: "A few clients a month, paid into your own account."
options.then: "Small, but mine. I can live with that." He seems lighter.

options.text: "Keep a secret stash and don't tell her."
options.then: He frowns. "A secret from Sana? That would feel worse than asking her."

options.text: "Quit fully. Start again if things go wrong."
options.then: "Start again from zero, with no clients? That sounds like a lot."

steps.why: A little income in his own account keeps independence without hurting trust.

steps.prompt: A week later Imran says: "Sana says the freelancing is my call. Maybe I'm overthinking this."

options.text: "Maybe. She sounds supportive, so relax."
options.then: "Maybe." He shrugs. The easy way is still tempting.

options.text: "Then ask her to promise to support you forever."
options.then: "Promise? That feels odd. Can't we just trust each other?"

options.text: "Forget I said anything. It's between you two."
options.then: "Thanks, I think." He's still unsure what he'll do.

options.text: "Not overthinking. It's about choice, not distrust."
options.then: He smiles. "Right. I'll keep two clients and tell her why."

steps.why: Wanting independence is about choice and safety, never about distrust.

scenarios.relearn: Encourage a friend to keep their own income as a safety net.

scenarios.hook: You want to help a younger sibling value financial independence early.

steps.prompt: Your younger brother Aman receives festival money. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him money isn't his concern until he's older
options.then: He shrugs, and spends it all by the evening.

options.text: Take it to keep safe for him
options.then: He hands it over. He never sees it again, and forgets it.

options.text: Suggest he splits it: some to spend, some to save
options.then: He grins. "A bit for me, a bit for later. Okay."

options.text: Tell him to save every rupee and never spend
options.then: He looks crushed. He hides the money, and stops asking you.

steps.why: Letting him split his money teaches both the habit of saving and the joy of spending.

steps.prompt: Aman asks why you keep your own account. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's grown-up stuff he'll learn later
options.then: He loses interest. The question stays with him.

options.text: Say it's because you don't trust people
options.then: He looks worried. He starts to think money is a scary thing.

options.text: Show him your whole budget so he can copy it
options.then: He glances at it and says it looks boring.

options.text: Explain it's yours, and help him open one
options.then: He's curious. "Can I have one too?"

steps.why: An honest, simple answer makes owning money feel normal and safe to him.

steps.prompt: Aman wants to borrow for a game and pay later. What do you do?

options.text: Show him how saving beats borrowing, together
options.then: He smiles. "Three weeks. I can do that."

options.text: Lend it without asking when he'll repay
options.then: He thanks you. The money doesn't come back.

options.text: Tell him borrowing is wrong and leave it there
options.then: He sulks. He finds another way to get the game.

options.text: Buy it for him so he stops asking
options.then: He's delighted. He learns he doesn't need to plan.

steps.why: Planning and saving teach independence better than borrowing or being handed things.

scenarios.hook: A friend is drowning in debt and feels too ashamed to ask for help.

steps.prompt: She finally tells you about it, in tears. What do you do?

options.text: Say she should have been a lot more careful
options.then: She looks down and says little. Days later she texts you anyway.

options.text: Quietly lend her some money and say nothing
options.then: She's relieved for a month. The debt and the shame are both still there.

options.text: Promise to keep it a secret from everyone
options.then: She trusts you fully. The secret keeps her away from real help.

options.text: Listen, say she's not alone, offer real help
options.then: She cries harder, then breathes out. "I thought you'd think less of me."

steps.why: Kindness and real help, without shame, get her moving.

steps.prompt: A few days later she says she can't even look at the numbers. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to just ignore the numbers for now
options.then: It feels better for a day. The numbers keep growing.

options.text: Offer to sit with her as she lists each loan
options.then: It takes an hour. The total is a number now, not a monster.

options.text: List everything yourself and set the plan
options.then: It's fast. She feels more lost, because she wasn't part of it.

options.text: Tell her it's really not that bad
options.then: She feels unheard, and doesn't tell you the rest.

steps.why: Facing the numbers together makes them smaller.

steps.prompt: You wonder who can give proper help. What do you suggest?

options.text: A friend who 'knows about money'
options.then: He means well. His advice fits his own life, not hers.

options.text: A social media 'debt fix' account
options.then: It promises to wipe her loans for a fee.

options.text: A bank, or a qualified, trusted source
options.then: She books a call. A plain plan is on paper within a week.

options.text: Waiting until her salary rises
options.then: The salary rises a little. The interest grows faster.

steps.why: A qualified, trusted source can give a plan that fits her case.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, she asks how to avoid ending up here again. What do you say?

options.text: Never borrow again, not even in emergencies
options.then: It sounds firm. A true emergency would leave her stuck.

options.text: Build a small fund and track your spending
options.then: She notes one small amount to set aside each payday. It's a start.

options.text: Just earn more. That solves everything
options.then: Her earnings rise. So do her spends, and the pattern stays.

options.text: Avoid talking about money with anyone
options.then: Silence is how it grew. The next slip would hide too.

steps.why: A small cushion and tracking make a slip easier to survive.

scenarios.debrief: Debt shame keeps people stuck; a non-judgmental nudge toward help is what frees them.
scenarios.relearn: Reassure a friend in debt and point to real help, without shame.
