myth.un: A budget only works if you never spend on yourself.
myth.re: A good budget plans some fun money in on purpose, so the plan is one you'll actually keep.
myth.why: A budget with zero joy is the one people quit by week two.

scenarios.relearn: Plan a little fun money in on purpose; that's the budget you'll keep.

scenarios.hook: "Tracking spending is for people who are bad with money."

myth.un: Tracking spending is for people who are bad with money.
myth.re: Tracking is how anyone sees where money actually goes; it's the first step to controlling it.
myth.why: You can't direct money you've never looked at.

scenarios.relearn: Tracking spending is the first step to control, not a sign you're bad with money.

scenarios.hook: "Budgeting is pointless when prices keep rising."

myth.un: Budgeting is pointless when prices keep rising.
myth.re: When costs climb, a budget matters more: it shows what to protect and what to trim.
myth.why: A plan is how you make a tighter month still cover the essentials.

scenarios.relearn: When prices rise, a budget matters more, it shows what to protect and what to trim.

scenarios.hook: "If there's money in my account, I can afford it."

myth.un: If there's money in my account, I can afford it.
myth.re: Money sitting there is often already promised to rent, bills or savings; a budget shows what's truly free.
myth.why: The balance isn't the same as spare money.

scenarios.relearn: Your balance isn't spare money; a budget shows what's truly free to spend.

scenarios.hook: "Saving is whatever's left at the end of the month."

myth.un: Saving is whatever's left at the end of the month.
myth.re: There's usually nothing left, so saving works best as a fixed line you set aside first.
myth.why: Pay yourself first, then live on the rest.

scenarios.relearn: Treat savings as a fixed line you set aside first, not the leftover.

scenarios.hook: "A budget is just one spending limit to remember."

myth.un: A budget is just one spending limit to remember.
myth.re: A budget splits money into jobs: needs, wants and savings, so each rupee has a place.
myth.why: Giving money a job is what stops it quietly vanishing.

scenarios.relearn: A budget gives each rupee a job across needs, wants and savings.

scenarios.hook: "My income's too small to bother budgeting."

myth.un: My income's too small to bother budgeting.
myth.re: A small income is exactly when a plan helps most; it stretches every rupee further.
myth.why: The tighter the money, the more a plan matters.

scenarios.relearn: A small income is when a budget helps most; it stretches every rupee further.

scenarios.hook: Sort: spotted by tracking spending, or a fix that follows?

items.text: Setting a weekly cap on eating out

scenarios.relearn: Tracking shows the leaks; the fixes (caps, cancelling, saving first) are what you do about them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: belongs in the savings line, or the wants line?

items.text: Money toward a course you want
A new pair of branded shoes
A fancier phone than you need

scenarios.relearn: An emergency fund, a course and a cushion are savings; trips and upgrades are wants.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real budgeting move, or a budgeting myth?
scenarios.relearn: Giving rupees jobs, saving first and reviewing are real; 'later', 'no fun' and 'balance = spare' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Sort: which costs are easy to trim, and which are hard?

items.text: Daily cab when a bus works

scenarios.relearn: Cabs, food apps and impulse carts trim easily; rent, groceries and getting to college are harder needs.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps your plan survive payday, or wrecks it?

items.text: Moving savings the day you're paid
Listing this month's fixed bills first
Lending big sums you can't spare
Keeping a small buffer for surprises
Spending the whole stipend week one

scenarios.relearn: Saving on payday, listing bills and a buffer help; free-for-alls, over-lending and blowing it week one wreck the plan.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a fact about the 50/30/20 guide, or a misread of it?

items.text: You can tweak it to your life
You must hit it to the rupee
Savings is its own fixed slice

scenarios.relearn: The 50/30/20 split is a rough, tweakable guide with savings as a fixed slice, not a strict rule or a leftover.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a sign your budget is working, or a warning sign?

items.text: Savings grows a little each month
You dread opening your bank app
You know roughly where money goes
You borrow before the next stipend
You've no idea what you spent

scenarios.relearn: Growing savings, knowing where money goes and calm surprises mean it's working; dread, borrowing and blanks are warnings.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a step in setting up a first budget, or not part of it?

items.text: Guess and hope it works out

scenarios.relearn: Note income, list needs, save first and leave room for wants; don't just guess or wait to earn more.

scenarios.hook: Match the budgeting term to what it means.
scenarios.relearn: Needs, wants, fixed, flexible and pay-yourself-first each have a clear meaning.

scenarios.hook: Match the money problem to the budgeting fix.

pairs.right: Save a slice on payday first
Set aside a little each month

scenarios.relearn: Each common money problem has a simple budgeting fix.

scenarios.hook: Match each item to the budget label that fits it.
scenarios.relearn: Rent and transport are needs, movies and top-ups are wants, an emergency fund is savings.

scenarios.hook: Match the budgeting phrase to what it really means.

pairs.right: Assign all your income on purpose
Saving toward a known future cost

scenarios.relearn: Budgeting phrases like buffer, sinking fund and lifestyle creep each name a real habit.

scenarios.hook: Match the budget review question to why it helps.

pairs.right: Links spending to what you want

scenarios.relearn: A monthly review of a few questions keeps a budget honest and useful.

scenarios.hook: Your stipend lands and three apps are showing tempting sales.

steps.prompt: A flash sale ends tonight on something you like. What do you do?

options.text: Grab the deals now and sort the bills later
options.then: The parcel is on its way. Rent and bills are still waiting.

options.text: Buy one thing now and skip savings this month
options.then: It's just one thing. The savings line stays empty for the month.

options.text: Pay needs and savings first, then see what's left
options.then: After needs and savings, a small amount remains. It covers a smaller item.

options.text: Ask a friend if the deal is really worth it
options.then: She says everyone is buying. It's hard to tell what you can spare.

steps.why: Needs and savings first leaves real room for treats.

steps.prompt: A week later, another sale alert arrives. What do you do?

options.text: Pick one item and fix an amount for it
options.then: You set a fun limit. The alert no longer feels urgent.

options.text: Delete every shopping app for good
options.then: The alerts stop. A month later you overspend in a shop instead.

options.text: Buy on the EMI offer since the price is split
options.then: It looks small each month. The payments pile up behind it.

options.text: Use the bill money and refill it later
options.then: The refill slips. Then a bill is due and the gap shows.

steps.why: A fixed fun amount lets you enjoy sales without panic.

steps.prompt: A friend's birthday is next week and you have only a little fun money left. What do you do?

options.text: Take it from your savings line for one gift
options.then: It's one gift. The savings habit now has a gap.

options.text: Skip her birthday completely to save money
options.then: She notices you weren't there. It stings both ways.

options.text: Buy an expensive gift on EMI
options.then: The gift is a hit. The payments arrive monthly for a while.

options.text: Pick a small gift or plan something together
options.then: She loves the thought. Your plan stays whole.

steps.why: A small, thoughtful gift keeps both the friendship and the plan.

scenarios.debrief: Treats are fine, after needs and savings are set aside, not before.
scenarios.relearn: Cover needs and savings first, then treat yourself from what's left.

scenarios.hook: You realise you have no idea what you spent last month.

steps.prompt: Your balance looks low again. What do you do?

options.text: Decide it's too late to bother
options.then: You close the app. The same question returns next month.

options.text: Guess a total and move on
options.then: You note a number. Whether it's close, you can't tell.

options.text: Ask a friend to compare her spending with yours
options.then: Her total is very different. It doesn't show where yours went.

options.text: Scroll your bank and UPI history and add it up
options.then: The real picture appears line by line, with a few surprises.

steps.why: A quick look at your own history shows the truth.

steps.prompt: When you finally go through your history line by line, a few payments look unfamiliar. What do you do?

options.text: Skip the ones you can't place
options.then: Those stay a mystery, and the total stays fuzzy.

options.text: Check each one against your chats and bills
options.then: Most turn out to be shared meals and a forgotten subscription.

options.text: Call them all mistakes and ignore them
options.then: The money is still gone, and you learn nothing from it.

options.text: Lump them under 'miscellaneous' and stop
options.then: The total looks tidy, but miscellaneous is now your biggest line.

steps.why: Checking against your chats and bills fills in the gaps.

steps.prompt: A new month starts. How will you keep track this time?

options.text: Note your spends each week so surprises show early
options.then: Five minutes each Sunday keeps the picture fresh.

options.text: Track every rupee perfectly or not at all
options.then: By day nine you miss a day and quietly stop.

options.text: Do another big look back at month-end
options.then: It shows the truth again, only a month late.

options.text: Trust your memory now that you've seen it
options.then: By week three the details blur again.

steps.why: A short weekly check catches leaks while they are small.

scenarios.debrief: A quick look back at your own transactions is the fastest way to see the truth.
scenarios.relearn: Scroll your own UPI and bank history to see where money really went.

scenarios.hook: A friend invites you to a pricey dinner that would break your week's budget.

steps.prompt: She asks if you're coming on Friday. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest a cheaper place, or come just for chai
options.then: She laughs and picks a dhaba. You still get your evening together.

options.text: Say yes and quietly skip groceries to cover it
options.then: The dinner is lovely. Your fridge is nearly empty by Sunday.

options.text: Say you're busy and skip it
options.then: She's disappointed. You save money and feel a bit left out.

options.text: Say yes and put it on a card for later
options.then: The swipe is easy. The bill shows up at month-end.

steps.why: Offering a cheaper plan keeps the friendship and the budget.

steps.prompt: A week later, the group plans another meal and says they'll split the bill evenly. What do you do?

options.text: Go along with equal splitting so nobody fusses
options.then: You pay for dishes you didn't order. Nobody notices.

options.text: Order what the others do to fit in
options.then: The table looks fun. Your share ends up well above your plan.

options.text: Say you'll order light and pay for your own share
options.then: Someone agrees. "Same, honestly." The bill splits by what each person ate.

options.text: Ask a friend to cover you for now
options.then: She pays. You owe her, and no one has said when.

steps.why: Paying for what you ordered is fair and protects your plan.

steps.prompt: A friend says she has stopped joining plans because the costs pile up. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her she should just save more
options.then: She nods but looks away. She doesn't plan to join the next one.

options.text: Say you've felt it too and suggest cheaper plans
options.then: She smiles. "Really? I thought it was only me."

options.text: Offer to pay for her every time
options.then: She's touched, and a little uneasy about relying on it.

options.text: Say it's not a big deal and everyone copes
options.then: She stops talking about it. The next plan goes ahead without her.

steps.why: Naming your own limits makes it easier for others to name theirs.

scenarios.debrief: You can protect both a friendship and a budget by naming what you can do.
scenarios.relearn: You can stay social and keep your budget by suggesting a cheaper option.

scenarios.hook: Your stipend just went up a bit.

steps.prompt: The new amount shows in your account. What do you do?

options.text: Upgrade your lifestyle to match the new amount
options.then: Everything feels nicer. By month-end you have no extra left.

options.text: Raise your savings line and keep spending steady
options.then: You move part of the raise to savings on payday. The cushion grows.

options.text: Spend it all this month and save from next month
options.then: The treat month is fun. Next month looks like the old one.

options.text: Wait and see if it lasts before deciding
options.then: You leave it in the account. It slowly goes in small spends.

steps.why: Moving part of the raise to savings on day one stops it melting into small spends.

steps.prompt: A friend hears about it and says you must celebrate big. What do you do?

options.text: Throw a big party since you earned it
options.then: It's memorable. The party eats most of the raise.

options.text: Refuse any celebration to protect your savings
options.then: Friends are surprised. You feel dutiful but a bit flat.

options.text: Put the party on a credit card
options.then: The night is great. The bill arrives and the raise is spoken for.

options.text: Plan a modest celebration from your fun line
options.then: You do a nice dinner. The plan covers it with no stress.

steps.why: Celebrating from your fun line keeps both the joy and the plan.

steps.prompt: Three months on, the raise feels like normal income. What do you do?

options.text: Let it settle and stop thinking about it
options.then: The money goes where it always goes. The cushion stays the same.

options.text: Move to a pricier flat to match your new level
options.then: The flat is nicer. The rent now takes a bigger bite each month.

options.text: Check your savings line and raise it if you can
options.then: You move a little more on payday. The pot starts growing month by month.

options.text: Lend to friends freely since you earn more now
options.then: You help a few people. You have less for yourself, and some is not repaid.

steps.why: Reviewing your savings line lets a raise keep working for you.

scenarios.debrief: A raise is a chance to save more, not just spend more.
scenarios.relearn: When income rises, raise your savings line before your spending.

scenarios.hook: You overspent this week and feel like giving up on the budget.

steps.prompt: It's Sunday night and the numbers look bad. What do you do?

options.text: Scrap the whole budget in frustration
options.then: You close the sheet. The coming week has no plan at all.

options.text: Stop looking at the numbers for a while
options.then: Out of sight, out of mind. The balance keeps dropping unseen.

options.text: Adjust next week's amounts and carry on
options.then: You trim a few lines. The month is still within reach.

options.text: Spend nothing at all next week as a punishment
options.then: You last three days. Then one small spend feels like a huge failure.

steps.why: A budget bends around a bad week, so adjusting keeps you in control.

steps.prompt: A week later, you are about to overspend again. What do you do?

options.text: Pause and check what's left for the week
options.then: You see a little room. You spend a bit and skip the rest.

options.text: Spend now and fix it from next month's stipend
options.then: It feels fine until the stipend is already half spoken for.

options.text: Tell yourself you're bad with money and stop checking
options.then: The label sticks. Checking feels pointless from then on.

options.text: Ask a friend to hold your card for the week
options.then: She agrees awkwardly. You still don't know your own limits.

steps.why: A quick check before spending keeps one slip from becoming many.

steps.prompt: The month ends and you ran over in two lines. What do you do?

options.text: Decide budgets don't work for you
options.then: The budget is dropped. Spending goes back to guesswork.

options.text: Promise to be perfect next month
options.then: The promise feels good. Nothing in the plan has changed.

options.text: Blame the busy week and leave it as is
options.then: It was a busy week. The same thing is likely to happen again.

options.text: Note what caused it and change those lines
options.then: Two lines get new limits. The next month runs closer to plan.

steps.why: Learning from the overspend lets you fix the lines that caused it.

scenarios.debrief: A budget can bend around a bad week. It doesn't have to break.
scenarios.relearn: One overspend isn't failure; adjust and keep going.

scenarios.hook: You're setting up your very first monthly budget.

steps.prompt: You open a blank sheet. Where do you start?

options.text: Cap your fun spending first and guess the rest
options.then: Fun is neat. Rent and travel are left floating.

options.text: List everything you want to buy this month
options.then: The list is long. It's unclear how any of it gets paid.

options.text: Copy a friend's sheet exactly
options.then: Her rent and pay are different. Some of her lines don't apply to you.

options.text: Write what comes in, then your needs
options.then: The top line shows your stipend. Rent and food come next.

steps.why: Starting from what comes in and what you must pay keeps the plan real.

steps.prompt: A few days later, you return to the sheet. How do you finish it?

options.text: Fill wants first, since they are easiest
options.then: Wants fill up nicely. The savings line shows zero.

options.text: Fill income, needs and savings, then wants
options.then: Every rupee gets a place. Wants get a clear share.

options.text: Leave the rest blank and see how the month goes
options.then: The month goes on, and the blank space goes quickly.

options.text: Put a big round number for savings
options.then: The number looks impressive. There isn't enough left to reach it.

steps.why: Needs and savings before wants gives every rupee a place.

steps.prompt: Halfway through the month, a forgotten bill arrives. What do you do?

options.text: Add it to needs and trim a want line to cover it
options.then: The sheet shifts a little. The month still balances.

options.text: Pull it from savings and forget to put it back
options.then: The bill is paid. Savings is now short with no plan to refill.

options.text: Pay it from whatever is there and skip the sheet
options.then: You pay it. The sheet no longer matches your account.

options.text: Delay it and hope for a late fee waiver
options.then: A reminder arrives with a late fee. The amount is now higher.

steps.why: Adjusting one line keeps the sheet true when a surprise arrives.

scenarios.debrief: Build a budget in order: what comes in, what you must pay, what you save, then the rest.
scenarios.relearn: Build a budget in order: income, needs, savings, then wants.

scenarios.hook: Three small subscriptions auto-renew and you barely use two of them.

steps.prompt: The renewal alerts arrive today. What do you do?

options.text: Cancel the two you barely use
options.then: It takes five minutes. Next month a little more stays with you.

options.text: Leave them since it's only a little each
options.then: Each charge is small. Together they appear on the statement again.

options.text: Plan to cancel them next month
options.then: Next month comes and the same alerts arrive again.

options.text: Keep all three and try to use them more
options.then: You watch more for a week. Interest drops as before.

steps.why: Cutting unused subscriptions frees money every month with no effort.

steps.prompt: A month later, a free trial offer asks for your card details. What do you do?

options.text: Sign up and trust yourself to remember
options.then: You forget. A charge appears and you notice three weeks later.

options.text: Take the yearly plan for the discount
options.then: The monthly price looks lower. You paid a large sum upfront for something you may not use.

options.text: Set a cancel reminder before you sign up
options.then: You set it the moment you join. The trial ends with no charge.

options.text: Use a friend's card instead
options.then: She lets you. You both forget, and she is charged later.

steps.why: A cancel reminder stops a free trial from turning into a charge.

steps.prompt: You decide to check all your recurring charges. Where do you look?

options.text: Check only your email receipts
options.then: You find some. Autopay charges don't show up there.

options.text: Go through your bank and UPI autopay list
options.then: You find two forgotten ones and an old gym plan.

options.text: Think about it and list them from memory
options.then: You list four. The statement shows seven.

options.text: Wait for the charges to show up by themselves
options.then: They show up when the money has already gone.

steps.why: Your bank and autopay list shows every recurring charge, even forgotten ones.

scenarios.debrief: Small recurring charges are easy to ignore and easy to cut, and cutting them wins.
scenarios.relearn: Cancel subscriptions you don't use; small recurring charges add up.

scenarios.hook: You want a big purchase in four months but can't afford it now.

steps.prompt: The shop offers an easy EMI today. What do you do?

options.text: Buy now on the easy EMI
options.then: It's yours today. The payments run for months after the thrill fades.

options.text: Save a set amount each month and buy in four
options.then: The plan fits on one line in your budget. You move money on payday.

options.text: Buy a cheaper version now on EMI
options.then: It costs less, but it is still borrowed money. The payments are just smaller.

options.text: Wait and see if the price drops
options.then: You watch the price each week. You haven't saved anything meanwhile.

steps.why: Saving up for a want avoids debt and its hidden extra cost.

steps.prompt: Two months on, a surprise expense leaves the month tight. What do you do?

options.text: Take a small app loan to cover the month
options.then: It's quick. Interest now adds to what you owe.

options.text: Skip this month's money for the purchase
options.then: Next month the gap is bigger, and catching up feels harder than it sounded.

options.text: Put this month's extras on buy now, pay later
options.then: The month feels fine. Next month starts with a new bill.

options.text: Trim wants this month and keep to your money plan
options.then: It's tight, but the plan holds.

steps.why: Trimming wants for a month keeps you on track without new debt.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend asks if she should buy a laptop upgrade she wants on an easy EMI. What do you say?

options.text: Say EMIs are basically free if the monthly amount is small
options.then: She signs up that week. The interest never comes up.

options.text: Tell her she'd be foolish to even consider it
options.then: She stiffens. The chat ends on a cold note.

options.text: Say an EMI is debt, and saving first avoids the interest
options.then: She pauses. "Okay. I never counted the interest."

options.text: Say it depends and change the subject
options.then: She shrugs, still unsure what to do.

steps.why: An EMI is debt with extra cost, and saying so plainly helps a friend choose.

scenarios.debrief: Saving up for a want beats borrowing for it, because debt for wants is a trap.
scenarios.relearn: Save up for a want over months instead of putting it on EMI.

scenarios.hook: Rent is due next week but your money is already half spent.

steps.prompt: You look at your balance and the rent date. What do you do?

options.text: Hope something comes through before the date
options.then: You keep checking your phone. Nothing arrives.

options.text: Ask the landlord for more time, with no date in mind
options.then: He says maybe. He doesn't know when you'll pay and neither do you.

options.text: Set the rent aside today and pause other spending
options.then: The rent amount sits apart from your daily money. Other spends wait.

options.text: Borrow from a friend and sort it out later
options.then: A friend sends the amount. You haven't said when you'll return it.

steps.why: Setting rent aside first keeps your home secure.

steps.prompt: Next payday arrives. What do you do the moment the money lands?

options.text: Move the rent amount aside before anything else
options.then: Rent sits in its own place for the month. You feel calmer.

options.text: Pay bills and treats first, then see what's left
options.then: By the third week, the rent amount is hard to find.

options.text: Wait until mid-month to decide about rent
options.then: The days pass and other spends eat into it.

options.text: Set aside half the rent now and half later
options.then: Half is safe. The second half keeps getting borrowed from.

steps.why: Rent is your most important fixed bill, so it moves first.

steps.prompt: A friend asks to borrow a large sum right after payday. What do you do?

options.text: Lend the full amount and trust it works out
options.then: She thanks you warmly. The rent money is now in doubt.

options.text: Refuse and lecture her about planning
options.then: She leaves upset and doesn't ask again, or reach out.

options.text: Say you'll decide later
options.then: Days pass with no answer. You're stuck with the question.

options.text: Keep the rent safe and offer a smaller amount
options.then: She says that's fair. "Even a little helps."

steps.why: Rent stays safe first, and you can still help within your means.

steps.prompt: You want rent to feel easier each month. What do you do?

options.text: Promise yourself you'll remember
options.then: You remember two months out of three.

options.text: Set a payday reminder to move rent first
options.then: The reminder pings on payday. Rent moves before anything else.

options.text: Keep rent in the main balance and watch it
options.then: It's mixed with everything else, and it gets spent.

options.text: Pay rent a week late each month for a buffer
options.then: The buffer feels useful. Late fees and tense talks begin.

steps.why: A routine on payday protects rent without relying on memory.

scenarios.debrief: Protect your most important fixed bill by setting it aside first.
scenarios.relearn: Ring-fence your rent the moment you're paid, before other spending.

scenarios.hook: You keep running out of money in the last week of the month.

steps.prompt: Another month ends with you broke. What do you do?

options.text: Try harder to spend less somehow
options.then: You feel determined. Without numbers, it fades by week two.

options.text: Borrow to cover the last week
options.then: It gets you through. Next month starts with less.

options.text: Ask a friend how she makes her month last
options.then: She says she just doesn't spend much. It doesn't help you plan.

options.text: Split the monthly budget into weekly amounts
options.then: Four weekly amounts appear, each with its own limit.

steps.why: Weekly amounts make each week's limit visible, so week four survives.

steps.prompt: Midweek, a friend wants to get food after class. What do you do?

options.text: Spend it and borrow from next week
options.then: Next week starts lighter. Borrowing forward is easy to repeat.

options.text: Check what's left for this week first
options.then: There's enough for a small meal. You go and stay within it.

options.text: Dip into the money set for travel
options.then: The travel money is gone. You walk more than you'd like.

options.text: Put it on UPI credit and pay later
options.then: It works for now. The bill lands early next month.

steps.why: Checking what's left for the week keeps spending inside it.

steps.prompt: You reach the end of week three with some money still left. What do you do?

options.text: Carry it into week four or save some
options.then: Week four feels easier for once.

options.text: Spend it because it's there
options.then: It goes on small things. Week four has less to work with.

options.text: Lend it to a friend who asks
options.then: She's grateful. She hasn't said when she'll return it.

options.text: Forget about it until the month ends
options.then: The leftover gets absorbed by small spends you didn't notice.

steps.why: A leftover carried forward gives the tight weeks some room.

scenarios.debrief: Breaking a month into weeks makes a budget far easier to actually follow.
scenarios.relearn: Split your budget into weekly amounts so the last week isn't empty.

scenarios.hook: Your family expects a chunk of your stipend, and you also want to save.

steps.prompt: Your family asks how much you can send home this month. What do you do?

options.text: Send whatever they ask and save nothing
options.then: They are pleased. Your own account stays empty.

options.text: Send a random amount without saying anything
options.then: It's not what they expected. The silence makes it awkward.

options.text: Say you can't send anything at all
options.then: They are hurt and confused. The talk ends badly.

options.text: Offer a set amount and say you're saving some too
options.then: They nod. "That's sensible. Start with that."

steps.why: Two set lines let you support home and build your own savings.

steps.prompt: At a family function, a relative says young people who save for themselves are selfish. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and plan to send everything home from now on
options.then: She's satisfied. Nothing of your own is left for later.

options.text: Say you'll help within your means, and saving keeps you secure
options.then: She listens. "I hadn't thought of it that way."

options.text: Argue that she has no right to judge you
options.then: She bristles. By evening the family hears about your attitude.

options.text: Smile and change the subject
options.then: The remark hangs in the air and returns at the next gathering.

steps.why: Saving is a way to stay secure, not selfish, and you can say so calmly.

steps.prompt: An emergency hits at home and they need more this month. What do you do?

options.text: Send what you can spare and talk about next month
options.then: The help reaches them. You tell them what you can manage next.

options.text: Send all your savings without asking any questions
options.then: They are relieved. You have no cushion if something happens to you.

options.text: Refuse, since you already have a plan
options.then: They feel shut out. It's a hard week at home.

options.text: Take a loan from an app to cover it
options.then: The money arrives. The loan adds a new bill to your own month.

steps.why: Helping within your means supports family and keeps you secure.

scenarios.debrief: Supporting family and saving for yourself can both be planned lines, not either/or.
scenarios.relearn: You can plan both family support and your own savings as set lines.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kavya is short of money this month and wants to borrow from you.

steps.prompt: Your pay lands, and within minutes she messages about shopping and the loan. What do you do?

options.text: Move savings first, then see what's truly spare
options.then: After savings and bills, a small spare amount remains.

options.text: Say yes to everything and check the balance later
options.then: You lend and shop. By evening the balance is a surprise.

options.text: Lend the money now and skip the shopping
options.then: She's happy. You haven't checked whether you can spare it.

options.text: Ignore her messages until tomorrow
options.then: She sends three more. The pressure only builds.

steps.why: Deciding what is spare first keeps your own needs safe.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Kavya says her rent is short and asks for more than you can spare. What do you do?

options.text: Lend the full amount and cover it from savings
options.then: She's thrilled. Your savings line now has a hole.

options.text: Lend it all, as long as she repays next week
options.then: She promises. Your own week is now tight, and it rests on her word.

options.text: Offer a smaller amount you can afford to lend
options.then: She says thanks. The smaller amount doesn't disturb your plan.

options.text: Take a small loan so you can help her fully
options.then: You help. A new payment joins your list.

steps.why: Lending only what you can afford keeps the friendship and your plan.

steps.prompt: A week later, she hasn't mentioned repaying. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing to keep the friendship easy
options.then: The weeks pass. The money is a small knot between you.

options.text: Ask calmly when she can pay it back
options.then: She says she'd forgotten. "Sorry. Friday?"

options.text: Hint in a joke and hope she picks it up
options.then: She laughs along. She says nothing about the money.

options.text: Ask mutual friends to remind her
options.then: It gets back to her by evening. She feels embarrassed and cold.

steps.why: Asking calmly is fair, and it stops small loans from souring.

scenarios.debrief: Decide what's spare before you commit it, not after.
scenarios.relearn: Move savings first, then commit only what's genuinely spare.

scenarios.hook: A new budget app promises to "auto-manage" your money for you.

steps.prompt: The app asks for your netbanking ID and password. What do you do?

options.text: Enter the login so it's automatic
options.then: The app connects. You can't tell who can see your bank details now.

options.text: Skip it and track in a simple note or sheet
options.then: You open a note and list the month's spends. It's simple and private.

options.text: Read the app's reviews and then decide
options.then: The reviews are mixed. You still aren't sure it's safe to share a login.

options.text: Ask a friend to try it first
options.then: He says it works fine. He may not have noticed a problem yet.

steps.why: You never need to share a bank login to budget, because a list works.

steps.prompt: A friend says her budgeting app has been fine and you should link your bank to it too. What do you do?

options.text: Link your bank to her app for a week
options.then: You sign in. The app now holds your bank details for good.

options.text: Tell her off for being careless
options.then: She gets defensive and stops talking to you about money.

options.text: Ask her how much the app has saved her
options.then: She says it's hard to say. It doesn't answer whether your login is safe.

options.text: Say you won't share your bank login with her app
options.then: She shrugs. "Suit yourself." No new app gets your login.

steps.why: You can decline kindly, and keep your login away from more apps.

steps.prompt: A text claiming to be from a budget app says your account is locked. It has a link and asks for an OTP. What do you do?

options.text: Send the OTP to unlock it fast
options.then: The account wasn't locked. Money leaves your bank within minutes.

options.text: Reply asking who they are
options.then: They reply fast, pushing you to act. The chat is now open to them.

options.text: Don't share the OTP and report the message
options.then: You keep the message, report it, then block the number. Nothing leaves your phone.

options.text: Click the link to check
options.then: The page looks real. It asks for your card details next.

steps.why: No real bank or app texts you asking for an OTP. It's never your fault: report it on 1930.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, you still want an easier way to track. What do you do?

options.text: Try a sheet you fill in weekly
options.then: It takes five minutes each Sunday. You control every bit of it.

options.text: Try another app that asks for your bank login
options.then: It has a different logo. It asks for the same login.

options.text: Use a free app that asks for your card number
options.then: It says the card is to 'verify' you. Card details are as risky as a login.

options.text: Give up on tracking since it's too much work
options.then: You go back to guessing, and the month blurs again.

steps.why: A simple sheet updated weekly does the job without the risk.

scenarios.debrief: You never need to share a bank login to budget. A basic list does the job.
scenarios.relearn: Budget with a simple note or sheet; never hand over a bank login.

scenarios.hook: You get paid weekly, not monthly, and the usual budget tips feel off.

steps.prompt: A guide says to plan your whole month in one go. What do you do?

options.text: Force it into a monthly plan and hope
options.then: It looks neat. The big bills fall in the wrong weeks.

options.text: Skip budgeting until you're paid monthly
options.then: You keep spending week to week with no plan in sight.

options.text: Build the budget around each pay cycle
options.then: Each week gets its own bills, savings and spending amounts.

options.text: Average your pay into a monthly number
options.then: It feels smooth. In a weak week there is nothing to average.

steps.why: A budget shaped around how you're paid is one you can follow.

steps.prompt: Rent is due monthly, but your pay comes weekly. What do you do?

options.text: Set aside a slice of each week's pay for rent
options.then: Each week a slice moves. When rent day comes, it's ready.

options.text: Pay rent from whichever week feels easiest
options.then: That week is very tight. Everything else waits.

options.text: Cover it from the last week's pay only
options.then: The last week is heavy. The other weeks feel like free money.

options.text: Borrow for rent and repay it weekly
options.then: It fits the pay rhythm. The debt sits underneath the month.

steps.why: Setting aside a slice each week gets a monthly bill ready.

steps.prompt: One week's pay comes in smaller than usual. What do you do?

options.text: Skip savings that week to cover everything
options.then: It balances for the week. The savings habit loses a beat.

options.text: Borrow against next week's pay
options.then: It covers this week. Next week starts short.

options.text: Pay bills and ignore the budget that week
options.then: Bills are paid. The plan for the rest of the month is unclear.

options.text: Trim wants and protect bills and some savings
options.then: You pay bills, keep a small savings and skip a treat.

steps.why: Trimming wants protects bills and the savings habit in a thin week.

scenarios.debrief: Shape the budget around how you're actually paid, not a fixed template.
scenarios.relearn: If you're paid weekly, budget per pay cycle, not by the calendar month.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget is just you telling your money where to go, instead of wondering where it went. Sit with that?
scenarios.affirm: Directing your money on purpose is exactly what taking charge of it feels like.
scenarios.relearn: A budget is you directing your money, instead of wondering where it went.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: paying yourself first, saving a slice before you spend, quietly builds a cushion. How does that sit?
scenarios.affirm: Saving a slice before anything else is how the cushion actually gets built.
scenarios.relearn: Pay yourself first: save a slice before you spend the rest.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget with a little room for joy is one you'll actually keep. Does that match you?
options: I need some fun in it
scenarios.affirm: A realistic budget that includes some fun is the kind that actually lasts.
scenarios.relearn: A budget with room for some joy is one you'll actually keep.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing where your money goes can feel like 'oh, so that's where it went'. Recognise that?
scenarios.affirm: That moment of seeing where it went is the start of taking control.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing where your money goes is freedom, not restriction.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget isn't a punishment, it's choices you get to make on purpose. How does that feel?
scenarios.affirm: A budget is choices you make on purpose, that's freedom, not deprivation.
scenarios.relearn: A budget is control and choices, not deprivation or punishment.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: even a rough budget beats no budget. You don't need it perfect to start. Sit okay with that?
scenarios.affirm: A rough plan you actually use beats a perfect one you never start.
scenarios.relearn: A rough budget you use beats a perfect one you never start.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the goal isn't to spend less on everything, it's to spend on what matters to you. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: A budget is about funding what matters to you, not cutting everything you enjoy.
scenarios.relearn: Budgeting is funding what matters to you, not cutting everything.

options: I want to look without dread
scenarios.affirm: Your balance is information you can use, not a verdict to fear.
scenarios.relearn: Checking your balance is information to use, not something to dread.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a budget you build yourself fits your life better than any template. How does owning it feel?
scenarios.affirm: A budget you shape yourself fits your real life, and you're the expert on that.
scenarios.relearn: A budget you build for your own life fits better than any template.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: saving for something you want is itself a plan, not just self-denial. Does that reframe help?
scenarios.affirm: Saving toward a goal is actively going for it, the opposite of deprivation.
scenarios.relearn: Saving toward a want is a plan to get it, not self-denial.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two budgeting myths hiding in this group chat.

scene.text: "Track a month and you'll find the leaks"
"Just budget once you start earning big"
"Save a slice on payday before bills"
"Your whole balance is spare money"
"A budget can include some fun money"

scenarios.why: 'Budget later when you earn more' and 'balance = spare money' are the myths; the rest are solid moves.
scenarios.relearn: Start budgeting now at any income, and your balance isn't all spare money.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that quietly break a budget.

scene.text: You saved a slice the day you were paid
You upgraded your lifestyle when income rose
You listed your fixed bills first
You stopped opening your bank app
You kept a small buffer for surprises

scenarios.why: Lifestyle creep and avoiding your bank app are the budget-breakers; the others keep the plan healthy.
scenarios.relearn: Lifestyle creep and avoiding your balance quietly break a budget.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two wants pretending to be needs in this list.

scene.text: Hostel rent for the month
The newest phone, because mine's 'old'
Bus fare to college
Daily food delivery to save effort
Basic groceries for the week

scenarios.why: A new phone when yours works, and daily delivery for convenience, are wants dressed as needs.
scenarios.relearn: Upgrades and convenience are wants, even when they feel essential.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two budgeting moves that are actually traps.

scene.text: Set savings as a fixed line
Borrow a little for everyday wants
Review the plan each month
Leave saving for whatever's left over
Give each rupee a clear job

scenarios.why: Borrowing for wants and saving only the leftover are traps; the rest are solid budgeting moves.
scenarios.relearn: Don't borrow for wants or leave saving as the leftover.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two excuses for not budgeting.

scene.text: "I'll budget when I earn more"
"A rough plan today is enough to start"
"Finance is too hard for someone like me"
"I can track spending in a simple note"
"Even small amounts are worth planning"

scenarios.why: 'When I earn more' and 'too hard for me' are excuses; budgeting is learnable and best started now.
scenarios.relearn: Budgeting is learnable and worth starting now, not later or only for experts.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two costs that are easiest to cut when money's tight.

scene.text: Basic groceries for the week
A daily cab when a bus runs the route
Rent for your room
Three food-app orders this week
Medicine you actually need

scenarios.why: The daily cab and food-app orders are the easy cuts; groceries, rent and medicine are needs.
scenarios.relearn: Trim convenience like cabs and food apps before touching real needs.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that aren't real steps in setting up a budget.

scene.text: Write down your monthly income
Wait until your salary is bigger
List the bills you must pay
Just guess and hope it balances
Set a savings slice before wants

scenarios.why: 'Wait for a bigger salary' and 'guess and hope' aren't steps; noting income, bills and savings are.
scenarios.relearn: Setting up a budget is income, bills, savings, not waiting or guessing.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two signs a budget is quietly failing.

scene.text: Savings inches up most months
You borrow before the next stipend
Surprises don't trigger panic
You've no clue what you spent
You roughly know where money goes

scenarios.why: Borrowing before payday and not knowing what you spent are the failing signs; the rest are healthy.
scenarios.relearn: Borrowing before payday and not knowing your spending mean the budget needs a rethink.

scenarios.hook: A friend nudges you to join a weekend trip you didn't budget for.
scenarios.setup: She calls you, excited.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Come on, figure out the money later. Just say yes."

options.text: "Yeah okay. I'll sort the money out somehow. Count me in."
options.then: "Yes! I'll book once all confirm." The trip is on, and so is a hole in your month.

options.text: "Let me check if my family can help me pay for this."
options.then: "Sure, but ask soon." You feel uneasy about asking them.

options.text: "I'll think about it and tell you later tonight."
options.then: "Don't take too long. Everyone is deciding tonight."

options.text: "Not this one. It's not in my budget. Something cheaper?"
options.then: She pauses. "Hmm. Are you sure? Hear the price first."

steps.why: Saying no to the price, with another idea, keeps the friendship and the plan.

steps.prompt: She says: "Final price is four thousand each, all in. Everyone's paying it, so you can too, right?"

options.text: "Sure. I don't want to be the boring one. I'll pay it."
options.then: She cheers. You feel a knot about the money.

options.text: "I'm not saying no to you. I'm saying no to this price."
options.then: She softens. "Okay. That's fair."

options.text: "It's my money. Stop pushing me about it every time."
options.then: Her voice cools. "Fine. I was just asking."

options.text: "Maybe next month. Ask me again then, all right?"
options.then: "Okay. I'll remember you said that."

steps.why: Naming what you're refusing, and why, keeps it from feeling personal.

steps.prompt: A week later, she asks: "What could we plan next time that works for you?"

options.text: "A day trip or a picnic. I can do that without stress."
options.then: "Oh, that could be fun. Let's plan it."

options.text: "Nothing really. I'll skip all plans this month and stay in."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Okay, I'll ask the others then."

options.text: "Anything, as long as someone else pays for it."
options.then: She laughs, not sure if you mean it. The plan stays vague.

options.text: "You choose and I'll join if I can manage it."
options.then: "Hmm. Okay." The choice goes back to her, and the costs may too.

steps.why: Offering a real alternative keeps you in the plans on terms you can afford.

scenarios.relearn: You can say no to an unbudgeted splurge and still suggest a cheaper plan.

scenarios.hook: Your roommate teases you for writing down every expense.
scenarios.setup: Tonight she spots your notebook on the desk.

steps.prompt: Your roommate says: "Why bother counting? You're being so stingy."

options.text: "It's not stingy. It's me knowing where my money goes."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Hm. Really?"

options.text: "Yeah, maybe I'm overthinking it. I'll stop for now."
options.then: "There you go." Still, she picks up the notebook and flips through it.

options.text: "Mind your own business. It's my money, not yours."
options.then: She stiffens. "Okay, okay. Just a joke."

options.text: "I only do it because I'm broke. That's the truth."
options.then: "Oh. Sorry." She looks awkward, and tracking now sounds like a failure.

steps.why: Tracking isn't stingy. It's knowing where your money goes.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Does writing it all down actually change anything?"

options.text: "Not sure yet. I'm just trying it for a month."
options.then: "Okay. Let me know if it works." She isn't convinced.

options.text: "It beats wasting money the way you do, honestly."
options.then: Her face tightens. "That was unnecessary."

options.text: "Yes. I found two leaks last month and fixed them."
options.then: "Two? Really? Which ones?"

options.text: "It would help you too, but you never listen."
options.then: "I don't need lectures." She walks off.

steps.why: A real example of a leak shows tracking works better than a comeback.

steps.prompt: The next evening, short of money herself, she asks: "Where would I even start tracking?"

options.text: "Get an app I found online. It does everything."
options.then: "Which one?" You realise you'd be sending her to an app you haven't checked.

options.text: "Write each spend down for a week. Then look at it."
options.then: "That's it? Alright. I'll try from tomorrow."

options.text: "Use my sheet exactly as it is. It works for me."
options.then: She looks at your rows. "This is too detailed for me."

options.text: "Don't start unless you'll be serious about it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Then maybe I won't."

steps.why: A simple first step is easier to say yes to than a whole system.

scenarios.relearn: Tracking spending is taking control, not being stingy.

scenarios.hook: You keep putting off starting a budget.
scenarios.setup: Tonight you open your notes app, and a familiar doubt stirs.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "You'll never stick to it. Why even start?"

options.text: "You're right. I'll wait until I'm more organised."
options.then: Relief comes first. The same voice returns next week.

options.text: "A rough plan I use beats no plan. I'll start today."
options.then: The voice goes quiet. You type three lines: income, needs, savings.

options.text: "I'll start on the first of next month instead."
options.then: The first is three weeks away. The date slips by.

options.text: "I'll find the perfect app before I begin at all."
options.then: You spend the evening comparing apps. No budget is written.

steps.why: Starting rough today gets you further than waiting to feel ready.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "Your spending is all over the place. How can you budget that?"

options.text: "True. I'll wait for a month with clean numbers."
options.then: Next month brings new changes. No neat month arrives.

options.text: "I'll ask a friend to do the budget for me instead."
options.then: She offers to help. She can't know what you actually spend.

options.text: "I'll budget only the big bills and skip the rest."
options.then: The big bills are set. The small stuff keeps drifting.

options.text: "Rough numbers are fine. I can fix them as I go."
options.then: You put in estimates. The sheet is messy, but it exists.

steps.why: Rough numbers are enough to begin, and you can fix them later.

steps.prompt: A week later, your inner voice says: "You're already behind. See? You can't do this."

options.text: "You were right. This just isn't for me after all."
options.then: You close the notes app. The voice feels proven.

options.text: "I'll begin again next Monday, properly."
options.then: You wait for Monday. Days pass without a line written.

options.text: "Being behind isn't failing. I'll pick up again today."
options.then: You jot rough numbers for the week and move on.

options.text: "I'll catch up on every missed day tonight, all exact."
options.then: It takes two hours. You are worn out and skip the next day.

steps.why: Falling behind is normal, and you can simply pick up again.

scenarios.relearn: A rough budget you start now beats a perfect one you keep delaying.

scenarios.hook: You're in a shop to buy the model you planned for.
scenarios.setup: The assistant steps closer as you reach for it.

steps.prompt: The assistant says: "For just a bit more, you get the premium one. Everyone takes it."

options.text: "I guess a little more won't hurt. Show me that one."
options.then: "Of course." He fetches it. The bill will be higher than planned.

options.text: "Let me ask my friends which one they'd pick."
options.then: You text a friend. She says to go premium since it lasts longer.

options.text: "Thanks, but I budgeted for this one. I'll take it."
options.then: "Sure. I'll ring it up." He moves to the counter.

options.text: "Can I pay for the premium one in easy EMIs?"
options.then: "Of course, we have plans." The monthly number sounds small.

steps.why: You can stay with the model you budgeted for without apologising.

steps.prompt: The assistant says: "It has a longer warranty. It will pay for itself."

options.text: "Maybe, but this one fits what I need and planned."
options.then: He nods. "Fair enough. Let me show you this one's warranty."

options.text: "Oh, then it must be worth it. Let's get that one."
options.then: He picks up the premium box, then sees you hesitate at the price tag.

options.text: "Can you give me a discount on the premium one?"
options.then: He offers a small one. The premium is still above your plan.

options.text: "Warranties are a scam anyway. Everybody knows that."
options.then: He frowns. "Not always. Would you like to read the terms?"

steps.why: Extra features only matter if you need them and can afford them.

steps.prompt: The assistant says: "Only today, this price is valid. Tomorrow it goes up."

options.text: "Oh. Then I'd better get the premium one now."
options.then: You sign for the premium. The queue moves on.

options.text: "Hold the premium for me and I'll pay half today."
options.then: He says it needs full payment. You feel rushed.

options.text: "I'll take the premium and return it later if needed."
options.then: He says returns have conditions. The queue behind you grows.

options.text: "Then I'll take the one I planned for today."
options.then: "Alright. Card or UPI?"

steps.why: A time-limited price is a nudge to spend, not a reason to.

scenarios.relearn: You can hold to your budgeted choice against an upsell.

scenarios.hook: Your family asks for more of your stipend than you can spare.
scenarios.setup: They call you after dinner.

steps.prompt: A relative says: "Surely you can send a bit extra."

options.text: "Okay. I'll send extra and figure out my bills later."
options.then: "Good." They sound relieved. The month ahead looks tight.

options.text: "I don't have it. Please stop asking me for more."
options.then: The line goes quiet. "We only asked."

options.text: "I'll try. I'll see what's left at month-end then."
options.then: "Okay, but don't forget." They expect it now.

options.text: "I can send the usual. I'm also building my own savings."
options.then: "Hmm. Well, at least send that on time."

steps.why: A clear usual amount plus your own savings line is honest and steady.

steps.prompt: They say: "We have a bill this month and it worries us."

options.text: "Take it from my savings. I'll rebuild them later."
options.then: "Thank you." Your savings line drops to almost nothing.

options.text: "What's the bill? Let's see what we can cover together."
options.then: They tell you the amount. It's smaller than you feared.

options.text: "That's for you to handle, not me. I have my own."
options.then: Silence. Then: "We didn't mean it like that."

options.text: "Take a loan for it. I'll pay the EMI every month."
options.then: They are relieved. Now you also carry a debt.

steps.why: Asking about the need lets you help within your means.

steps.prompt: They ask: "Prices keep rising. Can you send more every month from now on?"

options.text: "Let's fix a monthly amount today that I can keep up."
options.then: They agree on a number. "That helps us plan too."

options.text: "Sure. Whatever you need each month is fine with me."
options.then: They say thanks. There is no number, and the amount may grow.

options.text: "No. The usual is all you'll ever get from me."
options.then: They sound hurt. The matter stays unresolved.

options.text: "I'll send extra when I can, without a fixed amount."
options.then: They nod, but the uncertainty stays. Both sides keep guessing.

steps.why: A fixed, agreed amount lets both sides plan.

scenarios.relearn: You can support family and still protect your own savings line.

scenarios.hook: You join friends on a night out and choose cheaper things.
scenarios.setup: As you order, one friend laughs at you.

steps.prompt: A friend says: "Don't be boring. Just spend like the rest of us."

options.text: "I'm still here and having fun. Just within my plan."
options.then: He laughs. "Okay, okay. Fair."

options.text: "Fine. I'll spend more so nobody thinks I'm cheap."
options.then: The table cheers. Your bill climbs as the round goes on.

options.text: "Some of us have rent to pay. Not everyone's loaded."
options.then: He goes quiet. The mood dips.

options.text: "Okay, next time I'll spend more. I promise you."
options.then: "Deal!" You've promised something you haven't planned.

steps.why: You can join the fun and keep your plan, without apology.

steps.prompt: He says: "Everyone's ordering another round. Come on, one more."

options.text: "Okay. One more won't hurt, I guess. Order for me."
options.then: It is one more. Then someone orders again.

options.text: "I'll have one, but someone else pays my share."
options.then: "Why me?" says one. "We said split equally."

options.text: "I'm good with what I have. You go ahead."
options.then: "Suit yourself." Someone else cracks a joke, and he moves on.

options.text: "Fine. Put it on my card and I'll see later."
options.then: The card comes out. A charge you haven't planned is on its way.

steps.why: Saying what you're having keeps it simple and within your budget.

steps.prompt: At bill time he says: "Let's just split it equally. It's simpler."

options.text: "Sure. Equal is easy. I don't want to seem petty."
options.then: You pay well above what you ordered. Nobody mentions it.

options.text: "I'll pay for what I had. It's easier for me to track."
options.then: "Fine by me." Two others say the same.

options.text: "Someone pay for me, and I'll settle up later."
options.then: "Sure." There's no date and no amount, just a promise.

options.text: "Equal's unfair. You lot always order the pricey stuff."
options.then: Heads turn. The bill gets paid in stiff silence.

steps.why: Paying for what you had is fair and easy to track.

scenarios.relearn: You can join in and stay within your budget without apology.

scenarios.hook: This month feels costly, and your savings look easy to cut.
scenarios.setup: It's payday evening and you're moving money around.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "Skip the savings this time. You can catch up later."

options.text: "One skip won't matter. I'll save double next month."
options.then: It feels fair. Next month brings its own expenses.

options.text: "Savings first, even a small slice. That's the habit."
options.then: You move a small slice. It feels small but steady.

options.text: "I'll save whatever is left at month-end instead."
options.then: At month-end nothing is left, and the thought repeats.

options.text: "I'll buy something I can resell later, as savings."
options.then: You buy it. Reselling turns out to be slow and for less.

steps.why: Saving first, even a little, builds the habit that counts.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "Saving tiny amounts is pointless. Why even bother?"

options.text: "True. I'll start when I can afford to put in a lot."
options.then: That day doesn't arrive. The month goes by again.

options.text: "I'll put in one big amount this month and then stop."
options.then: You drain your balance for one big deposit and struggle later.

options.text: "I'll save only in months when I feel a bit richer."
options.then: Those months are rare. The habit never forms.

options.text: "A small slice adds up, and the habit grows with me."
options.then: You set a small fixed amount. It's easy to keep.

steps.why: Small amounts add up, and the habit matters more than the size.

steps.prompt: Two weeks later, money is tight. Your inner voice says: "Forget saving. You need every rupee."

options.text: "Fine, just this once. I'll put it all back later."
options.then: Anything set aside gets spent. The refill keeps slipping.

options.text: "I'll stop saving until next month feels easier."
options.then: Next month has its own squeeze. The habit slips away.

options.text: "I'll trim a few wants and keep saving, even a little."
options.then: You cut a few treats. A small amount still goes aside.

options.text: "I'll keep everything in one wallet so it's easy."
options.then: Nothing is kept apart. It all drains before the month ends.

steps.why: Trimming wants in a tight month keeps the saving habit alive.

scenarios.relearn: Keep saving a slice first; the habit matters more than the amount.

scenarios.hook: Someone tells you budgeting is too complicated for you.
scenarios.setup: A relative says it over chai.

steps.prompt: A relative says: "Finance stuff isn't for people like us. Forget it."

options.text: "You're probably right. It all feels too confusing for me."
options.then: She nods. "Good. I know just who could manage it for you."

options.text: "You just don't want me to have any money of my own."
options.then: She looks stung. "That's not what I said."

options.text: "It's income minus needs and savings. I can learn this."
options.then: She blinks. "Oh. When you say it like that..."

options.text: "I'll ask someone who knows and do what they say."
options.then: "Good idea." You hand over your decisions without learning any.

steps.why: Budgeting is simple maths you can learn, so you don't need an expert.

steps.prompt: She says: "Your cousin Vikram handles the family's money. Let him do yours."

options.text: "I'd like to learn it myself. You can still advise me."
options.then: She thinks. "Well, you can ask me things."

options.text: "Okay. I'll let him handle all my money for me then."
options.then: She is satisfied. You can't see your own account's numbers.

options.text: "Don't tell me what to do with my own money, please."
options.then: She frowns. "I'm only trying to help."

options.text: "I'll think about it and get back to you later on."
options.then: She nods, and the offer stays open for later.

steps.why: You can welcome advice and still keep hold of your own money.

steps.prompt: A week later, she asks: "If you did want to learn, where would you even start?"

options.text: "With a course that explains everything in a day."
options.then: "Sounds expensive," she says. Nothing starts.

options.text: "With investing. That's where the money is."
options.then: She looks worried. "That sounds risky."

options.text: "I don't know yet. I'll figure it out later."
options.then: She shrugs. The plan stays vague.

options.text: "With my own account and a simple list of spends."
options.then: "That sounds doable," she admits.

steps.why: Start small with your own account and a list, and build from there.

scenarios.relearn: The money basics are learnable by anyone; budgeting isn't only for experts.

scenarios.hook: "A woman's salary is just pocket money for extras."

myth.un: A woman's salary is just pocket money for extras.
myth.re: Her income is real income: savings, independence and a safety net, exactly like anyone's.
myth.why: Calling it 'pocket money' quietly shrinks her financial power.

scenarios.relearn: A woman's income is real income, not 'pocket money'.

scenarios.hook: "You should be grateful for any offer and never ask for more."

myth.un: You should be grateful for any offer and never ask for more.
myth.re: Gratitude and a fair ask aren't opposites: you can be glad and still discuss the figure.
myth.why: Staying quiet just to seem grateful can leave money on the table.

scenarios.relearn: You can be grateful for an offer and still ask about the pay.

scenarios.hook: "Asking your salary range upfront makes you look desperate."

myth.un: Asking the salary range upfront makes you look desperate.
myth.re: Asking the range early is normal and respects everyone's time: it's information, not desperation.
myth.why: Knowing the band early saves you chasing a role that can't pay fairly.

scenarios.relearn: Asking the pay range early is normal, not desperate.

scenarios.hook: "If you're good at the work, the raise will come on its own."

myth.un: If you're good enough, the raise just comes on its own.
myth.re: Good work helps, but raises usually follow a clear ask backed by what you've delivered.
myth.why: Waiting silently to be noticed often means waiting a long time.

scenarios.relearn: Raises usually follow an ask, not silent good work alone.

scenarios.hook: "Talking about pay with colleagues is shameful and forbidden."

myth.un: Talking about pay with colleagues is shameful and forbidden.
myth.re: Sharing pay info with people you trust helps everyone spot unfair gaps.
myth.why: Secrecy around pay mostly protects whoever's underpaying.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing pay info with trusted peers helps spot unfair gaps.

scenarios.hook: "A higher gross figure always means more money in hand."

myth.un: A higher gross figure always means more in hand.
myth.re: Two offers can have the same take-home if deductions differ: check the net, not just the gross.
myth.why: Comparing only the headline number can mislead you.

scenarios.relearn: Compare take-home (net) pay across offers, not just gross.

scenarios.hook: "An internship or first job is free training, so unpaid is fair."

myth.un: A first job is just free training, so unpaid is fair.
myth.re: Real work has real value; ongoing unpaid 'work experience' is often a way to get labour for nothing.
myth.why: You can value learning and still expect to be paid for work done.

scenarios.relearn: Real work has value; ongoing unpaid 'experience' is a red flag.

scenarios.hook: "Negotiating once means they'll just take the offer away."

myth.un: If you negotiate, they'll just take the offer away.
myth.re: A polite, prepared ask rarely loses an offer: employers expect a conversation about pay.
myth.why: Fearing withdrawal keeps many people stuck below their worth.

scenarios.relearn: A polite pay negotiation rarely loses an offer.

scenarios.hook: "Knowing your worth is something you're just born with."

myth.un: Knowing your worth is something you're just born with.
myth.re: It's research: check fair rates for the role, the city and the experience. Anyone can learn it.
myth.why: Treating it as innate stops people from doing the easy homework.

scenarios.relearn: Knowing your worth is research anyone can do, not a born trait.

scenarios.hook: "Men ask for raises; for women it just looks pushy."

myth.un: Men can ask for raises but for women it just looks pushy.
myth.re: A clear, evidence-based ask is professional for anyone: the discomfort is the bias, not the ask.
myth.why: Backing off 'to be liked' is part of how the pay gap stays open.

scenarios.relearn: An evidence-based pay ask is professional for anyone.
