scenarios.hook: You've researched the role, and HR has set up a first call.
scenarios.setup: The call starts with a few friendly questions.

steps.prompt: HR says: "Before we go ahead, what's your salary expectation?"

options.text: "Oh, whatever you think is fair is fine with me."
options.then: "Okay. We'll decide then." The number is now hers.

options.text: "Quite high, since I've had other offers too."
options.then: "Hm. Okay." She sounds unconvinced and makes a note.

options.text: "About the same as what I earn at the moment."
options.then: "Okay. That's noted as your figure."

options.text: "From my research, ₹4.5 to 5 lakh a year."
options.then: "Thanks. That's useful to know."

steps.why: Giving a researched range beats leaving the number to them.

steps.prompt: HR says: "Our budget for this role is on the lower side, just so you know."

options.text: "Yes, sure. I'll take whatever you can offer me."
options.then: "Great. Then we'll go with our range."

options.text: "Could we look at the full package, not only salary?"
options.then: "Sure. Let me share benefits, leave and growth."

options.text: "Then it's not worth my time. I need far more."
options.then: "Then we may not be a match."

options.text: "That's fine. Pay isn't a big deal for me."
options.then: "Thank you. That helps us."

steps.why: Looking at the full package keeps the talk open without giving in.

steps.prompt: HR says: "Okay. Could you share your current salary too?"

options.text: "I'd rather focus on the role's market rate, if that's fine."
options.then: "Understood. I'll note that."

options.text: "Sure. I'll share it now. Please keep it private."
options.then: "Noted. That helps us set the offer."

options.text: "I can't remember it exactly. Maybe I'll check."
options.then: "No problem. You can send it later."

options.text: "That's private. Please don't ask me again."
options.then: "Alright. Sorry. I'll move on."

steps.why: Focusing on the role's rate keeps your past pay from capping the offer.

steps.prompt: HR says: "We'll be in touch with next steps this week."

options.text: "Great, thanks so much. I'll wait to hear from you."
options.then: "Perfect. Speak soon." Nothing is written down.

options.text: "Can you tell me what others were offered?"
options.then: "I can't share that. Sorry."

options.text: "Thanks. Could you email me what we discussed?"
options.then: "Yes, I'll send it after the call."

options.text: "Please call me tomorrow with the answer."
options.then: "I can't promise tomorrow. The process takes time."

steps.why: A written note of what was discussed is easy to refer back to.

scenarios.relearn: Give a researched range when asked your expectation, not 'whatever you think'.

scenarios.hook: A friend has a job offer and worries about looking pushy.
scenarios.setup: She tells you this over tea.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I'll just take the first number. I don't want to seem difficult."

options.text: "Asking isn't being difficult. Let's find a fair number."
options.then: She smiles, a little relieved. "You think so? Okay."

options.text: "Yeah, maybe just take it so you don't annoy them."
options.then: "Right. No point making things awkward." She stirs her tea, still unsure.

options.text: "They'd take advantage of you then. Be tougher."
options.then: "Tougher? I'm not sure I can do that."

options.text: "I'll ask them for you. You stay out of it."
options.then: "Really? I'm not sure that's okay."

steps.why: Asking about pay is normal, and finding a fair number together helps.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Even if I did ask, how would I know what's fair?"

options.text: "Ask your friends what they earn and copy the highest."
options.then: "They might not want to share. And jobs differ."

options.text: "Just ask for double. They'll meet you in the middle."
options.then: "Double? That seems unrealistic."

options.text: "Check the market rate for the role. Look at a few sources."
options.then: "I can do that tonight."

options.text: "Honestly it doesn't matter. Any number will be fine."
options.then: "Then I'll stay with theirs," she says, not sounding sure.

steps.why: The market rate gives you a fair number instead of a guess.

steps.prompt: A few days later, she says: "I looked up a range. Should I ask for the top?"

options.text: "Ask for the lowest to be safe. They'll like you."
options.then: "Then I'd earn less. Hmm."

options.text: "Ask near the top and give your reasons."
options.then: "Reasons. I have a few. Okay."

options.text: "Ask for the top and refuse to budge at all."
options.then: "That sounds stiff. Is that wise?"

options.text: "Ask for the middle so nobody is upset."
options.then: "Nobody upset. Except maybe me."

steps.why: A researched ask with reasons is polite and strong.

steps.prompt: She asks: "And if they say they can't go higher?"

options.text: "Walk away angrily and don't reply again."
options.then: "That feels extreme for a first offer."

options.text: "Take it without asking about anything more."
options.then: "So I'd be back where I started."

options.text: "Tell them you'll go to another company."
options.then: "What if they say go ahead?"

options.text: "Ask about other parts: a review date, leave or training."
options.then: "Oh, I hadn't thought of those. Good."

steps.why: Other parts of the package can still move when the figure can't.

scenarios.relearn: Asking about pay isn't 'being difficult'; help a friend find a fair number.

scenarios.hook: You get an offer below the range they first mentioned.
scenarios.setup: The HR executive sends the letter and calls to confirm.

steps.prompt: HR says: "Did you get the letter? We're happy to have you."

options.text: "Got it, thanks. I'll sign it and send it back today."
options.then: "Wonderful. Welcome aboard." You pick up a pen, with a small knot.

options.text: "Thanks. The figure is below the range we discussed."
options.then: "Oh. Let me see what we can do."

options.text: "This is way too low. I expected a lot more than this."
options.then: "I'm sorry you feel that way. It's what we approved."

options.text: "Thanks. I'll ask my family what they think of it."
options.then: "Of course. Please let us know soon."

steps.why: Naming the gap calmly is the first step to closing it.

steps.prompt: HR says: "Just so you know, the range we mentioned earlier was only an estimate."

options.text: "Oh. Then I'll just hope it rises after I join."
options.then: "Maybe. I'll mention it to my manager."

options.text: "You promised the range. That's a broken promise."
options.then: "I never promised it. Please don't put it that way."

options.text: "Then I'll decline right now. I won't work for less."
options.then: "I'm sorry to hear that. I'll pass it on."

options.text: "I see. Can we get closer to the range we discussed?"
options.then: "Let me check with my manager."

steps.why: Asking to get closer keeps the talk open and respectful.

steps.prompt: A day later, HR says: "I checked. There's a little room. What would you need?"

options.text: "Anything you can add would help. You choose the number."
options.then: "Okay, I'll choose something small."

options.text: "The top of the range we discussed, or I'll walk away."
options.then: "That's too firm. I can't promise that."

options.text: "Something near the lower end of the original range."
options.then: "That's possible. Let me confirm."

options.text: "Let's keep it as it is. Sorry for the trouble."
options.then: "No trouble at all." Nothing changes.

steps.why: A specific, reachable number gives them something they can approve.

steps.prompt: HR says: "I'll send a final letter today. Can you sign by tomorrow?"

options.text: "Yes, once I've checked the figure in the letter."
options.then: "Sounds fair. You'll have it by evening."

options.text: "Sure. I'll sign whatever comes and read it later."
options.then: "Great." You sign without checking what figure it states.

options.text: "Thanks. Can you confirm by phone instead?"
options.then: "We usually send letters. A call is informal."

options.text: "Thanks. I'll post about the new job right away."
options.then: "Please wait until the letter is signed."

steps.why: Signing only after you've checked the figure in writing protects the deal.

scenarios.relearn: If an offer drops below the discussed range, name it and ask to close the gap.

scenarios.hook: You feel your pay doesn't match your work, and you want it looked at.
scenarios.setup: You asked for a quiet word about your pay.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "I hear you. But budgets are tight right now."

options.text: "Okay. I'm sorry I brought it up at all, then."
options.then: "No, it's fine," she says. "I do want to understand what you're after."

options.text: "I understand. Could we set a date and goals to revisit?"
options.then: "That's fair. Let's agree something."

options.text: "Budgets are always tight. That's just an excuse."
options.then: She stiffens. "It's not an excuse. It's the situation."

options.text: "Fine. I'll ask you again next week, then."
options.then: "Please give it some time. It won't change by then."

steps.why: A date and goals turn a closed door into a next step.

steps.prompt: She asks: "If money frees up, how should we decide what change is fair?"

options.text: "Any raise at all will do. I'm not fussy."
options.then: "That's helpful, but I can't promise one."

options.text: "I'll know it when I see it. You decide."
options.then: "Hmm. That doesn't give me much to go on."

options.text: "Whatever my friend earns at her company. The same."
options.then: "Another company's pay doesn't tell me much. Her role may differ from yours. What about your own role?"

options.text: "Clear targets, a review date, and who decides."
options.then: "All right. I can work with that."

steps.why: Clear targets and a named decider make the promise trackable.

steps.prompt: Three months later, she says: "Things are still tight, honestly."

options.text: "Then I guess nothing will ever change here."
options.then: She sighs. "That's not what I'm saying."

options.text: "Then I'll start looking at other companies now."
options.then: She looks worried. "Please give us a chance first."

options.text: "I hear that. Can we go through my results together?"
options.then: "Yes. Let me pull up the numbers."

options.text: "Fine. Let's talk again in another three months."
options.then: "All right." The matter goes round again with no change.

steps.why: Going through results keeps the talk on evidence, not on feelings.

steps.prompt: At your next check-in, she says: "I can offer a small raise now and a review in six months."

options.text: "Thank you. Could we put both in writing?"
options.then: "Yes. I'll send it this week."

options.text: "That's not enough. I'll decline and wait for more."
options.then: "I understand. The offer will stay open a short while."

options.text: "Okay, thanks. I won't expect anything more."
options.then: "Good. Let's leave it there." Nothing is recorded.

options.text: "Make it double and we're done. No review needed."
options.then: She sighs. "I can't go that far. Let's not drop the review."

steps.why: Writing down the raise and the review date makes the deal clear.

scenarios.relearn: If 'budgets are tight', ask for a clear date and goals to revisit pay.

scenarios.hook: You've started earning, and relatives don't take your job seriously.
scenarios.setup: At a family function, an aunt pulls up a chair beside you.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says: "You studied for marriage anyway. The job hardly matters."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. It probably isn't a big deal."
options.then: She smiles, pleased. "Good. Then listen to me on this too."

options.text: "Please don't say that here in front of everyone."
options.then: She looks away. The remark has already been heard.

options.text: "My income is my independence. The job matters to me."
options.then: She blinks. The others fall quiet for a moment.

options.text: "Did you ask my parents what they think?"
options.then: She shrugs. "They agree with me, you know."

steps.why: Your income is your independence, and you can say it calmly.

steps.prompt: She says: "A good family will look after you. Why do you need money?"

options.text: "Having my own money means I always have choices."
options.then: She pauses. "I never thought of it that way."

options.text: "You're right. A good family makes it unnecessary."
options.then: She smiles. You're left with a small, uneasy feeling.

options.text: "Maybe it's selfish of me to want my own money."
options.then: "It's not selfish, but it's not needed either."

options.text: "Don't judge me. You know nothing about my life."
options.then: "I'm only saying what everyone thinks."

steps.why: Your own money is about choices and safety, not about trust.

steps.prompt: She says: "People will talk if you put a job ahead of family."

options.text: "You're right. I should think about what people say."
options.then: "Exactly. Family name matters."

options.text: "You're all old-fashioned. Nobody thinks like this."
options.then: "Old-fashioned? Watch your tone."

options.text: "Maybe I'm bringing gossip on the family by working."
options.then: "That's what I'm saying." She watches you, and the topic hangs.

options.text: "I can value family and my job. They can both matter."
options.then: She looks unsure. "Hmm. Perhaps."

steps.why: You can care about family and about your work at the same time.

steps.prompt: That evening, another relative says: "Keep the job if you must, but give us your salary to manage."

options.text: "Maybe I can't handle money well enough myself."
options.then: "Yes, that's why we should do it."

options.text: "I'll help at home. My salary stays in my own account."
options.then: They frown. "We only want to help." You stay calm.

options.text: "A good daughter hands over her salary without asking."
options.then: Your aunt nods along. You feel uneasy, and the demand is still open.

options.text: "If all elders do this, maybe it's just normal."
options.then: They nod, pleased. The demand stays on the table.

steps.why: Taking your salary is financial control, not help. It is yours, and you can still help at home.

steps.prompt: A trusted friend says: "You've seemed tense. Is something going on at home?"

options.text: "They want my salary. I need help working out what to do."
options.then: She listens. "That's not okay. Want to call the Women Helpline 181 together?"

options.text: "It's nothing. I shouldn't cause trouble for the family."
options.then: "Okay. But I'm here if you want to talk."

options.text: "It's probably my fault for wanting my own money."
options.then: She frowns. "Wait. Why would that be your fault?"

options.text: "Every family does this. It's not worth talking about."
options.then: "Maybe. But it sounds hard. I'm here if you want me."

steps.why: You deserve support, and it is never your fault when someone controls your money.

scenarios.relearn: Your own income is your independence: it matters, whatever others say.

scenarios.hook: In your review, your manager lists your wins but says nothing about pay.
scenarios.setup: She finishes and starts closing her laptop.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "Great work this year. That's all from me."

options.text: "Thank you so much. It's lovely to hear all that."
options.then: "You're welcome." She closes the laptop. Pay isn't mentioned.

options.text: "Thanks. I was kind of hoping you'd bring up pay."
options.then: "Oh. Pay wasn't on my list today."

options.text: "Good. I expect a raise after all that work, obviously."
options.then: She pauses. "Let's not assume anything."

options.text: "Glad the work landed well. I'd like to discuss my pay too."
options.then: "Oh. Sure. Let's find a moment."

steps.why: Opening the pay talk yourself is normal after good feedback.

steps.prompt: She says: "I've got another meeting now. Anything else before I go?"

options.text: "No problem. We'll leave pay for some other time."
options.then: "Good. Thanks for understanding." Nothing is set.

options.text: "Could we set ten minutes this week to talk pay?"
options.then: "Let's do Thursday. Bring what you have."

options.text: "Pay has to be today. I can't wait any longer."
options.then: She frowns. "I'm not prepared for that."

options.text: "I'll just ask HR about my pay directly."
options.then: "Please talk to me first." She looks uneasy.

steps.why: Asking for a set time respects her schedule and keeps pay on the table.

steps.prompt: At your next one-to-one, she asks: "So, about pay. What are you hoping for?"

options.text: "A raise based on my results and the market rate."
options.then: "That's reasonable. Show me what you have."

options.text: "Whatever you think is fair. I trust you completely."
options.then: "All right. I'll see what I can do."

options.text: "More than everyone else, since I work the hardest."
options.then: "I can't compare you with others like that."

options.text: "Double what I earn now. I deserve it, honestly."
options.then: She looks startled. "That's far from what's possible."

steps.why: Results and the market rate make a clear and fair ask.

steps.prompt: She says: "I'll look into it and get back to you."

options.text: "Thanks. I'll trust that you'll remember on your own."
options.then: "Of course." Two busy weeks go by.

options.text: "Please decide before the month ends, or else."
options.then: "There's no need for that tone."

options.text: "Thanks. Could we agree on a date for your answer?"
options.then: "Yes. Two weeks from today."

options.text: "Thanks. I'll check with you again next week."
options.then: "A week is too soon. Give me a little longer."

steps.why: Agreeing a date keeps the promise from fading.

scenarios.relearn: After good review feedback, open the pay conversation yourself.

scenarios.hook: A "recruiter" offers great pay but wants a fee first.
scenarios.setup: The chat pings while you're at work.

steps.prompt: The recruiter writes: "Great news, you're selected! Pay the registration fee to confirm."

options.text: "Real jobs don't charge me to join. I won't pay any fee."
options.then: "Fee is required. This is our policy."

options.text: "Okay, thank you so much! Where do I send the fee?"
options.then: "Here's the account. Please pay in the next hour."

options.text: "Can I pay half now and the other half after I start?"
options.then: "Yes, half now. The rest before you join."

options.text: "Send me the offer letter first. Then I'll decide."
options.then: A polished letter arrives. It has no address or signatures.

steps.why: Real jobs don't charge you to join, so refuse any fee.

steps.prompt: The recruiter writes: "Only two seats left. Pay the fee within the hour to keep yours."

options.text: "I'll pay now. I can't risk losing this seat."
options.then: "Received! One last step to finish your joining."

options.text: "Everyone pays a fee these days. I'll send it."
options.then: "Great. Once it's in, we need a few details from you."

options.text: "I'll check the company first. I won't pay."
options.then: "Don't take long. Others are waiting."

options.text: "Give me a discount and I'll pay right now."
options.then: "Okay, a small discount if you pay in ten minutes."

steps.why: A rush to pay is a pressure tactic, so check first.

steps.prompt: The recruiter writes: "Send your ID copy and bank details so we can register you."

options.text: "Sure. Here's my ID. I'll keep the bank details."
options.then: "Fine, thanks." Your ID is now in unknown hands.

options.text: "No. I'm not sharing those with someone I can't verify."
options.then: The chat turns angry, then silent. Your details stay yours.

options.text: "Here's everything. I really hope this is real."
options.then: "Received." Soon you get odd messages.

options.text: "I'll send a blurred ID copy. That should be safe."
options.then: "Blurred is useless. Send the clear one."

steps.why: Never share ID or bank details with someone you can't verify.

steps.prompt: A friend messages you: "Heard you got a job offer? Can I apply too?"

options.text: "Yes, definitely apply! The pay looks really great."
options.then: "Brilliant. Send me the link."

options.text: "Maybe. Wait and see if it works out for me first."
options.then: "Okay. I'll wait for your update."

options.text: "Sure. They want a small fee, but it's worth paying."
options.then: "A fee? Fine. I'll pay it."

options.text: "Wait. They asked for a fee. Let's check them first."
options.then: "A fee? That sounds off. Thanks for telling me."

steps.why: Telling a friend early protects her from the same trap.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend sends a news story about job-fee scams and asks: "Isn't this the same thing? What do we do?"

options.text: "Reply and scold them so they stop doing this."
options.then: "They'll only block us. It won't change much."

options.text: "Ignore it all and hope they leave us alone."
options.then: "Okay." The number stays unreported, and the chat is still there.

options.text: "Stop replying, keep the chat and report the number."
options.then: "Okay. Let's report it on the cybercrime helpline, 1930."

options.text: "Ask them politely to return any money we paid."
options.then: "They'll only ask for another fee."

steps.why: Reporting and keeping the chat helps. Being targeted, or having paid, is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Real jobs don't charge a fee to join; refuse and verify the company.

scenarios.hook: You're early in your career and feel you can't negotiate yet.
scenarios.setup: You're drafting a reply to a first offer.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "You're too junior. Better not say anything."

options.text: "You're right. I'm too junior to say anything at all."
options.then: It feels safe. The offer stays as it is.

options.text: "Even early on, I can ask once, politely, with my research."
options.then: The voice pauses. A small, steady plan forms.

options.text: "I'll wait until I have more experience to ask."
options.then: The wait feels safe. It has no end date.

options.text: "I'll ask a senior to speak up for me instead."
options.then: You imagine him saying it's your call, and your face warms.

steps.why: Even early in your career, one polite, researched ask is fair.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "What if they withdraw the offer if you ask?"

options.text: "It's possible, so I shouldn't risk anything at all."
options.then: The worry grows. Still, part of you wonders what you'd say.

options.text: "They'd never do that. So I can be blunt with them."
options.then: You picture a blunt message. It wouldn't land well.

options.text: "I'll just hint and see if they offer more on their own."
options.then: You imagine hinting. They may never catch it.

options.text: "A polite, prepared ask is normal. The worst is usually a no."
options.then: You breathe out. Most likely, a no leaves you where you are now.

steps.why: A polite, prepared ask is a normal part of hiring.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "Even if you asked, what would you actually say?"

options.text: "I'll write a long explanation of my life story."
options.then: You write for an hour. The message is long and unfocused.

options.text: "I'll say I need more because I have expenses."
options.then: It's true, but it says nothing about the role.

options.text: "Thanks. From my research, could we revisit the figure?"
options.then: You type it out. It sounds polite and clear.

options.text: "I'll copy a ready-made message from the internet."
options.then: It reads oddly formal. It doesn't sound like you.

steps.why: A short, researched line is easier to send than a long story.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "They said they'll think about it. Now you wait."

options.text: "I'll thank them and ask when they'll reply."
options.then: You send a short note. A date comes back.

options.text: "I'll check my phone every five minutes until they do."
options.then: Every buzz is a false alarm. The wait feels long.

options.text: "I'll accept before they can change their minds."
options.then: You reply yes. The question about the figure closes.

options.text: "I'll message them every day until they answer."
options.then: By day three, they seem irritated.

steps.why: A thank-you with a date keeps the wait calm and polite.

scenarios.relearn: Even early in your career you can make one polite, researched ask.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Nikhil has strong views on what your teammate Kavya should be paid.
scenarios.setup: You're having chai with Nikhil after a long shift.

steps.prompt: Nikhil says: "Kavya earns enough for a woman. Why ask for a raise?"

options.text: "Pay is the rate for the work. Same job, same number."
options.then: Nikhil blinks. "Huh. I never thought of it as a rate."

options.text: "She's good at her work, so she can ask."
options.then: He nods. "True. She's good. For a woman, I mean."

options.text: "Arre, leave it. That's between her and the manager."
options.then: Nikhil shrugs and sips his tea. His view stays as it was.

options.text: "That's a sexist thing to say. Grow up, Nikhil."
options.then: Nikhil bristles. "I was only saying it. Why attack me?"

steps.why: Naming pay as the rate for the work is calm, sharp and hard to argue with.

steps.prompt: Nikhil says: "But the guys here have families to support. Isn't that different?"

options.text: "Some do, yes. She's just as good though."
options.then: He nods, but says the men's needs come first. The question stays open.

options.text: "Pay follows the work. Kavya may support a family too."
options.then: He pauses. "I didn't think about her side. Fair."

options.text: "Okay, fair enough. Maybe the men should get a bit more."
options.then: Nikhil grins. "Exactly." The old idea sits a little firmer.

options.text: "Let's not get into who supports whom."
options.then: He laughs it off. The idea is still there, unchallenged.

steps.why: The job sets the rate, so who supports whom doesn't change what the work is worth.

steps.prompt: Nikhil asks: "Kavya's review is next week. Am I supposed to do anything about it?"

options.text: "Nothing. That's for the manager to sort out."
options.then: He nods, relieved. Nothing changes for Kavya.

options.text: "Tell her to be grateful she has a job at all."
options.then: Nikhil frowns. "That sounds harsh, even to me."

options.text: "If she asks, back her with the work she's done."
options.then: He thinks. "I can do that. She fixed our worst bug last month."

options.text: "Start a group chat and shame the manager."
options.then: He looks alarmed. "That will blow up on all of us."

steps.why: Backing a colleague's ask with facts about her work is a simple, fair way to help.

scenarios.relearn: Fair pay is the rate for the work, not 'enough for a woman'.

scenarios.hook: Your first job offer comes with no written breakdown of the pay.
scenarios.setup: It's Friday afternoon and your phone rings.

steps.prompt: Mrs Iyer, the recruiter, says: "We'll pay ₹30,000 a month. Shall I confirm Monday?"

options.text: "Sounds great. Please confirm me for Monday."
options.then: "Wonderful. I'll mail the joining details and the pay breakdown."

options.text: "Could you send gross, deductions and in-hand in writing first?"
options.then: "Of course. I'll email the full breakdown within the hour."

options.text: "Is ₹30,000 what lands in my account?"
options.then: "Roughly. A few deductions apply. I'd have to check."

options.text: "Let me ask a friend there what they get."
options.then: "Sure, but roles differ. I'll send your breakdown anyway."

steps.why: Asking for it in writing means you work from real numbers, not a verbal figure.

steps.prompt: Mrs Iyer says: "Here is the breakdown. In-hand is lower than gross because of deductions."

options.text: "Fine. As long as the gross matches."
options.then: "It does." Nobody mentions what you'll actually take home.

options.text: "That's far too low. I'll look elsewhere."
options.then: "I understand. Most payslips show some deductions. The offer stays open."

options.text: "Thanks. Could you explain each deduction?"
options.then: "Yes. Part is tax and part goes to your provident fund."

options.text: "Okay. I'll plan my budget on the gross."
options.then: "Noted." She doesn't say you won't see that number monthly.

steps.why: Knowing each deduction lets you plan your budget on the in-hand figure.

steps.prompt: Mrs Iyer says: "The offer letter is ready. Would you like to sign it today?"

options.text: "Yes, I'll sign now. Questions can wait."
options.then: She says she'll send the e-sign link. Your questions stay unasked.

options.text: "Let me show my uncle. He'll decide."
options.then: "Of course." She waits, though it is your contract.

options.text: "No need to read it. All offer letters say the same."
options.then: She sends the e-sign link. Nobody checks what this one says.

options.text: "I'll read it tonight and sign if it matches."
options.then: "That's sensible. Send it back by Sunday night and we're set."

steps.why: Reading the letter fully before signing protects you from surprises.

scenarios.relearn: Ask for the pay breakdown in writing: gross, deductions and in-hand.

scenarios.hook: You have two offers: one with a higher gross, one with higher take-home.

steps.prompt: The bigger gross number looks exciting. What do you do?

options.text: Compare take-home and the full package
options.then: You list both side by side. The higher gross offer takes home less than you thought.

options.text: Lean toward the bigger gross figure on instinct
options.then: It feels like a win. You haven't looked past that one number.

options.text: Lean toward the one your family likes
options.then: They like the brand name. Nobody has looked at the numbers.

options.text: Ask a friend which company sounds cooler
options.then: She names the trendier one. It doesn't show what lands in your account.

steps.why: Take-home plus the full package shows the real money.

steps.prompt: One offer lists "benefits" but gives no amounts. What do you do?

options.text: Assume the benefits are worth a lot and count them
options.then: Your comparison looks rosy. Some benefits turn out to be small.

options.text: Ignore anything you can't count
options.then: You leave out health cover, which would have cost you later.

options.text: Ask for the numbers behind each benefit
options.then: HR sends a simple breakdown. Some benefits are worth more than they sounded.

options.text: Ask the recruiter if it's a good offer
options.then: She says it's very competitive. It still gives you no number.

steps.why: Numbers behind benefits show what they are really worth.

steps.prompt: Both offers need an answer by Friday. What decides it for you?

options.text: The higher number, whatever else is in it
options.then: You pick it. Two months later the hours and commute wear you down.

options.text: Take-home, benefits and growth together
options.then: You choose with the whole picture in mind and feel settled.

options.text: Whichever sounds more impressive to relatives
options.then: They are pleased. Your budget is not.

options.text: Whichever you feel least nervous saying yes to
options.then: The decision feels easy. You haven't compared the money at all.

steps.why: Looking at the whole picture beats any single number.

scenarios.debrief: The honest comparison is net pay plus the full package, because gross alone can mislead.
scenarios.relearn: Compare take-home and the full package across offers, not just gross.

scenarios.hook: You learn a peer in the same role earns clearly more than you.

steps.prompt: A colleague mentions it in passing. What do you do with that?

options.text: Quietly fume and tell no one
options.then: You carry it around. Your work gets a little colder.

options.text: Check the market rate for your role
options.then: The range suggests your pay is lower than typical.

options.text: Confront the peer about why she earns more
options.then: She's stunned and defensive. It isn't her decision, and the mood sours.

options.text: Tell the team it's unfair
options.then: The room goes silent. Word reaches your manager, without any facts.

steps.why: Checking the market rate turns a feeling into something you can use.

steps.prompt: You decide to raise it. How do you prepare?

options.text: List everything that feels unfair about it
options.then: The list is long and emotional. There's little you can show.

options.text: Get a colleague to back you up in the meeting
options.then: She hesitates. Bringing her in makes it feel like a fight.

options.text: Plan to quote the peer's exact salary
options.then: You'd be using information she never shared with you. It could backfire.

options.text: Gather your wins and the market rate
options.then: You have five results and a range. It feels solid.

steps.why: Wins plus the market rate make a fair case, without using anyone's pay.

steps.prompt: Your manager asks what the meeting is about. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's nothing, just a chat
options.then: She's surprised when pay comes up. She hasn't prepared.

options.text: Hint that you're thinking of leaving
options.then: She looks worried, and the meeting starts on the wrong foot.

options.text: Say you'd like to discuss your pay and role
options.then: She says okay and blocks half an hour.

options.text: Skip the meeting and raise it over a message
options.then: A message is easy to misread. The reply is short and cool.

steps.why: Being open about the topic keeps the meeting calm and useful.

steps.prompt: Your manager replies that she'll look into it. What do you do next?

options.text: Thank her and agree on when you'll hear back
options.then: You both settle on a date. You write it down.

options.text: Leave it open and hope she remembers
options.then: Busy weeks pass. The matter stays open.

options.text: Ask for an answer on the spot
options.then: She feels cornered and gives a vague answer.

options.text: Ask your peer to help push it along
options.then: She's uncomfortable. It turns into a bigger dispute.

steps.why: Agreeing a date makes sure the conversation goes somewhere.

scenarios.debrief: Evidence plus a professional ask turns resentment into a fair conversation.
scenarios.relearn: Gather evidence and raise a pay gap professionally instead of fuming silently.

scenarios.hook: A "work from home" job offers big pay for forwarding parcels and links.

steps.prompt: The recruiter's message promises high pay for a few easy tasks. What do you do?

options.text: Try it once since the pay sounds great
options.then: The first task pays a tiny amount. The next asks for a deposit.

options.text: Ask for a company name and website first
options.then: They send a slick page. It has no address or real people.

options.text: Refuse and report it as a likely scam
options.then: You report the number. Nothing is lost, and the chat goes quiet for now.

options.text: Reply asking how they found you
options.then: They reply instantly with a long friendly message. Now they know you read it.

steps.why: Easy money for vague tasks is a scam pattern, so refuse and report.

steps.prompt: Next day, a new message says many people earn daily, with screenshots as proof. What do you do?

options.text: Treat the screenshots as bait and step away
options.then: Screenshots are easy to fake. You mute the chat.

options.text: Ask to speak to someone who earns from it
options.then: They produce a "member". She sounds convincing and is part of the script.

options.text: Join their group to see what happens
options.then: The group is full of happy posts. The pressure to join in builds.

options.text: Share it with friends so you can all earn
options.then: Two friends join. Now they are at risk too.

steps.why: Screenshots and testimonials are easy to fake, so don't trust them.

steps.prompt: Days later, another message says you can "unlock" a bonus by paying a fee. What do you do?

options.text: Pay a small fee to see the bonus
options.then: The fee goes through. A bigger fee is now asked.

options.text: Pay but plan to stop after this one
options.then: One fee becomes several before you can stop. Each has a reason.

options.text: Ask a friend to pay it while you're short
options.then: She pays. Now both of you are out of pocket.

options.text: Stop and pay nothing
options.then: They send angry messages, then fall silent. You keep your money.

steps.why: Real jobs don't charge you to release your pay.

steps.prompt: A friend messages you the same offer, excited. What do you say?

options.text: Tell her to check the company herself
options.then: She'll check, but she won't know what to look for.

options.text: Tell her it looks like a scam and show how to spot one
options.then: She stops. "Thank you. I was about to send money."

options.text: Say nothing since it's her decision
options.then: She goes ahead. You hear about it too late.

options.text: Say it's probably fine if the pay is small
options.then: She tries. The tasks lead her to a fee.

steps.why: Helping a friend spot a scam protects her money.

scenarios.debrief: Easy money for vague tasks is a scam pattern, so verify and report instead of trying it.
scenarios.relearn: 'Too good' pay for vague online tasks is a scam: refuse and report.

scenarios.hook: Your manager praises you, but the promised raise keeps slipping each quarter.

steps.prompt: Another quarter ends and the raise is still "coming". What do you do?

options.text: Keep waiting and hope it lands
options.then: The quarter ticks over. Nothing is written or decided.

options.text: Mention it casually by the coffee machine
options.then: She nods and says soon. Nothing is recorded.

options.text: Ask for a written timeline and clear targets
options.then: She agrees to write it down. "Fair. I'll send something this week."

options.text: Complain to colleagues about the delay
options.then: They sympathise. Word of your mood reaches your manager, not your request.

steps.why: A written timeline turns "soon" into something you can follow.

steps.prompt: A month later, she mentions the raise again and says only "by year end". What do you do?

options.text: Ask which targets and who approves it
options.then: She names three targets and the person who signs off.

options.text: Take it as settled and relax
options.then: It's vague enough that nothing is actually decided.

options.text: Thank her and say nothing more
options.then: The chat ends politely. You're no further along.

options.text: Ask HR without telling your manager
options.then: HR says it's the manager's call. Your manager hears about it.

steps.why: Clear targets and an approver make a vague promise trackable.

steps.prompt: Near the date she gave, you have clear results to show. What do you do?

options.text: Wait quietly for her to bring it up herself
options.then: Weeks pass. She has a full calendar and doesn't.

options.text: Accept a small one-time bonus and drop the raise
options.then: It helps this month. Your base pay stays the same.

options.text: Send her a long email listing all your complaints
options.then: She reads the complaints more than the results.

options.text: Request a meeting with your results and the timeline
options.then: She agrees and reviews your results. "You've earned this."

steps.why: Results plus the agreed timeline make the ask fair and easy to grant.

scenarios.debrief: A vague 'soon' becomes real only with a date and clear targets.
scenarios.relearn: Turn a slipping raise promise into a written timeline and clear targets.

scenarios.hook: Your current pay is very low, and you're looking for a better role.

steps.prompt: A recruiter wants your current salary to set the new offer. What do you say?

options.text: Share the low number and let it set the offer
options.then: She notes it down and says an offer will follow.

options.text: Give a higher number than your real pay
options.then: She notes it, and mentions they check payslips before joining.

options.text: Say you can't share it, then go quiet
options.then: She says it's needed and asks you to think it over.

options.text: Say you'd like to focus on the role's market rate
options.then: She pauses, then says she'll pass that on to the team.

steps.why: Anchoring on the role's market rate protects you from a past low.

steps.prompt: The next day, she says the team usually bases offers on last pay. What do you do?

options.text: Go along with it, since that's how it's done
options.then: The offer tracks your old pay, not the role.

options.text: Say your past pay shouldn't cap your future value
options.then: She hears you out. "Hmm. Let me check the band for this role."

options.text: Accept, but ask for a raise after six months
options.then: She agrees to look at it later. Nothing is written down.

options.text: Argue that the practice is unfair
options.then: She gets defensive. The call turns tense and the offer stalls.

steps.why: Your past pay shouldn't cap your future, and you can say so politely.

steps.prompt: She comes back with an offer well below the role's market rate. What do you do?

options.text: Point to the market rate and ask for a closer number
options.then: She says she'll take it back to the team.

options.text: Accept it so you don't lose the job
options.then: You say yes. That number will follow you into later jobs.

options.text: Counter with a number far above the market rate
options.then: She sounds taken aback. The call turns cold.

options.text: Say you'll think it over and let the silence decide
options.then: She waits, then moves on to other candidates.

steps.why: Market evidence gives you a fair basis for a counter.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, how do you prepare for your next pay talk?

options.text: Hope the next recruiter doesn't ask about pay
options.then: They ask, as most do. You have no answer ready.

options.text: Plan to claim a higher past salary next time
options.then: You carry the worry of being caught.

options.text: Note market rates and your value to cite next time
options.then: You build a one-page note you can reuse.

options.text: Apply only through referrals to skip the question
options.then: Referrals help a bit. The pay question still comes up.

steps.why: A reusable note of your value makes the next talk easier.

scenarios.debrief: Your past pay shouldn't cap your future: anchor on the role's fair rate.
scenarios.relearn: Anchor a new offer on the role's market rate, not your old low pay.

scenarios.hook: A family member wants you to quit your paid job for an unpaid family role.

steps.prompt: They say the family needs you at home more than at work. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want to keep some income of your own
options.then: They are surprised. "We just thought family came first." They listen.

options.text: Wonder whether your income matters less than theirs
options.then: The thought grows heavier. You don't say it to anyone.

options.text: Blame yourself for making the family worry
options.then: You feel guilty. You can't tell if they are asking too much.

options.text: Assume elders always know what's best for you
options.then: You stop saying what you want. Their plan starts to feel settled.

steps.why: Your own income is your safety net, and wanting it is not selfish.

steps.prompt: They say a job is unnecessary because they will provide for you. What do you do?

options.text: Decide independence is only for people who don't trust family
options.then: You feel ashamed of wanting your own money. The wish stays.

options.text: Ask a cousin to convince them for you
options.then: She tries. They nod politely, but she can't speak for you.

options.text: Say your own income matters to you, whatever they provide
options.then: They look unsure. "We didn't think of it that way."

options.text: Believe an allowance from them is as good as a salary
options.then: It sounds generous. The money would still depend on them.

steps.why: Your income matters to you, and that stays true however well they provide.

steps.prompt: A week later, your family suggests part-time work as a middle path. What do you do?

options.text: Believe putting family first means dropping your own plans
options.then: Your own wishes start to feel wrong. Nothing is decided.

options.text: Weigh what hours you want, then tell them your decision
options.then: You choose what suits you. They're unsure, but they hear it from you.

options.text: Let an uncle decide your hours, since elders know best
options.then: He says he'll sort your hours for you. Nothing is settled yet.

options.text: Decide that wanting your own income is selfish
options.then: The guilt grows. The pressure at home stays the same.

steps.why: Your hours and income are your call. Deciding for yourself protects both.

steps.prompt: The topic comes up again at home and you feel stuck. Who do you turn to?

options.text: Keep it to yourself so you don't cause trouble
options.then: You hold it in. The worry follows you to work and to bed.

options.text: Tell yourself every family does this and wait
options.then: Weeks go by. The pressure doesn't ease and you feel more alone.

options.text: Ask an online group for advice
options.then: Some advice is kind. Some pushes you to extremes. None of them knows your family.

options.text: Someone you trust, or call the Women Helpline 181
options.then: You tell a cousin you trust. She listens and says the helpline is there if you need it.

steps.why: You don't have to carry this alone, and it is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Your own income is your safety net: worth protecting even amid family pressure.
scenarios.relearn: Protect some income of your own rather than giving it all up.

scenarios.hook: You feel underpaid but think asking might make you look bad.

steps.prompt: You've felt this for weeks. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing to avoid looking bad
options.then: The days pass quietly. The feeling doesn't go away.

options.text: Prepare your case and ask once, politely
options.then: You gather your results and the market rate. You feel steadier.

options.text: Drop hints in casual talk that you're underpaid
options.then: People laugh along. Nobody takes it as a request.

options.text: Ask a senior colleague to raise it for you
options.then: He says it's not his place. He suggests you ask yourself.

steps.why: One prepared, polite ask is normal and professional.

steps.prompt: At your next one-to-one, your manager asks if anything is on your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Wait for her to notice your work without asking
options.then: She praises your work and moves on. Pay never comes up.

options.text: Say you want to discuss pay and show your results
options.then: She listens and says she'll look at it before appraisals.

options.text: Joke that you're working for peanuts
options.then: She laughs. It doesn't land as a real request.

options.text: Say you'll leave unless your pay changes
options.then: She tenses. The talk turns to whether you're committed.

steps.why: Naming the topic with your results is the clearest, calmest way to ask.

steps.prompt: At appraisal time, she offers a small raise, below the market rate. What do you do?

options.text: Accept it and feel quietly resentful
options.then: You say thanks. The resentment shows up in small ways later.

options.text: Turn it down and walk out upset
options.then: She's startled. The talk ends with no raise at all.

options.text: Ask what it would take to reach a fair figure
options.then: She says what she'd need to see. You get a clear goal.

options.text: Take it and get nothing in writing
options.then: It's agreed verbally. Two months later it is "still pending".

steps.why: Asking what closes the gap turns a half yes into a plan.

scenarios.debrief: One calm, prepared ask is normal professional behaviour, not a black mark.
scenarios.relearn: Prepare and make one polite ask rather than staying silent to 'look good'.

scenarios.hook: An offer's pay sounds fine but there's no written contract, just a handshake.

steps.prompt: They say you can start Monday and the paperwork will follow. What do you do?

options.text: Start on trust, without anything written
options.then: You say yes to Monday. Nothing written says what you'll be paid.

options.text: Jot down what they said and just start
options.then: Your notes are yours alone. They prove little if pay is disputed.

options.text: Ask for the terms in writing before you start
options.then: They look surprised, then agree to send something.

options.text: Ask a friend at the company if it's legit
options.then: He says people work there happily. He doesn't know your terms.

steps.why: A handshake isn't proof, so get pay terms in writing.

steps.prompt: Before Monday, they say the letter will come after the first month. What do you do?

options.text: Ask for a short email with pay and start date
options.then: They send two lines with pay, date and role. It's enough to refer back to.

options.text: Agree because the boss seems honest and friendly
options.then: You start. The warm talk is all you have to show.

options.text: Start now and ask for it after your first payday
options.then: Payday arrives. The paperwork still doesn't.

options.text: Insist on a full legal contract or nothing
options.then: They say a small team can't do that. Needing the work, you start with nothing written.

steps.why: Even a short email gives you a record to point to.

steps.prompt: Your first pay arrives lower than you were told. What do you do?

options.text: Complain in person and hope they remember
options.then: They say they'll look into it. Weeks later nothing has changed.

options.text: Accept it so you don't cause any trouble at work
options.then: You let it go. The gap repeats the next month.

options.text: Quit on the spot and tell everyone you know
options.then: You feel relieved for a day. The unpaid gap remains unsettled.

options.text: Raise it calmly and share whatever is in writing
options.then: They check what's on record and agree to fix it next month.

steps.why: A calm ask backed by a record fixes pay errors faster.

scenarios.debrief: A handshake isn't proof: written terms are basic self-protection.
scenarios.relearn: Get pay terms in writing before starting, not just a handshake.

scenarios.hook: You want a raise but only have a vague feeling you deserve more.

steps.prompt: You decide to ask soon. What do you do first?

options.text: Ask with just the feeling and nothing to back it
options.then: Your manager asks why. You can't say.

options.text: Wait until you're really annoyed and then ask
options.then: By then it comes out sharp. The talk is tense from the start.

options.text: Ask colleagues what they think you deserve
options.then: Answers range widely. None is based on your role's rate.

options.text: List your concrete wins and the market rate
options.then: You find four results and a rate range. The feeling now has a base.

steps.why: Concrete wins and the market rate turn a feeling into a strong ask.

steps.prompt: Your manager asks what number you have in mind. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll happily take whatever she thinks is fair
options.then: She names a low figure, since you gave her nothing to go on.

options.text: Name a range based on the market and your results
options.then: She nods. "That's reasonable. Let me see what I can do."

options.text: Name a round number that simply feels good to you
options.then: It has no reasoning behind it. She counters much lower.

options.text: Say it's not really about the number for you
options.then: She says it's hard to help without one.

steps.why: A range backed by facts is easier to agree to than a vague number.

steps.prompt: She says any raise needs sign-off, and asks for something in writing to show. What do you do?

options.text: Send a short summary of results and the market range
options.then: She reads it in two minutes. "This is clear. Thank you."

options.text: Send a long email about how hard you've worked lately
options.then: It's a lot to read. She can't find the results.

options.text: Say a good worker shouldn't need to prove anything
options.then: She pauses. The meeting ends with no next step.

options.text: Promise to send something later when you have time
options.then: Days pass. The moment cools and the ask fades.

steps.why: A short, clear summary makes the decision easy.

scenarios.debrief: Evidence of your wins plus the market rate is what makes a raise ask land.
scenarios.relearn: Back a raise ask with concrete wins and the market rate, not a vague feeling.

scenarios.hook: A new role pays the same but offers a skill that's clearly in demand.

steps.prompt: You compare it with your current job. What do you weigh?

options.text: Earning power over time, plus today's pay
options.then: You weigh both, and the skill starts to look like real value.

options.text: Only what lands in your account this month
options.then: The pay is equal, so it looks like a tie, and staying feels easier.

options.text: Which brand name sounds better on a resume
options.then: The brand sounds good. It says little about what you'll learn.

options.text: What your friends think of the move
options.then: Opinions split. None of them know your field.

steps.why: A skill in demand can grow your earning power beyond today's number.

steps.prompt: You like the skill but worry it might not pay off. What do you do?

options.text: Go for it on a hunch, without checking
options.then: You lean toward yes. It feels exciting, and a bit shaky.

options.text: Lean toward staying, since change feels risky
options.then: Staying feels safe. The skill question keeps nagging you.

options.text: See how many roles want it and what they pay
options.then: You find plenty of listings, and most pay more than you earn.

options.text: Ask the recruiter whether the skill is valuable
options.then: She says it's very valuable. She is also trying to fill the role.

steps.why: Checking demand and pay replaces a guess with facts.

steps.prompt: The new company formally offers you the role. How do you handle the pay?

options.text: Take the same pay and never mention it again
options.then: You start. The pay stays the same even as your skill grows.

options.text: Ask about a review date tied to the new skill
options.then: She says six months. You note what good looks like by then.

options.text: Demand a much higher salary to start right away
options.then: She sounds surprised. The offer is now in question.

options.text: Accept and assume a raise will just happen
options.then: Nothing is planned. Six months on, no one mentions it.

steps.why: A review date tied to the skill links your pay to your growth.

scenarios.debrief: Earning power grows with skills: sometimes the smarter pay move is the skill.
scenarios.relearn: Weigh a role's skill and future earning power, not just today's salary.

items.text: A monthly payslip you can read

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds your earning power, or doesn't?

'Women earn for extras, not the family'
A real pay gap is worth closing

Threatening to quit on the spot

scenarios.relearn: Research, results, timing and peers are smart prep; blurting or threatening is a misstep.

items.text: Your salary in your own account
Letting someone else 'handle all of it'
Never seeing your own pay details

scenarios.affirm: A pay ask is a learnable script: practising it makes the real one far easier.
scenarios.relearn: A polite pay ask is a normal, practisable professional conversation.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your income landing in your own account is a quiet kind of independence. Sit with that?
scenarios.affirm: Your earnings in your own name are a real foundation of independence.
scenarios.relearn: Your income in your own account is a foundation of independence.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a skill that's genuinely yours travels with you to any job. Worth investing in?
scenarios.affirm: A skill you own is portable earning power no employer can take back.
scenarios.relearn: A skill that's yours is portable earning power across any job.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'I don't just have to accept this pay' is a fair thing to feel. Recognise it?
scenarios.affirm: You don't have to silently accept a number: asking is a legitimate, empowering stance.
scenarios.relearn: 'I don't have to just accept this pay' is a fair, empowering stance.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: finance and fair pay are learnable by someone exactly like you, not a born talent. Believe that?
scenarios.affirm: Pay literacy is learnable by anyone: it's homework and practice, not a gift you're born with.
scenarios.relearn: Pay literacy is learnable by anyone, not a born talent.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: comparing pay notes with people you trust isn't gossip: it's how unfairness gets caught. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Sharing pay info with people you trust is how quiet pay gaps get spotted.
scenarios.relearn: Comparing pay with trusted peers is how unfairness gets caught.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two manipulative pay lines a fair job would never use.

scene.text: "Your salary's in writing: gross, deductions, in-hand."
"Pay a small joining fee and the high salary's yours."
"We can revisit pay at your review."
"Tell no one your pay: it's strictly secret here."
"Your contract lists the full breakdown."

scenarios.why: A joining fee is a scam and forced pay secrecy hides unfairness.
scenarios.relearn: A joining fee and forced pay secrecy are manipulation, not fair pay.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that quietly talk you out of fair pay.

scene.text: "I researched the market rate for this role."
"Asking for more would just make me look greedy."
"I'll bring my results to the conversation."
"I should be grateful and never bring up money."
"A polite ask is normal; the worst is a 'no'."

scenarios.why: 'It's greedy' and 'just be grateful' are the self-talk that keeps you underpaid.
scenarios.relearn: 'It's greedy' and 'just be grateful' talk you out of fair pay.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two job-scam red flags among these offer lines.

scene.text: "We'll send a written offer and contract."
"Just share your OTP to 'verify' your salary account."
"Salary is paid monthly with a payslip."
"Pay ₹2000 now to lock this high-paying seat."
"You can ask us anything about the role."

scenarios.why: Real jobs never need your OTP or an upfront payment: both are classic scam asks.
scenarios.relearn: A job asking for your OTP or an upfront fee is a scam: never share or pay.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two gendered pay myths hiding among these lines.

scene.text: "Same role should mean the same rate."
"Her salary's just pocket money, so it's fine if it's low."
"Knowing your worth is research anyone can do."
"Pay talks are really for the men to handle."
"A real pay gap is worth naming and closing."

scenarios.why: 'Just pocket money' and 'pay talks are for men' are gendered myths that keep women underpaid.
scenarios.relearn: 'Just pocket money' and 'pay talks are for men' are myths, not truths.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that misread a payslip.

scene.text: "Net pay is what actually reaches my account."
"My gross is exactly what I take home."
"Provident fund is saving deducted now."
"Deductions are just made-up lines I can ignore."
"CTC is bigger than my in-hand amount."

scenarios.why: Gross isn't take-home, and deductions are real: misreading both leads to nasty surprises.
scenarios.relearn: Gross isn't take-home and deductions are real; misreading a payslip surprises you.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two 'too good to be true' earning traps here.

scene.text: "Steady pay that grows as my skills grow."
"Earn ₹50000 a week from home, no skills needed."
"A clear contract and monthly payslip."
"Recruit three friends and your 'salary' doubles."
"Pay tied to real work I actually do."

scenarios.why: Huge effortless pay and 'recruit to double it' are scam patterns, not real earning.
scenarios.relearn: Huge effortless pay and recruit-to-double offers are scams, not real earning.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two high-pressure tactics rushing you to accept low pay.

scene.text: "Take your time to think the offer over."
"Decide in the next hour or the offer's gone."
"Happy to share the pay breakdown in writing."
"Don't ask around. Just trust us on the number."
"You're welcome to compare other offers first."

scenarios.why: A forced deadline and 'don't ask around' are pressure tactics, not fair pay.
scenarios.relearn: A forced deadline and 'don't ask around' are pressure tactics to rush a low offer.

scenarios.hook: "A wife's salary is just pocket money; the household runs on his."

myth.un: A wife's salary is just pocket money.
myth.re: Her income is real income and her own to decide on, equal to any earner's.
myth.why: Calling it 'pocket money' is a way to dismiss her financial say.

scenarios.relearn: A woman's earnings are real income and hers to decide on, not 'pocket money'.

scenarios.hook: "If he pays for everything, it's romantic that I don't touch money."

myth.un: It's romantic to never deal with money yourself.
myth.re: Knowing and accessing your own money is independence; never touching it is a quiet vulnerability.
myth.why: Not knowing your finances leaves you stuck if things go wrong.

scenarios.relearn: Knowing your own money is independence, not unromantic.

scenarios.hook: "Real love means sharing one account and one password."

myth.un: Love means one shared account and password.
myth.re: Fair money means shared decisions and transparency, while each keeps their own access too.
myth.why: Sharing everything but your own access removes your safety net.

scenarios.relearn: Fair money is shared decisions plus each keeping their own access.

scenarios.hook: "A good partner manages the money so you never have to learn it."

myth.un: A good partner means you never learn money yourself.
myth.re: Money basics are learnable by anyone, and both partners keeping the knowledge is what's fair.
myth.why: Keeping you in the dark, even kindly, is still dependence.

scenarios.relearn: Both partners keep money knowledge; staying in the dark isn't safety.

scenarios.hook: "Asking your partner about the joint money means you don't trust them."

myth.un: Asking about the joint money shows distrust.
myth.re: Both partners knowing where the money is, is normal transparency, not suspicion.
myth.why: Open books are how fair money works; secrecy is the warning sign.

scenarios.relearn: Both knowing the finances is normal transparency, not distrust.

scenarios.hook: "He stopped me working because he earns enough, that's him providing."

myth.un: Being stopped from working is just being provided for.
myth.re: Blocking a partner from earning is economic control, a recognised form of abuse, not providing.
myth.why: Cutting off your income removes your means to leave.

scenarios.relearn: Blocking you from earning is economic control, not 'providing'.

scenarios.hook: "Dowry pressure is a family matter, not financial abuse."

myth.un: Dowry pressure is just a family matter.
myth.re: Demanding money or goods as a marriage condition is economic coercion, and demanding dowry is illegal in India.
myth.why: Naming it matters; it's pressure on you, not tradition you owe.

scenarios.relearn: Dowry demands are economic coercion and illegal, not 'family matters'.

scenarios.hook: "If I keep my own savings secret from my partner, I'm being shady."

myth.un: Keeping your own savings means you're being shady.
myth.re: Keeping your own account and an emergency fund is independence everyone is entitled to.
myth.why: Your own safety net is healthy, not a betrayal.

scenarios.relearn: Keeping your own account and emergency fund is independence, not deceit.

scenarios.hook: "Once you marry, your salary should go straight to the in-laws."

myth.un: After marriage your salary belongs to the in-laws.
myth.re: Your earnings are yours; sharing is a choice you make, not a handover others can demand.
myth.why: Demanding your whole income is financial control, not a custom you owe.

scenarios.relearn: Your earnings stay yours; sharing is your choice, not a demand.

scenarios.hook: "He checks every UPI payment I make so we 'stay on budget'."

myth.un: A partner checking your every payment keeps you on budget.
myth.re: Policing every rupee you spend is financial control; a shared budget is agreed together, not surveilled.
myth.why: Monitoring isn't budgeting; it's control over your choices.

scenarios.relearn: Policing your every spend is control; a real budget is agreed, not surveilled.

scenarios.hook: "Letting your husband be the only name on the home loan protects you."

myth.un: Being left off the loan and assets protects you.
myth.re: Knowing what's in your name and being on shared assets protects your stake; being kept off can leave you with nothing.
myth.why: Invisible ownership is a vulnerability, not a shield.

scenarios.relearn: Know what's in your name; being kept off shared assets is a risk, not protection.

scenarios.hook: "If you love someone, you give them your ATM PIN and OTPs."

myth.un: Love means sharing your PIN and OTPs.
myth.re: Your PIN and OTP are yours alone; sharing them isn't proof of love and a real partner won't demand it.
myth.why: Handing over access is how control, and fraud, get a foothold.

scenarios.relearn: Your PIN and OTP stay yours; demanding them isn't love.

scenarios.hook: "A woman who insists on her own bank account doesn't trust the marriage."

myth.un: Wanting your own account means you doubt the marriage.
myth.re: Your own bank account is the foundation of financial independence, for everyone, married or not.
myth.why: Independence and trust aren't opposites; both can be true.

scenarios.relearn: Your own account is the base of independence, married or not.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two red flags of financial control in this relationship.

They take your salary and hand back an 'allowance'

You openly discuss what you each earn

scenarios.relearn: Taking your earnings or blocking your account is financial control.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that are economic abuse, not love.

scene.text: "Let's plan our savings goal together this year."
"You don't need a job, just ask me for money."
"Keep your own emergency fund, it's smart."
"Sign here, don't read it, just trust me."
"Tell me if a bill feels too tight for you."

scenarios.why: Cutting off your income and making you sign blind are economic control; the others respect your independence.
scenarios.relearn: Cutting off your income or making you sign blind is economic abuse.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that pressure you into money you don't owe.

scene.text: "Take a loan in your name to prove you love me."
"Let's split the rent fairly between us."
"A real wife gives her whole salary over."
"Want to set a savings goal together?"
"Your money is yours to share or not."

scenarios.why: Coerced debt 'to prove love' and 'give your whole salary' are pressure; the rest are fair.
scenarios.relearn: Pressure to take debt or hand over all your pay is coercion, not love.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two demands that are control dressed as care.

scene.text: "Forward me every OTP so I can manage our money."
"Shall we review our budget together on Sunday?"
"You can't go to work; I'll provide everything."
"Keep your salary in your own account, of course."
"Let's agree who pays which bill this month."

scenarios.why: Demanding your OTPs and forbidding you to work are control; the rest keep your access and choice intact.
scenarios.relearn: Demanding your OTPs or forbidding work is control, not care.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two signs a partner is making you depend on them.

scene.text: They want you to keep earning and saving
They pressure you to quit your job
They want you both to know the finances
They hide all accounts and debts from you
They're fine with your own savings

scenarios.why: Pressuring you to quit and hiding all finances build dependence; the rest support independence.
scenarios.relearn: Pressure to quit and hidden finances are warning signs of dependence.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two red flags in how this partner handles a scam.

scene.text: They ask for your bank OTP 'to fix it'

They blame you and say you must pay alone
They check the message calmly with you
They agree never to share an OTP

scenarios.relearn: Never share an OTP; a fair partner reports scams together, not blames you.

Reading any document before you sign it

You both can see the savings
Only they can touch the money

scenarios.hook: Sort each marriage money belief: a healthy frame, or a control myth?

"Give your whole salary to the family."
