scenarios.hook: You've never had a bank account in your own name, and a friend offers to walk you through opening one.

steps.prompt: Tara has a free afternoon on Thursday. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll do it later, once you earn more
options.then: Tara shrugs. "Okay, but the offer stands." It doesn't get done.

options.text: Say a family member's account is fine for now
options.then: Tara raises an eyebrow. "It's still not yours."

options.text: Ask her to open one for you and hold it
options.then: She laughs. "It has to be you at the bank."

options.text: Say yes, and open one in your own name
options.then: Tara gives a thumbs up. "Bring ID and a photo. It's simple."

steps.why: An account in your own name is the foundation: open it now and grow into it.

steps.prompt: Your mother says she can just add you to hers. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her, and still open one in your own name
options.then: She sighs. "As you wish. Just be careful."

options.text: Say yes, since it saves a trip to the bank
options.then: She smiles. You'll share her account, and her rules.

options.text: Say you'll think about it while you decide
options.then: She nods. It takes weeks, and a nudge from Tara, before you open one.

options.text: Say yes now, and open your own later
options.then: She agrees. The second account tends not to happen.

steps.why: An account in your name means the access and decisions are yours.

steps.prompt: A cousin asks to borrow your card and PIN for an online order. What do you do?

options.text: Lend it, since she's family
options.then: She uses it. You find out the amount afterwards.

options.text: Say no politely, and keep your PIN to yourself
options.then: She pouts. "Fine. I'll ask someone else."

options.text: Lend the card, and tell her the PIN later
options.then: She says thanks. You spend the day worrying.

options.text: Say yes, but only if she sends you the order details
options.then: She sends them. The card is still in her hands.

steps.why: Your card and PIN are yours alone, whoever is asking.

scenarios.debrief: An account in your own name is the foundation: open it now, grow into it later.
scenarios.relearn: Open your own account now; it's the foundation of independence.

scenarios.hook: A partner suggests you stop working since they earn enough for both of you.

steps.prompt: Your contract is up for renewal, and they bring it up again. What do you do?

options.text: Renew it, and say your income is your safety net
options.then: They look puzzled. "A safety net from what?" But they hear you.

options.text: Let it lapse, since they've offered to cover everything
options.then: They're delighted. Your income ends on the last day of the month.

options.text: Ask them to decide whether you should renew
options.then: They choose to let it go. You realise you've handed over the call.

options.text: Renew it, and don't tell them until later
options.then: They find out a week later, and feel shut out of the news.

steps.why: Your own income is your safety net, independent of how much you trust anyone.

steps.prompt: They say they'll put a monthly amount into your account instead. What do you do?

options.text: Accept, since the amount sounds generous
options.then: The first transfer is generous. You wait for the next one each month.

options.text: Say you'd rather keep earning and share costs fairly
options.then: They sigh. "I'm only trying to help." They ask how you'd share them.

options.text: Ask for the amount in writing, then stop working
options.then: They're amused, but they agree. Your pay check stops anyway.

options.text: Ask them to raise the amount before you agree
options.then: They raise it slightly. It remains their money, given to you.

steps.why: Money given to you is a gift on their terms, while your own pay is yours to keep.

steps.prompt: A former colleague offers you a job with more hours and better pay. What do you do?

options.text: Turn it down to keep them happy
options.then: They hug you. The offer goes to someone else.

options.text: Ask them whether you're allowed to take it
options.then: They think about it. "If you want to." You feel smaller.

options.text: Look at it on its merits, and talk it through with them
options.then: They frown at the hours, and agree to help with the week.

options.text: Take it without telling them at all
options.then: You sign the papers. A week later, the silence shows.

steps.why: A job offer is your career decision, and you can make it with your partner, not for them.

scenarios.debrief: Your own income is your safety net: independent of how much you trust anyone.
scenarios.relearn: Keep your own income; it's your safety net regardless of trust.

scenarios.hook: You could lean on family money indefinitely or build a small income of your own, and leaning is easier.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says a print shop needs a part-time helper. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since family already covers your costs
options.then: You spend the evenings relaxing. Your own income stays at zero.

options.text: Ask about hours, and take it if classes allow
options.then: The shop wants three evenings a week. It fits, just.

options.text: Say you'll apply once the semester is over
options.then: The semester ends. The position has already been filled.

options.text: Take it for a week and quit if it gets tiring
options.then: The first shift is long. You start thinking about the exit.

steps.why: Even a small part-time income starts independence that family money can't give.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a small paid job comes your way, and the pay is less than you hoped. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it, since it's really not worth the effort
options.then: You're free on Saturdays. Your own income stays at zero.

options.text: Ask family to top you up so you needn't bother
options.then: They agree easily. The habit of asking gets stronger.

options.text: Take it, and put a fixed slice in your own account
options.then: The slice is small. It's the first money that's yours alone.

options.text: Take it, and spend it all, since it's so little
options.then: A fine evening out, and nothing left of it by Sunday.

steps.why: Saving a fixed slice from the first pay builds a habit, even when the pay is small.

steps.prompt: Your father says the family may struggle with next semester's fees. What do you do?

options.text: Say nothing about money, so he doesn't expect your help
options.then: He doesn't know what you could offer. You carry a quiet guilt with you.

options.text: Tell him to sort it out, since you're busy
options.then: He looks tired. The problem falls back on him.

options.text: Offer every rupee you have without checking the numbers
options.then: He's moved, and so worried. Whatever you have is gone in a week.

options.text: Share what you have and your plan, and look at options together
options.then: He's surprised and touched. Together you sketch what could work.

steps.why: Having your own money lets you help your family by choice, with a clear plan.

scenarios.debrief: Even slow progress toward your own income beats indefinite reliance.
scenarios.relearn: Build your own income, even slowly: it's real independence.

scenarios.hook: Your marriage is being arranged, and the plan is that you'll stop studying and not work after.

steps.prompt: The families meet again to settle the plan. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself speaking up would look ungrateful
options.then: The thought feels heavy. You sense the plan is being fixed around you.

options.text: Think the family must know best about your future
options.then: It's a comforting thought. It also leaves your own wishes out of the plan.

options.text: Say keeping your own income matters to you
options.then: The room goes quiet. Your father asks everyone to hear you out.

options.text: Tell your mother privately and ask her to say it
options.then: She listens and says she'll try. The meeting starts before she can raise it.

steps.why: Naming your own income early makes it a shared plan. Wanting it is never selfish or your fault.

steps.prompt: His family says they 'don't need' a working wife. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself you can sort out work after the wedding
options.then: It feels like a way to keep the peace. The wedding date comes up first.

options.text: Think stopping for now won't matter if you can restart
options.then: It sounds harmless. Later is easy to promise and hard to claim.

options.text: Think it's fair that your match should decide
options.then: It sounds fair to you. It also makes it their decision.

options.text: Tell your mother, then say working is your choice
options.then: Your mother stands with you. His family looks surprised. "Fair. You two can talk."

steps.why: Working is your choice, and a trusted person beside you helps. Wanting it is never your fault.

steps.prompt: You get to speak to your match alone. What do you ask?

options.text: How they see money, work and decisions in a marriage
options.then: Your match thinks. "I've never been asked that. Let me think."

options.text: What they earn, and what they expect you to earn
options.then: They answer, and ask the same. It's a start, and a narrow one.

options.text: Whether they like your family
options.then: They laugh. "They seem nice." Nothing new about the plan.

options.text: If they can talk their mother round for you
options.then: They say they'll try. The plan is still theirs to bend.

steps.why: Asking how they see money, work and decisions shows whether you're on the same page.

scenarios.debrief: Your own income and a say in your life are worth naming, early, and out loud.
scenarios.relearn: Your own income and a say in your life are worth naming early.

scenarios.hook: You keep avoiding anything about money because it feels too complicated for you.

steps.prompt: A friend asks if you want to learn budgeting together. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, since numbers aren't your thing
options.then: She shrugs. You lose a chance to learn with a friend.

options.text: Say maybe later, when you're less busy
options.then: "Sure." Later doesn't have a day attached.

options.text: Say yes, but only if she does all the work
options.then: She laughs. "Then it's not learning for you."

options.text: Say yes, and start with what a budget is
options.then: She grins. "A budget is just a plan for your money."

steps.why: Starting with one simple idea makes money feel learnable.

steps.prompt: Later, a budgeting article lands in your feed, and you meet a word you don't know. What do you do?

options.text: Look it up, jot it down, and carry on
options.then: It takes a minute. The page makes more sense afterwards.

options.text: Close the page, since you knew it was too hard
options.then: The page closes. The idea that it's too hard stays.

options.text: Ask a friend to explain everything for you
options.then: She explains it well. You forget it by the next day.

options.text: Copy someone's budget without understanding it
options.then: It looks tidy. It doesn't fit your real spending.

steps.why: Looking up one word at a time builds understanding, not just copies.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks you to help plan a trip budget. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll let her do it all
options.then: She does it well. You learned nothing new.

options.text: Try it, and ask questions where you get stuck
options.then: You make a list and ask two questions. It comes together.

options.text: Say you can't, since you're bad at this
options.then: She sighs. "You're not. You just haven't tried."

options.text: Put in a number quickly and hope for the best
options.then: The number is a guess. The trip runs short of money.

steps.why: Trying it and asking questions proves the money basics are learnable by anyone.

scenarios.debrief: Learn one basic at a time; the money basics are learnable by anyone.
scenarios.relearn: Learn the basics one at a time; they're learnable by anyone.

scenarios.hook: Your first salary has landed, and the family has views on where it should go.

steps.prompt: Your uncle suggests you hand the whole salary to the family. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it in your own account, and offer a set amount
options.then: He's a little surprised. "A set amount? Hmm. Tell me the amount."

options.text: Think handing it all over would show respect
options.then: You picture asking for cash each time, and waiting days for it.

options.text: Think half to the family and half in cash is fair
options.then: You picture the cash at home going within weeks.

options.text: Ask your mother to hold it until you decide
options.then: She agrees. Weeks later, you still haven't decided.

steps.why: Your salary in your own account lets you help by choice, not by demand.

steps.prompt: Your aunt says a good child gives everything and keeps nothing. What do you do?

options.text: Give a little more, to show respect
options.then: She beams. Your contribution has crept up again.

options.text: Say you'll help by choice, and name how much
options.then: She purses her lips. Your father adds that it sounds fair.

options.text: Tell yourself a good child shouldn't answer back
options.then: The thought stays with you. The question isn't answered.

options.text: Say your salary is yours and nobody should ask
options.then: She's offended. The argument reaches the whole family.

steps.why: Helping is your choice, and so is the amount. Keeping your own earnings is never wrong.

steps.prompt: A month later, a family member needs money for an urgent bill. What do you do?

options.text: Give whatever they ask for, without checking
options.then: It's gone in a day. You've left little for your own rent.

options.text: Say you'll never give anything, so don't ask again
options.then: They're hurt, and the whole family hears. The real need is still there.

options.text: Help from your own account, with an amount you decide
options.then: They thank you warmly. Your budget still has room.

options.text: Ask them to wait until your next salary
options.then: The bill is urgent. The wait makes everyone uncomfortable.

steps.why: Helping your family is a choice that works best from your own account.

scenarios.debrief: Helping your family is a choice: it works best from your own account, on your terms.
scenarios.relearn: Keep your earnings in your own account; contribute by choice.

scenarios.hook: You've started thinking about having a little money that is only yours, just in case.

steps.prompt: You notice you couldn't reach any money quickly if you had to leave. What do you do?

options.text: Assume you'd figure it out if it ever happened
options.then: The thought passes. The gap is still there.

options.text: Decide to start a small fund only you can reach
options.then: You decide the first amount. It takes a little courage.

options.text: Keep spare cash in a drawer the family knows about
options.then: It's easy to reach. So is it for everyone at home.

options.text: Ask a relative to hold your money, just in case
options.then: She agrees warmly. You can't reach it without asking her.

steps.why: A fund only you can reach gives you real choices, and planning ahead isn't wrong.

steps.prompt: You have a little money to set aside. Where do you keep it?

options.text: In cash in a drawer that others share
options.then: It's handy. A few notes vanish by the weekend.

options.text: With a friend who says she'll return it any time
options.then: She means it. She's also not always reachable.

options.text: In an account only you can open, with your own PIN
options.then: You note the steps. Your name is on it, and only yours.

options.text: You don't set anything aside this month
options.then: The month goes by. The gap stays as wide as before.

steps.why: An account in your own name keeps the fund safe and within your reach.

steps.prompt: A family member asks why you've become careful with money. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself showing them everything would clear suspicion
options.then: You imagine them looking, then asking to borrow some of it.

options.text: Think spending it on something visible would stop questions
options.then: You imagine the money gone, and your cushion with it.

options.text: Think handing your savings to them would settle things
options.then: You imagine them thanking you, and your reach to the money gone.

options.text: Say it's a savings habit, and tell a trusted friend the real reason
options.then: Your friend says you can call 181 or 1091 for help planning safely, whenever you like.

steps.why: A private fund is smart, and it's never your fault if home doesn't feel safe. Help exists.

scenarios.debrief: Money only you can reach is the difference between feeling stuck and being able to choose.
scenarios.relearn: A small fund only you can access is real freedom to choose.

scenarios.hook: A mate is hurt by how his girlfriend handles her money, and you think he's reading it wrong.

steps.prompt: Dev tells you she's opened her own savings account without asking him. What do you do?

options.text: Agree that it's a bit insulting of her
options.then: Dev nods. He feels backed up, and a little more hurt.

options.text: Say it's their business and change the subject
options.then: Dev shrugs. He's still stewing when the subject changes.

options.text: Tell him: her own money is smart, not distrust
options.then: Dev scowls. "Smart? She's hiding it from me." But he keeps listening.

options.text: Tell him to ask her to prove she trusts him
options.then: Dev likes the idea. He isn't sure how to ask without a fight.

steps.why: Her own savings are a safety net. They say nothing about whether she trusts him.

steps.prompt: Dev says she even keeps an emergency fund. What do you say?

options.text: Say she probably expects him to let her down
options.then: Dev's jaw tightens. He says nothing more.

options.text: Say it's a bit cold of her, to be honest
options.then: Dev nods slowly. "Right? That's how it feels."

options.text: Say all girls do that, so don't take it personally
options.then: He laughs and relaxes. The idea that it's a "girl thing" hangs in the air.

options.text: Say a safety net protects both, and ask if he has one
options.then: He pauses. "I don't. Maybe I should. But hers still bugs me."

steps.why: An emergency fund protects both people. It isn't a verdict on the partner.

steps.prompt: Later, Dev texts to ask if he should just tell her to close hers. What do you say?

options.text: No. Tell him it's hers, and not about trust
options.then: Dev texts back: "Hmm. I hadn't thought of it as just hers."

options.text: Yes. Tell her to close it to show trust
options.then: Dev replies with a thumbs up. The argument waits for her to hear it.

options.text: Tell him to ask to see her balance instead
options.then: Dev texts back: "Isn't that the same as checking up on her?"

options.text: Say nothing and let him work it out
options.then: Dev waits for a line that doesn't come.

steps.why: Her savings are hers and no verdict on him. Seeing that keeps trust alive.

scenarios.debrief: A partner's own savings are independence, not distrust: they protect both people.
scenarios.relearn: A partner keeping her own money is smart independence, not distrust.

scenarios.hook: Your employer has a plan for how you'll be paid, "to keep it safe".

steps.prompt: Your employer says your wages will go to your uncle. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself your uncle will keep it safe
options.then: It sounds safe. You'd be relying on your uncle to hand over your money.

options.text: Ask him to send half to your uncle and half to you
options.then: He agrees. Half your pay still goes through your uncle.

options.text: Ask your uncle to sort it out with the employer
options.then: Your uncle says he will. Your uncle will also decide.

options.text: Ask to be paid into your own account
options.then: He frowns. "Everyone else is fine with it." But he listens.

steps.why: Wages that reach you directly are yours. Your own account is how you keep them.

steps.prompt: A few weeks on, he says the bank is too far and it's simpler to pay everything in cash to your uncle. What do you do?

options.text: Ask to be paid yourself, by account or cash with a slip
options.then: He sighs. "I'll see what I can do."

options.text: Think cash to family sounds practical
options.then: It's easier for him. You wouldn't see a record.

options.text: Ask your uncle to keep a notebook of every payment
options.then: Your uncle agrees. The notebook is his, not yours.

options.text: Ask him to pay you a month in advance instead
options.then: He laughs. "That won't work."

steps.why: Wages that reach you directly, with a record, show exactly what you earned and were paid.

steps.prompt: Payday comes and the amount is less than agreed. What do you do?

options.text: Assume you must have misread it somehow
options.then: You recheck. The numbers don't change.

options.text: Ask for a written breakdown, and tell a trusted person
options.then: Your trusted person says you're right to ask, and offers to come with you.

options.text: Shout at him at the gate in front of everyone
options.then: He's furious. Others watch, and he calls security.

options.text: Ask your uncle to go and argue it out for you
options.then: Your uncle goes. He comes back with a vague reply.

steps.why: It's never your fault. You're entitled to know your pay: ask for a written breakdown and tell a trusted person.

scenarios.debrief: Your wages should reach you: your own account is how you keep what you earn.
scenarios.relearn: Get paid into your own account so your wages stay yours.

scenarios.hook: Where you live has stopped feeling like your own choice.

steps.prompt: You feel stuck where you live, and can't picture affording to leave. What do you do?

options.text: Start building income and a small fund now
options.then: You pick a first small step. It feels like a door opening.

options.text: Tell yourself there's no other option
options.then: The thought settles in. Nothing around you changes.

options.text: Wait for things to get better on their own
options.then: Weeks pass. The feeling stays exactly where it was.

options.text: Daydream about a big win that would fix everything
options.then: It's a pleasant hour. Nothing has moved afterwards.

steps.why: Building income and savings now is the power to choose later.

steps.prompt: A chance comes up for some extra paid hours. What do you do?

options.text: Skip them, since it's too much trouble
options.then: You keep your evenings. Your fund stays at zero.

options.text: Take them, and keep the pay in your own account
options.then: The first payment is small. It's entirely yours.

options.text: Think the pay should go to the household anyway
options.then: You picture it vanishing into household costs. Your fund would still be zero.

options.text: Wait for a better-paying offer
options.then: The better offer doesn't come. The small one goes to someone else.

steps.why: Small extra income in your own account starts to make other choices possible.

steps.prompt: A relative says you should be grateful and never think of leaving. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself you should be grateful and stop wishing
options.then: It's a heavy thought. The wish comes back at night.

options.text: Argue loudly and say you'll go tonight
options.then: The house goes silent. Without a plan, tonight is hard to imagine.

options.text: Keep building quietly, and tell someone you trust how you feel
options.then: Your friend listens. "That sounds hard. I'm glad you told me."

options.text: Promise yourself you'll decide one day
options.then: The day stays vague. The feeling gets heavier.

steps.why: Money gives you choices, and feeling stuck is never your fault. Support exists.

scenarios.debrief: Money is the power to walk away: build it quietly, before you ever need it.
scenarios.relearn: Build income and savings now; they're the power to walk away.

scenarios.hook: First time living away from home, you suddenly control your own money and it's a bit overwhelming.

steps.prompt: Your allowance lands in your own account in your first month away. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your parents to control it again
options.then: They take it back, relieved. You feel smaller somehow.

options.text: List what you must pay first, then see what's left
options.then: It takes ten minutes. The remainder looks small but clear.

options.text: Spend freely, since it feels like freedom
options.then: The first week is wonderful. By the third, you're counting coins.

options.text: Send it all to a friend for safekeeping
options.then: She agrees. She's now responsible for money she didn't ask for.

steps.why: Listing needs first turns a scary lump of money into a plan.

steps.prompt: Midway through the month, you're nearly out. What do you do?

options.text: Ask your parents for extra without looking
options.then: They send it. You learn nothing about where it went.

options.text: Feel bad and stop checking your account
options.then: The dread grows. The account is still there.

options.text: Track where it went, and adjust next month
options.then: You see it: too many snacks and one big treat. You adjust.

options.text: Put a month's shopping on an easy EMI
options.then: Approval takes a minute. Now two payments are due monthly.

steps.why: Tracking where money went is how you learn to manage it.

steps.prompt: Your parents ask how you're managing. What do you say?

options.text: Say everything is fine, and leave it there
options.then: They believe you. You still have the same questions.

options.text: Ask them to take the money back
options.then: They hesitate. "Are you sure? You were doing well."

options.text: Blame the prices and the hostel
options.then: They sigh and say prices are hard everywhere.

options.text: Share what you learned and what you'll change
options.then: They're quietly proud. "You're figuring it out."

steps.why: Controlling your own money is a skill you can grow into, one month at a time.

scenarios.debrief: Controlling your own money is a skill you grow into: you're allowed to be a financial adult.
scenarios.relearn: Controlling your own money is a learnable skill; you can be a financial adult.

scenarios.hook: Someone close pressures you to put a big loan in your name 'because you have the cleaner record.'

steps.prompt: Your cousin says the loan is easier in your name. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself signing is the quickest way to avoid a fight
options.then: It feels like the easy way out. You haven't seen a repayment plan.

options.text: Think a repayment plan from him would make it safe
options.then: A plan on paper still leaves the debt in your name if he misses payments.

options.text: Decline, because a loan in your name is your debt
options.then: He looks annoyed. "It's only paperwork." You stay steady.

options.text: Ask your parents to decide it all for you
options.then: They say it's up to you. You're back at the start.

steps.why: A loan in your name is your debt and your risk, whoever spends the money.

steps.prompt: A few days on, he says you're selfish, and family always helps family. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself you're being selfish and should reconsider
options.then: You feel your footing slip.

options.text: Think guaranteeing only half would be a fair middle
options.then: It sounds fair. You'd owe that half if he stopped paying.

options.text: Tell yourself it can wait until after the festival
options.then: It feels like breathing room. The pressure would return after it.

options.text: Offer other help, but not a loan in your name
options.then: He scoffs. "Other ways don't pay the bills."

steps.why: You can help in many ways. Putting a loan in your name is not a test of loyalty.

steps.prompt: He says he'll tell the whole family you let him down. What do you do?

options.text: Stay firm, and tell a trusted person
options.then: Your friend says that's pressure, and you can call 181 or 1091 for advice.

options.text: Think a smaller loan might calm things
options.then: It sounds like a fair middle. It would still be yours to repay.

options.text: Tell everyone first in a long message
options.then: The family chat explodes. It helps no one.

options.text: Tell yourself he'll drop it if you stay silent
options.then: The silence feels safer. The pressure wouldn't go away.

steps.why: It's not your fault, and you don't owe anyone a loan. Help exists.

scenarios.debrief: Debt in your name is your risk: guarding your own footing is independence, not betrayal.
scenarios.relearn: A loan in your name is your debt and risk; guarding your footing is independence.

scenarios.hook: You're the first in your family in college, and money has suddenly become yours to manage.

steps.prompt: Your first stipend lands. What do you do with it first?

options.text: Spend it all, and save next year
options.then: Next year's plan arrives with another spending spree.

options.text: Send all of it home, and keep nothing
options.then: Home is grateful. By the tenth, you're out of your own money.

options.text: Keep it all in cash, and see what happens
options.then: It goes quickly, in small bills. You can't say where.

options.text: Move a fixed slice into your own account
options.then: The slice is small. It's the first money that's only yours.

steps.why: Saving a fixed slice from the start builds the habit that grows.

steps.prompt: A senior says a 'guaranteed doubling' scheme worked for him. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, and check with a bank or trusted source
options.then: He shrugs. The bank says guaranteed doubling is a warning sign.

options.text: Put in a little, just to see if it works
options.then: The small amount disappears. The senior stops replying.

options.text: Ask him to prove it works before you decide
options.then: He sends a screenshot. It proves nothing.

options.text: Put in more, since he really swears by it
options.then: He's pleased. You watch the balance go, and it doesn't come back.

steps.why: Guaranteed doubling is a scam sign. Real wealth builds slowly.

steps.prompt: Next month your stipend is late and money is tight. What do you do?

options.text: Decide saving can wait until things ease
options.then: It's easier this month. The habit never gets started.

options.text: Cut wants, stretch what you have, and start a small pot
options.then: The month is tight but doable. You see why a small pot of your own matters.

options.text: Borrow the gap on an easy EMI for now
options.then: Approval is instant. The EMI outlasts the problem.

options.text: Skip meals to stretch what you have
options.then: You hold out for days. You feel weaker, and it isn't sustainable.

steps.why: Cutting wants and building a small pot carries you through a tight patch without debt.

scenarios.debrief: A stipend in your own account, with a fixed saving slice, is independence starting now.
scenarios.relearn: Save a fixed slice of your income into your own account from now.

scenarios.hook: Home isn't an easy place to be, and you wonder what money of your own would change.

steps.prompt: You dread the holidays at home. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly start building your own money
options.then: You write a first step. It feels small, and entirely yours.

options.text: Tell yourself you just have to cope with it
options.then: You brace yourself. The dread doesn't lessen.

options.text: Wait for someone else to come and fix it
options.then: You wait. Nobody knows what needs fixing.

options.text: Think money of your own isn't for someone like you
options.then: You let the thought settle. The holidays still get closer, and nothing is yours.

steps.why: Your own income and savings turn coping into choosing.

steps.prompt: A paid internship comes up for the holidays. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself staying home to keep the peace matters more
options.then: The thought is heavy. Your own income stays at zero.

options.text: Apply, and keep the pay in your own account
options.then: You send the application. It's a first real step.

options.text: Apply, but plan to hand over the pay
options.then: You send the application, and plan to hand the pay to the household. You'd have no savings of your own.

options.text: Think you should only apply if home approves
options.then: You picture a week of waiting. The position might close.

steps.why: Even a short paid stint builds savings that are yours.

steps.prompt: As the holidays near, the dread builds. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself the feeling will pass if you ignore it
options.then: It might work for a day. It's louder the next.

options.text: Tell no one how hard home is, and plan to manage alone
options.then: Nobody knows what you carry, so nobody can help. The dread stays.

options.text: Talk to a counsellor or a trusted friend
options.then: They listen. You aren't alone in how you feel, and you make a plan.

options.text: Put off any plan until you earn more
options.then: It sounds sensible. The holidays arrive, and nothing has changed.

steps.why: Talking to someone you trust helps you plan, and it's never your fault if home is hard.

scenarios.debrief: Your own money turns 'I have to cope' into 'I can choose': build it for yourself.
scenarios.relearn: Your own income and savings turn coping into choosing.

scenarios.hook: Your sister has never had money of her own to manage.
scenarios.setup: She shrugs while folding clothes.

steps.prompt: Your sister says: "Why would I learn money stuff? Papa and Rahul handle it all."

options.text: "Yeah, leave that stuff to the men."
options.then: She nods, relieved. The subject closes and the cupboard door shuts.

options.text: "Your money is your freedom. Let's open an account."
options.then: She pauses. "Me, with an account? Would Papa mind?"

options.text: "At least ask Papa to show you the accounts."
options.then: "He'll say not to worry. He always does."

options.text: "That's such an outdated way to think."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "Don't start with your lectures."

steps.why: Her own account and saving habit are the start of her independence.

steps.prompt: A few days later she says: "Even if I wanted to, I wouldn't know where to start."

options.text: "Ask Rahul to set it all up. He knows this stuff."
options.then: "He'd do it in five minutes. I still wouldn't understand it."

options.text: "It's complicated. Don't stress about it. Ask Papa."
options.then: "See? That's what I said." She nods, though the question clearly still nags at her.

options.text: "Read up on every kind of investment first."
options.then: "Every kind? I'd give up by the weekend."

options.text: "An account in your name and a small monthly saving."
options.then: "That I can do." She opens a notes app and types a number.

steps.why: The basics are learnable in small steps, starting with an account in your name.

steps.prompt: Your sister says: "If I ever did open my own account, what would I tell Papa? I don't want a fight."

options.text: "You'd need Papa's permission first, I think."
options.then: She sighs. "Then it's never happening." The idea goes back in the drawer.

options.text: "Tell him you're opening it whether he likes it or not."
options.then: She goes pale. "Say that to Papa? I could never."

options.text: "Say it's a normal part of being an adult. I'll back you."
options.then: "A normal part of being an adult." She repeats it twice, then nods.

options.text: "Then skip it until you're married."
options.then: "Maybe later." The account stays unopened, and so does the subject.

steps.why: Owning your money is normal, and it helps to have someone backing you.

scenarios.relearn: Encourage the women around you to own their own money.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kavya has big news about her job and her partner Aman.
scenarios.setup: She tells you over a late lunch.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "Aman earns enough. I'm quitting next month and he'll manage everything."

options.text: "If you trust him, it's totally fine. Go ahead."
options.then: She lights up. "Right? I knew you'd understand."

options.text: "Keep some income, even part-time. It's a safety net."
options.then: She sighs. "I'm so tired I hadn't thought past quitting."

options.text: "Quitting is a big mistake. Please don't do it."
options.then: She stiffens. "You're not the one who's exhausted every day."

options.text: "Fine, but get him to promise to provide for you."
options.then: "A promise? Aman would just laugh and say of course."

steps.why: Income of your own is a safety net, however much you trust him.

steps.prompt: A few days later Kavya says: "I'm so tired of this job. Is wanting a break even allowed?"

options.text: "You'll regret it. Stick it out."
options.then: "Easy for you to say. I'm worn out."

options.text: "Take the break. Aman will cover it."
options.then: She relaxes, though the plan has no backup of her own.

options.text: "Of course. Plan the break around some income of your own."
options.then: "A little income of my own, even on a break. That feels much safer."

options.text: "Let him decide what's best for both of you."
options.then: "He'd say whatever I want to hear. That doesn't help."

steps.why: A break is fine, and a small income of your own makes it safer.

steps.prompt: Kavya says: "Aman says we may as well run everything from his account. Simpler, right?"

options.text: "Sure, it's the same money anyway. Why bother?"
options.then: "True. What's his is mine." She stops thinking about it.

options.text: "Simple, yes. Keep an account in your name too."
options.then: "Just one of mine, alongside. He can't mind that."

options.text: "That's a red flag. Break up with him right now."
options.then: She freezes. "Over an account? You're scaring me."

options.text: "Ask your parents what they think you should do."
options.then: "They'll say to do what Aman says. That's no help."

steps.why: Your own account keeps your access and your choices, whatever the set-up.

scenarios.relearn: Keeping your own income is a safety net regardless of trust.

scenarios.hook: Looking at your account, a familiar doubt creeps in.
scenarios.setup: It's a quiet evening and nobody is around.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "Money is too complicated. That's for people who studied commerce."

options.text: "You're right. This isn't for someone like me."
options.then: "Exactly. Close the app." The relief is quick, and so is the guilt.

options.text: "I'll get someone else to sort it all out."
options.then: "Good. Then you never have to look." You also never have to know.

options.text: "I can learn the basics one step at a time."
options.then: "One step? Fine. Which step?"

options.text: "I have to learn everything before I start."
options.then: "Everything? That takes years. Maybe tomorrow."

steps.why: Basics are learnable by anyone, one small step at a time.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "And if you do try, you'll get it wrong and feel silly."

options.text: "Better not to try, then."
options.then: "Safe." You also learn nothing, which quietly confirms the voice.

options.text: "Mistakes with small amounts are how I learn."
options.then: "Small amounts. I can live with that."

options.text: "I'll just copy what my friends do."
options.then: "Their rent and pay aren't yours." The copy doesn't quite fit.

options.text: "I'll wait until someone explains it all."
options.then: "Nobody is coming." The week passes with nothing learned.

steps.why: Small mistakes are cheap, and they are how everyone learns money.

steps.prompt: A few days later your balance is lower than you expected. Your inner voice asks: "So where would you even begin?"

options.text: "Note my spending for a week, then sort needs and wants."
options.then: "A week of notes. That I can do." You open a blank page.

options.text: "Watch hours of videos before I touch anything."
options.then: "Hours? You'll give up by day three."

options.text: "Jump straight to investing. That's where the money is."
options.then: "With no savings behind you? Ambitious."

options.text: "Start next month, when things calm down."
options.then: "Things never calm down." The page stays blank.

steps.why: Tracking spending for a week is a small, doable first step.

scenarios.relearn: The money basics are learnable by anyone, one step at a time.

scenarios.hook: Your salary has started coming in, and your family has opinions about it.
scenarios.setup: Your uncle raises it over dinner.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Give me your salary account details. I'll hold it. Simpler for everyone."

options.text: "Thanks, but my salary stays in my own account."
options.then: His smile tightens. "Only trying to help. Don't you trust family?"

options.text: "Isn't family money shared anyway? Maybe I'm wrong."
options.then: He smiles. "Exactly. That's why it's simplest if I hold it."

options.text: "Maybe it's rude to refuse an elder."
options.then: He nods. "Elders know these things. Send the details tonight."

options.text: "Only if you show me every transaction."
options.then: "Every transaction? That's a lot of fuss for family."

steps.why: Your salary belongs in your own account, and asking for that is reasonable.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Young people waste money. I'm only protecting you."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I do overspend sometimes."
options.then: He brightens. "See? Even you agree."

options.text: "My friend says elders holding pay is normal."
options.then: He nods. "Your friend is right." He asks for the details again.

options.text: "I'll set a fixed saving each month myself."
options.then: He sighs. "Hm. At least you have a plan."

options.text: "Then I'll ask my cousin to manage it instead."
options.then: "Your cousin? She's younger than you. That makes no sense."

steps.why: Learning to manage your own money is the best protection.

steps.prompt: At the next family function your uncle says: "Everyone thinks it's simpler my way. Why make it difficult?"

options.text: "Maybe I'm being selfish. Is it wrong to want it?"
options.then: The table goes quiet. Your uncle nods, and the pressure grows. Nothing is settled.

options.text: "Elders know best about money. I shouldn't push back."
options.then: Your uncle takes it as a yes. "Good. We'll talk details at home."

options.text: "Everyone should stay out of my money."
options.then: Voices rise. Your aunt calls you rude, and nothing is settled.

options.text: "I've told Mummy. She knows it stays with me."
options.then: Your mother, nearby, nods. "She's right. It's her money."

steps.why: A trusted person beside you helps, and wanting your own money is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your salary in your own account; it's your independence.

scenarios.hook: You've been putting a little aside each month, and your partner Dev has noticed.
scenarios.setup: It comes up after dinner.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "Why do you need savings of your own? That's selfish. We're a team."

options.text: "Wanting my own savings isn't selfish. It's safety."
options.then: Dev frowns. "Safety from what? From me?"

options.text: "You're right. Maybe I'm being selfish."
options.then: Dev relaxes. "Good. Then we'll put it all together."

options.text: "My friends say good couples pool everything."
options.then: Dev smiles. "Smart friends. Everyone I know does the same."

options.text: "Then you stop your own savings too."
options.then: Dev laughs. "That's different. I earn more, so I decide."

steps.why: Wanting savings of your own is about independence and safety, not selfishness.

steps.prompt: A few days later Dev says: "Most couples put everything together. That's just normal."

options.text: "Couples who fight about money don't last."
options.then: "Exactly. So let's not fight." He considers it settled.

options.text: "Ask a few couples how they do it first."
options.then: Dev waves it off. "Everyone's different. I'm asking about us."

options.text: "Maybe normal couples do put it all together."
options.then: Dev smiles. "Exactly. Let's sort it out this week."

options.text: "Shared goals are fine. I'll keep some money mine."
options.then: Dev pauses. "Some yours, some ours. We'll see."

steps.why: Couples can share goals while each keeps some money of their own.

steps.prompt: A week later Dev says: "One more thing. Give me your card and PIN, just for safekeeping."

options.text: "Maybe sharing my PIN is what trust looks like."
options.then: Dev nods. "Trust means no secrets." He doesn't offer his own card.

options.text: "My cousin says couples share cards. Maybe she's right."
options.then: Dev smiles. "Listen to your cousin." He asks again the next morning.

options.text: "No. They stay with me. I'll talk to my sister."
options.then: Dev goes quiet. You text your sister that night.

options.text: "Let's fix this together, with a counsellor."
options.then: Dev agrees to go, but says the card is the first step.

steps.why: Demanding your card and PIN is financial control, and it is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Wanting your own savings isn't selfish: it's independence and safety.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Nikhil is on a stipend and has a view on when to start saving.
scenarios.setup: You're splitting a samosa after class.

steps.prompt: Nikhil says: "A stipend's too small to save from. I'll start when I get a real job."

options.text: "Yeah, no point saving until you earn properly."
options.then: He nods happily. "Finally someone who gets it."

options.text: "Start now, even tiny. It's the habit that counts."
options.then: He scoffs, then pauses. "Even fifty rupees? That's nothing."

options.text: "Try investing it instead. It'll grow faster."
options.then: "Invest what? I don't even know where to begin."

options.text: "Wait for a raise, then save a big chunk."
options.then: "Right. A big chunk, later." Later has no date.

steps.why: The saving habit matters more than the amount, so start small and start now.

steps.prompt: A few days later Nikhil says: "My stipend landed and half of it is gone already. Why bother saving any?"

options.text: "True. Save when it's a number worth saving."
options.then: "Exactly my point." The stipend goes out as usual.

options.text: "Then save one big lump around the festival."
options.then: "Festival money, sure. If any is left by then."

options.text: "The habit is the point. The amount grows later."
options.then: "The habit, not the amount." He sets a reminder on his phone.

options.text: "Skip the small stuff. Chase a better gig."
options.then: "A better gig would help. But that's months away."

steps.why: A small saving builds the habit, and the amount can grow later.

steps.prompt: Nikhil says: "Okay. If I did start, when would I move the money, and how much?"

options.text: "Whatever's left at month-end."
options.then: "Month-end?" He laughs. "There's never anything left."

options.text: "On stipend day, a small fixed amount."
options.then: "Fixed amount, same day." He sets up a 200 rupee transfer.

options.text: "Whenever you feel rich. Then save big."
options.then: "I never feel rich." The feeling doesn't come.

options.text: "Ask your dad how much he'd put aside."
options.then: "Dad says save when you can. Very helpful."

steps.why: A small fixed amount on payday happens before spending can eat it.

scenarios.relearn: Start the saving habit now, even tiny; it's what compounds.

scenarios.hook: You earn from a part-time job, and your cousin has opinions about it.
scenarios.setup: It comes up at a family gathering.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "It's pocket money, not real income. Don't get ideas."

options.text: "Ha, yes. It's basically nothing."
options.then: He grins. "Good, you get it." The word 'nothing' stays with you.

options.text: "It's real income. It's my safety net."
options.then: He blinks. "A safety net? From a part-time job?"

options.text: "Let me show you my earnings to prove it."
options.then: He scrolls his phone. "I'm not judging. Calm down."

options.text: "It's pocket money, but I'm saving it anyway."
options.then: "Cute," he says. The word 'pocket' sticks.

steps.why: Part-time earnings are real income, and they start your independence.

steps.prompt: Later, over dessert, your cousin says: "Your father will always provide anyway. Why bother earning?"

options.text: "True. Dad will always provide."
options.then: "Exactly." He looks satisfied, and your savings go quiet.

options.text: "I earn only a little. Why bother, honestly?"
options.then: "See? You agree." He looks pleased with himself.

options.text: "It builds my independence. I'll keep going."
options.then: He shrugs. "Suit yourself." But he stops arguing.

options.text: "Let's not argue. I'll think about it."
options.then: "Think all you like." The subject hangs in the air.

steps.why: Your own earnings build independence, whoever else provides.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks: "So what will you even do with that money?"

options.text: "Put some in savings, some toward my own plans."
options.then: "Hm. A plan." He sounds less sure of himself.

options.text: "Spend it on fun before I lose it."
options.then: "Sounds right." He grins. You're not sure it does.

options.text: "Give it to Mummy to look after."
options.then: Mummy takes it kindly. After that, you have no say in where it goes.

options.text: "I haven't decided. I'll figure it out later."
options.then: "Later." He shrugs. Another month's earnings drift by.

steps.why: Giving your earnings a plan, even a small one, keeps them working for you.

scenarios.relearn: Your earnings are real income, not pocket money.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kabir has a hot take on couples and money.
scenarios.setup: You're with the boys after a match.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "Bro, only a weak guy lets his girlfriend keep her own money."

options.text: "Haha yeah, can't let her have her own money."
options.then: The boys laugh louder. Nobody asks what she would think.

options.text: "Strong move, actually. Two people on their own feet is secure."
options.then: Kabir snorts. "Secure? That's new." But he's listening.

options.text: "Every couple's different. I don't really care."
options.then: Kabir shrugs. "Fair." The joke stands.

options.text: "That's a disgusting thing to say. Grow up."
options.then: The laughter stops. Kabir says you've turned it into a lecture.

steps.why: Two people each on their own footing is the secure setup, not the weak one.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "And who decides the big spends in a couple? Someone has to be boss."

options.text: "The one who earns more, obviously."
options.then: "Obviously." The others nod along.

options.text: "Whoever's better with numbers takes charge."
options.then: "So, me." Kabir grins. The argument slides away from fairness.

options.text: "No boss. Big spends get decided together, openly."
options.then: Kabir frowns. "Sounds like a meeting." He doesn't laugh, though.

options.text: "Don't ask me. I'll work it out when I'm there."
options.then: "Sure." Kabir returns to his phone.

steps.why: Fair money means open, shared decisions, with no one playing boss.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "Here's a worse one. What if she earns more than me? That'd be embarrassing."

options.text: "Then you're lucky. Two incomes is a safety net."
options.then: He laughs. "Two incomes. That sounds less scary."

options.text: "True. Earn more first. Then it won't matter."
options.then: "That's the plan." He looks stressed just saying it.

options.text: "Then never bring up pay. Keep it light."
options.then: He nods. Saying nothing, he will carry the worry alone.

options.text: "Ha, then she pays for everything. Easy life."
options.then: The boys laugh. Kabir laughs too, but his worry stays unspoken.

steps.why: Two incomes are a shared strength, and there is nothing to be embarrassed about.

scenarios.relearn: Both partners keeping their own footing is the secure, strong setup.

scenarios.hook: You moved to the city alone for work.
scenarios.setup: Your boss calls you over on payday.

steps.prompt: Your boss says: "Wages go to your uncle from now on. It's safer that way."

options.text: "Please pay my wages into my own account. They're mine."
options.then: His smile tightens. "Your uncle arranged this. Why the fuss?"

options.text: "Maybe it really is safer if my uncle holds my wages."
options.then: He writes it down. "Your uncle will sort it out." He doesn't ask what you want.

options.text: "Maybe a man in the family should handle my money."
options.then: He nods. "Your uncle thinks so too." He turns back to his register.

options.text: "Let me ask my uncle what he wants me to do first."
options.then: "Do that." You're the last to be asked about your own pay.

steps.why: Wages belong to the person who earned them, paid into their own account.

steps.prompt: Your boss adds: "Your uncle says the city is costly. He'll send you a little each week."

options.text: "A little each week is probably enough for me."
options.then: He nods, pleased. Your pay would still go through your uncle first.

options.text: "If you write it in your book, my pay is safe."
options.then: He writes a line. A line in his book isn't money in your hand.

options.text: "My wages come to me. I'll talk to someone I trust."
options.then: He shrugs and turns away. That evening you call a friend and tell her everything.

options.text: "My roommate says never cross a boss. Maybe she's right."
options.then: He smiles. "Listen to her." He moves on to the next worker.

steps.why: Your wages are yours, and a trusted person can help you claim them.

steps.prompt: Next payday your boss says: "Sign here. Your wages go to your uncle, as arranged."

options.text: "Maybe I caused this by asking too many questions."
options.then: He taps the paper. "No more questions, then." The pen waits by your hand.

options.text: "Everyone signs these, so it must be normal."
options.then: He slides the paper closer. "Exactly. Everyone does."

options.text: "I won't sign. I'm calling 181 and a friend I trust."
options.then: He stops. "No need for all that. Let me see what I can do."

options.text: "Let me ask a coworker what she did."
options.then: She says to just sign. She has never seen her own pay either.

steps.why: Your wages are yours, and help is at 181. Held pay is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Your wages should be paid to you, in your own account.

scenarios.relearn: Money is choices, safety, the power to walk away, independence and equality.
scenarios.hook: Match each thing money is to what it really means.

A net under you in a crisis

scenarios.relearn: Every independence goal starts with one small, concrete first step.
scenarios.hook: Match each independence step to the small first move it starts with.

Save a fixed slice each month

scenarios.relearn: Fair money means transparency, shared decisions, and kept access and knowledge for both.
scenarios.hook: Match each fair-money idea to what it looks like in a relationship.
