pairs.right: A bank or qualified, trusted source
A small emergency fund of your own

scenarios.relearn: Taking your access or keeping you uninformed is control, not fair money.
scenarios.hook: A partner is talking about money. Spot the two lines that are really about controlling you.

scene.text: "Let's both keep our own accounts."
"Just give me your card, I'll handle it all."
"You don't need to know our finances."
"Let's decide the big spends together."
"Of course you can see the statements."

scenarios.why: Taking your card and keeping you in the dark are control; fair money means both keep access.

scenarios.relearn: Advice that strips your own money or net leaves you dependent.
scenarios.hook: Spot the two pieces of 'advice' that quietly leave you dependent.

scene.text: "Open an account in your own name."
"You don't need your own money if you trust him."
"Keep a little saving of your own."
"Just hand your whole salary to the family."
"Learn the basics, they're learnable."

scenarios.why: Both 'you don't need money' and 'hand it all over' strip your safety net and leave you dependent.

scenarios.relearn: 'Too complicated' and 'just pocket money' are dependence-myths, not truths.
scenarios.hook: Spot the two money myths hiding among true statements.

scene.text: "The basics are learnable by anyone."
"Finance is too complicated for someone like you."
"Your own income is your safety net."
"A woman's earnings are just pocket money."
"Money is the power to walk away."

scenarios.why: 'Too complicated for you' and 'just pocket money' are myths that keep people dependent: the rest are true.

scenarios.relearn: Wages routed away from you, or anyone asking your OTP, are red flags.
scenarios.hook: A 'helper' is arranging your pay. Spot the two lines that should worry you.

scene.text: "We'll pay into your own account."
"Your wages will go to your uncle to keep safe."
"Here's a payslip each month."
"Share your OTP so we can 'set up' your pay."
"You can ask about your pay anytime."

scenarios.why: Wages routed away from you, and anyone asking for your OTP, are red flags: your pay and OTP stay yours.

scenarios.relearn: Guilt-tripping your savings as 'distrust' or 'selfish' is manipulation, not concern.
scenarios.hook: Someone reacts to you wanting your own savings. Spot the two lines that are manipulation, not concern.

scene.text: "Good idea keeping your own savings."
"Wanting your own money means you don't trust me."
"Let's both keep a safety net."
"It's selfish to keep money from us."
"Your independence matters to me."

scenarios.why: 'You don't trust me' and 'it's selfish' twist independence into guilt.

scenarios.relearn: Handing over your card or all your savings gives your independence away.
scenarios.hook: First month managing your own money. Spot the two moves that hand your independence away.

scene.text: Set up your own bank account
Give a relative your card and PIN to 'manage' it
Track roughly where your money goes
Let someone else hold all your savings
Keep a small fund only you can reach

scenarios.why: Handing over your card/PIN and letting someone hold all your savings give away the control you just gained.

scenarios.relearn: Money you can't reach and needing permission remove the power to walk away.
scenarios.hook: Spot the two situations that would leave you unable to walk away if you needed to.

scene.text: You have a small fund only you control
All your money sits in someone else's account
You earn a small income of your own
You must ask permission for every rupee
You know how to reach your savings

scenarios.why: Money you can't reach, and needing permission to spend, are exactly what removes the power to walk away.

scenarios.relearn: Sole control of passwords or an allowance for handed-over wages isn't equal sharing.
scenarios.hook: A couple says they share money 'equally.' Spot the two lines that aren't equal at all.

scene.text: "We both see every statement."
"Only I know the passwords."
"We decide big spends together."
"She gives me her salary, I give her an allowance."
"We each keep our own account."

scenarios.why: One person holding all passwords, and an allowance for handed-over wages, is control dressed as sharing.

scenarios.hook: "Saving ₹100 a month is too small to bother with."

myth.un: Saving ₹100 a month is too small to bother with.
myth.re: Tiny regular amounts build the saving habit, and the habit is the part that lasts.
myth.why: What you repeat beats what you intend; small saved beats nothing saved.

scenarios.relearn: Even tiny regular saving builds the habit that lasts.

scenarios.hook: "I'll save whatever's left at the end of the month."

myth.un: I'll save whatever's left at the end of the month.
myth.re: Pay yourself first: move savings aside on payday, before spending starts.
myth.why: Treated as leftovers, savings vanish; treated as a fixed line, they stay.

scenarios.relearn: Pay yourself first on payday; don't save the leftovers.

scenarios.hook: "An emergency fund is only for people with real money."

myth.un: An emergency fund is only for people with real money.
myth.re: An emergency fund is built in small steps; aim for around three months of essentials.
myth.why: A small cushion turns a sudden cost from a crisis into an inconvenience.

scenarios.relearn: Build an emergency fund in small steps, aiming for around three months of essentials.

scenarios.hook: "Auto-debited savings means I can't touch my money if I need it."

myth.un: Auto-saving means I can't touch my money if I need it.
myth.re: A simple recurring transfer to savings is yours to pause or withdraw; it just removes the decision each month.
myth.why: Automating the move beats relying on willpower every payday.

scenarios.relearn: Automating a small savings transfer beats relying on monthly willpower.

scenarios.hook: "BNPL on a sale is basically a discount."

myth.un: Buy-now-pay-later on a sale is basically a discount.
myth.re: BNPL is borrowed money; splitting a payment doesn't lower the price, and missed instalments add fees.
myth.why: Delaying a payment isn't the same as being able to afford it.

scenarios.relearn: BNPL is debt, not a discount; missed instalments add fees.

scenarios.hook: "My credit card limit is money I have."

myth.un: My credit card limit is money I have.
myth.re: A card limit is how much you can borrow, not money you own; spending it is taking on debt.
myth.why: Treating a limit as savings is how balances quietly grow.

scenarios.relearn: A card limit is borrowing power, not your money.

scenarios.hook: "Topping up one app's loan with another keeps me afloat."

myth.un: Borrowing from one app to repay another keeps me afloat.
myth.re: Borrowing to repay a loan is a debt spiral; the total owed keeps climbing.
myth.why: New debt to clear old debt only moves the problem and adds interest.

scenarios.relearn: Borrowing to repay debt is a spiral, not a fix.

scenarios.hook: "A guaranteed-return crypto tip from a stranger online is a real chance."

myth.un: A guaranteed-return tip from a stranger online is a real chance.
myth.re: If a return is guaranteed and quick, it's a scam; real wealth builds slowly.
myth.why: No honest investment promises guaranteed quick riches.

scenarios.relearn: Guaranteed quick returns are a scam; real wealth builds slowly.

scenarios.hook: "Sharing one OTP to 'verify' my account is harmless."

myth.un: Sharing one OTP to verify my account is harmless.
myth.re: An OTP is a one-time key to your money; no real bank or app ever asks you to share it.
myth.why: Whoever has your OTP can move your money: that's the whole point of the scam.

scenarios.relearn: Never share an OTP; no genuine service asks for it.

scenarios.hook: "A subscription is too small to matter to my budget."

myth.un: A subscription is too small to matter.
myth.re: Forgotten subscriptions are a silent leak; a quick audit and cancel reclaims real money.
myth.why: Several small monthly charges add up to a chunk you never chose to spend.

scenarios.relearn: Audit and cancel unused subscriptions; small leaks add up.

scenarios.hook: "A 'processing fee' to release my approved loan is normal."

myth.un: A fee to release my already-approved loan is normal.
myth.re: Genuine lenders deduct fees from the loan; an upfront fee to 'release' money is an advance-fee scam.
myth.why: Real money never needs you to pay first to receive it.

scenarios.relearn: Paying an upfront fee to 'release' a loan or prize is a scam.

scenarios.hook: "A friend's investment group that pays me to add members is a side hustle."

myth.un: A group that pays me to recruit members is a side hustle.
myth.re: If the earnings come mainly from recruiting, not a real product, it's a pyramid scheme that collapses.
myth.why: Latecomers fund the early ones, then the whole thing falls apart.

scenarios.relearn: Recruit-to-earn schemes are pyramids; they collapse on the latecomers.

scenarios.hook: You want saving to actually happen this month, not stay a wish.

steps.prompt: The credit pings in your bank app, and the month is still unplanned. What do you do first?

options.text: Move a small fixed amount to savings the same day
options.then: You send a fixed sum to a separate account. The balance looks smaller but steadier.

options.text: Save whatever is left at month-end
options.then: Month-end arrives. A few coins are left, and you move them anyway.

options.text: Spend first, then save from what's left next week
options.then: By next week most of the stipend has slipped away on small things. You save what's left.

options.text: Save a big amount and live on very little
options.then: It feels strict. By day ten you're skipping meals out and feeling poor.

steps.why: Savings paid first happen before spending can eat them.

steps.prompt: Soon after, a friend invites you on an expensive outing. What do you do?

options.text: Dip into savings just this once
options.then: It's a great night. The savings shrink, and the next excuse comes easier.

options.text: Put it on a BNPL to pay later
options.then: You pay nothing tonight. Next month the bill arrives with everything else.

options.text: Go if you can afford it, or suggest something cheaper
options.then: You pick a plan that fits what you can spend. Nothing comes out of your savings.

options.text: Decline without saying why
options.then: You stay in without a word. Your friends can't tell it's about money, and the next invite comes slower.

steps.why: Fun can come from what you can spend, so savings stay safe.

steps.prompt: Next month's stipend is delayed by a week. What do you do?

options.text: Take a quick app loan to keep life normal
options.then: The loan lands in minutes. The interest lands soon after.

options.text: Stop the savings transfer for good
options.then: It's easier this month. The habit is gone by the next.

options.text: Use a little buffer for essentials
options.then: Rent and food are covered. The buffer has a small dent you'll refill.

options.text: Wait and hope it arrives soon
options.then: It arrives on day eight. The week before is spent borrowing rides and meals.

steps.why: A small buffer exists for moments like this.

steps.prompt: A month later your stipend goes up a little. What do you do?

options.text: Spend all of the raise on treats
options.then: It feels great. The habit stays the same small size.

options.text: Set a fixed saving on payday and nudge it up
options.then: The fixed amount feels fine. Your routine grows with your income.

options.text: Skip saving, since the raise is too small to matter
options.then: The raise melts into daily spending. The habit stalls.

options.text: Lend some to friends who ask
options.then: A few loans go out, and not all come back.

steps.why: A fixed payday amount, nudged up as you earn more, keeps the habit growing.

scenarios.debrief: Pay yourself first: move a small fixed amount on payday, before spending starts.
scenarios.relearn: Move a small fixed amount to savings on payday, before you spend.

scenarios.hook: A flashy phone you want is on an 18-month EMI you can't really afford.

steps.prompt: The banner says 'just a small amount a month'. What do you do?

options.text: Take the EMI. The monthly figure is small
options.then: You sign in five minutes. The phone is yours, and so are eighteen payments.

options.text: Ask your cousin to pay the EMI for now
options.then: He agrees. You now owe him, with no schedule.

options.text: Work out the full cost and save towards it
options.then: Eighteen instalments add up to more than the sticker price. You start a saving target.

options.text: Take the EMI and cancel early if it pinches
options.then: Closing early can cost a fee, and your budget stays tight until then.

steps.why: Working out the full cost shows what a small monthly figure hides.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later your friends show off newer phones and you feel the pull. What do you do?

options.text: Buy a new one on BNPL because it's 'interest-free'
options.then: Approval is instant. The first bill arrives while you're still paying other things.

options.text: Wait for the sale and take the EMI then
options.then: The sale price is lower. The EMI is still eighteen months long.

options.text: Trade in your phone and EMI the difference
options.then: The trade-in shaves a little. The EMI still runs for a long stretch.

options.text: Give a newer phone a budget line and save for it
options.then: The fund grows a little every payday, and the newer phone isn't going anywhere.

steps.why: A budget line turns a want into a plan instead of a debt.

steps.prompt: A month later a newer model launches and everyone talks about it. What do you do?

options.text: Set a budget for it and buy once you can pay outright
options.then: You pick a figure and a date. No instalments, and the phone does its job.

options.text: Switch to the newer model, whatever the price
options.then: The price is higher, and so is the pull. Each new launch moves the bar again.

options.text: Take the EMI on the new one. It's only a bit more
options.then: You sign fast. Now instalments pay for a want.

options.text: Give up and stay with your current phone forever
options.then: Your current phone stays. The plan is dropped, and so is the saving.

steps.why: Saving first and paying outright beats chasing each new model.

scenarios.debrief: Borrowing for a want locks up future income; saving for it first is cheaper and safer.
scenarios.relearn: Save for wants instead of putting them on EMI or BNPL.

scenarios.hook: An SMS says your account is blocked, and asks you to tap a link to verify.

steps.prompt: It says the account closes in one hour. What do you do?

options.text: Tap the link and enter details to be safe
options.then: The page looks just like your bank's. Minutes later, money moves out.

options.text: Ignore the link and check in the official app
options.then: The app shows no problem. The account is fine, and the SMS was bait.

options.text: Reply STOP to the message
options.then: The reply tells them your number is live. More messages arrive.

options.text: Call the number given in the SMS
options.then: A polite voice answers and asks for your card number to 'verify'.

steps.why: A link in an SMS is never the way to check your account.

steps.prompt: The next day a caller says it's your bank, following up. What do you do?

options.text: Stay on and confirm your name and date of birth
options.then: Now they know more than before, and use it to sound real.

options.text: Hang up and call the bank's official number yourself
options.then: The real bank says it sent no such SMS, and notes your report.

options.text: Give the last four card digits to prove it's you
options.then: Four digits are a start for them. The next ask is the OTP.

options.text: Ask them to hold while you check the app
options.then: They stay polite and stall, then ask for just the OTP.

steps.why: Calling the official number yourself puts you in control of the call.

steps.prompt: A hostel mate tapped a similar link yesterday. What do you tell her?

options.text: Tell her to wait and watch her balance
options.then: She waits. A small debit appears, then a bigger one.

options.text: Tell her she was careless
options.then: She goes quiet and doesn't call anyone.

options.text: Tell her to change her app password only
options.then: That helps a little. The card and OTP routes stay open.

options.text: Tell her to call her bank now and report on 1930
options.then: The bank freezes the card. She files a report the same hour.

steps.why: Acting fast with the bank and 1930 limits the damage, and blame helps no one.

steps.prompt: Your group chat fills with the same SMS. What do you do?

options.text: Post the link so people can see for themselves
options.then: Someone taps it to check. Now another phone is at risk.

options.text: Share the signs and say to use only the official app
options.then: Two friends delete the message. One says she nearly tapped it.

options.text: Mute the chat. It isn't your problem
options.then: You're safe. Others are left to guess.

options.text: Tell everyone to ignore every bank SMS
options.then: Someone ignores a real alert about a payment and misses it.

steps.why: Sharing the signs helps everyone, without hiding real alerts.

scenarios.debrief: Banks don't send reactivation links by SMS; verify only through the official app or branch.
scenarios.relearn: Don't tap 'verify your account' SMS links; check via the official app.

scenarios.hook: A buyer for your old bike sends a QR and says to scan it to receive payment.

steps.prompt: He messages again, impatient that you haven't scanned it yet. What do you do?

options.text: Scan it and enter your PIN since he seems genuine
options.then: The app asks for your PIN. A debit alert arrives instead of a credit.

options.text: Ask him to send a payment screenshot first
options.then: He sends one in seconds. Screenshots are easy to fake.

options.text: Refuse, and ask him to pay your UPI ID
options.then: He goes silent a minute, then says his app is 'having problems'.

options.text: Scan it and try a small test amount
options.then: The test amount leaves your account, and he says more will follow.

steps.why: Receiving money never needs a scan or a PIN.

steps.prompt: He now says you must pay a small 'verification' amount first. What do you do?

options.text: Pay it. It's only a small amount
options.then: The amount goes. He now asks for one more step.

options.text: Ask him to show how the payment works
options.then: His steps all end at a PIN screen, and every step asks you to pay.

options.text: Stop, and report his number on 1930
options.then: You file a report. He stops replying, and the bike stays yours.

options.text: Tell him he's a fraud and leave it there
options.then: He blocks you. Without a report, he moves on to the next seller.

steps.why: Refusing to pay in order to receive ends the trick, and a report helps others.

steps.prompt: A friend says she lost money the same way yesterday. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's not her fault, and to report on 1930
options.then: She files a report and tells her bank. The group hears and gets careful.

options.text: Tell her to wait a week and see if it returns
options.then: She waits. The window to freeze the transfer shrinks.

options.text: Tell her it's too late and to move on
options.then: She drops it. Her details stay with the scammer.

options.text: Tell her to message him for a refund
options.then: He says he'll refund if she sends one more payment.

steps.why: Reporting quickly helps, and being fooled is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Receiving money never needs a scan or a PIN; only paying does. Report fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930.
scenarios.relearn: Receiving money never needs your PIN or a scan; only paying does.

scenarios.hook: Your card bill is due, and you can only comfortably pay the minimum shown.

steps.prompt: The bill shows a full amount and a much smaller minimum. What do you do?

options.text: Pay just the minimum. It's the allowed amount
options.then: It clears in one tap. Next month the balance is almost as big, plus interest.

options.text: Pay as much above the minimum as you can
options.then: You pay a bit more than the minimum. Less is left to grow interest.

options.text: Pay nothing until next month
options.then: A late fee and interest land together. The bill grows.

options.text: Pay the minimum and swipe for small things
options.then: The balance now grows from both sides.

steps.why: Every rupee above the minimum shrinks the interest.

steps.prompt: Next month a friend's birthday dinner comes up, with the card still owing. What do you do?

options.text: Put the dinner on the card too
options.then: It's a good night. The balance and its interest both grow.

options.text: Skip every outing until the card is cleared
options.then: You clear it a bit faster. You also go quiet with your friends.

options.text: Go, keep it modest, and pay the card first
options.then: You split fairly and skip the extras. The card balance keeps shrinking.

options.text: Borrow from a loan app to clear the card
options.then: The card clears. The loan app's interest is often higher.

steps.why: You can enjoy a dinner without letting the card grow.

steps.prompt: A bonus lands, bigger than your card bill. What do you do?

options.text: Treat yourself first, then see what's left
options.then: The treat is nice. Little is left for the card.

options.text: Save it all and keep paying the minimum
options.then: Savings grow slowly. Card interest usually grows faster.

options.text: Pay half and put a new want on EMI
options.then: Half is paid. A new instalment takes its place.

options.text: Clear the card balance in full
options.then: The balance drops to zero and stops growing interest from here.

steps.why: Clearing high-interest debt first usually beats saving beside it.

scenarios.debrief: Paying only the minimum keeps high-interest debt growing; pay more than the minimum when you can.
scenarios.relearn: Pay more than the card minimum; minimum-only keeps the balance growing.

scenarios.hook: A 'work-from-home' offer asks you to pay a registration fee to start earning.

steps.prompt: The recruiter says the fee is refundable after week one. What do you do?

options.text: Pay, since the pay sounds great
options.then: The fee goes through. A second 'training kit' payment is asked for next.

options.text: Ask to pay the fee after your first salary
options.then: They insist on advance payment. That alone is odd for a real employer.

options.text: Walk away, since a real job pays you
options.then: You close the chat. The recruiter sends two more messages, then stops.

options.text: Ask for the company website and read it
options.then: The site is glossy, with no address or named people. The recruiter says to hurry.

steps.why: A real employer pays you. It never charges you to start.

steps.prompt: A classmate says she got the same offer and will pay. What do you do?

options.text: Wish her luck and stay quiet
options.then: She pays that evening. You hear nothing more about the job.

options.text: Ask her to pay first and tell you if it's real
options.then: She pays to 'check'. Her fee is gone by morning.

options.text: Offer to lend her the fee
options.then: She accepts. You've now lent money to a scam.

options.text: Tell her real jobs never charge, so don't pay
options.then: She frowns, then reads the offer again. She holds off.

steps.why: Telling her what you know can save her the fee.

steps.prompt: Another offer asks you to 'process payments' through your own account for a commission. What do you do?

options.text: Try it once with a small amount
options.then: Money lands in your account. The bank later asks why, and the trail leads to you.

options.text: Ask what happens if a payment is reversed
options.then: They say 'no risk'. They can't explain the gap.

options.text: Accept. It's just passing money along
options.then: You move money for strangers. The account may get frozen.

options.text: Decline, and report it on 1930
options.then: You block the number and file the report. No money left your account.

steps.why: Your account is yours, so never lend it to move strangers' money.

steps.prompt: You still want a real remote job. What do you do next?

options.text: Post your CV and ID on random groups
options.then: Your details spread. Fake offers multiply in your inbox.

options.text: Take whichever offer replies fastest
options.then: Fast replies are easy. Some turn out to be fake and ask you to pay.

options.text: Wait for offers to come to you
options.then: A few arrive. Most ask for money or your bank details.

options.text: Apply through verified job pages, and ask about pay
options.then: You get fewer replies, but each one is real and clear about pay.

steps.why: Real jobs are found through verified sources and are clear about pay.

scenarios.debrief: Real jobs pay you; an upfront fee is a fake-job scam. Report it on 1930.
scenarios.relearn: A real job never asks you to pay a fee to start.

scenarios.hook: You get a few thousand rupees you weren't expecting.

steps.prompt: It lands in your account as a relative's gift. What do you do?

options.text: Spend it all before it disappears
options.then: A big shopping trip. By the weekend it's gone, and the fun fades with it.

options.text: Put it toward a big purchase on EMI
options.then: The windfall becomes a down payment. A long EMI follows.

options.text: Top up the emergency fund, then enjoy a little
options.then: The fund grows, and you pick a small treat.

options.text: Leave it untouched with no plan
options.then: It sits there. By next month some has slipped into daily spending.

steps.why: A windfall is a chance to build the cushion first.

steps.prompt: A week later another small gift arrives from an uncle. How do you split it between your emergency fund and a treat?

options.text: Most to the fund, a small slice for a treat
options.then: The fund grows steadily. The treat is small and still feels good.

options.text: All to savings, no treat at all
options.then: The fund grows faster. There's no treat this time, and you notice.

options.text: A small slice to the fund, most for a treat
options.then: The treat is big. The cushion barely moves.

options.text: Decide the split later
options.then: Later never comes. A small part stays in the fund and the rest blurs into daily spending.

steps.why: Both can happen when the cushion comes first and the treat is small.

steps.prompt: A month later an urgent expense comes up. What do you do?

options.text: Take a loan app offer and keep the fund
options.then: It's fast. Interest starts at once.

options.text: Ask family for money and skip the fund
options.then: They help, with some worry. The fund is neither used nor grown.

options.text: Use what is in the fund, then refill it
options.then: The expense is paid without borrowing. You start refilling the fund.

options.text: Sell your old tablet cheap and leave the fund
options.then: You get less than the tablet is worth. The fund sits there untouched.

steps.why: An emergency fund is for moments like this, and you can refill it.

scenarios.debrief: A windfall is a chance to build your cushion first; then a small treat is fair.
scenarios.relearn: Use a windfall to build your emergency cushion first, then treat a little.

scenarios.hook: A 'guaranteed daily profit' trading app is going round your hostel.

steps.prompt: Friends say they've made money already. What do you do?

options.text: Try a small amount since friends are in
options.then: The app shows a nice profit on day two. You want to add more.

options.text: Ask a friend to show you her withdrawals
options.then: She shows the balance on screen. She hasn't actually withdrawn yet.

options.text: Ask the app for a guarantee in writing
options.then: A formal PDF arrives. A guarantee in a PDF is still not real.

options.text: Stay out. Guaranteed daily profit isn't real
options.then: Your friends tease you a little. Your savings stay where they are.

steps.why: Real investments never guarantee a daily profit.

steps.prompt: A friend says she can't withdraw and the app wants a 'tax fee'. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to pay the fee to free her money
options.then: She pays. The app asks for one more charge.

options.text: Suggest she add more to cover the loss
options.then: She adds more. The hole only gets deeper.

options.text: Tell her to stop paying and adding money
options.then: She hesitates, then pauses her deposits. It's a hard call for her.

options.text: Tell her to ask the app's support
options.then: Support is friendly, and says the tax is required.

steps.why: Paying to withdraw is the classic sign, so stop putting money in.

steps.prompt: Two hostel mates have put in their semester savings. What do you do?

options.text: Tell them off for being so foolish with money
options.then: They get defensive and stop discussing it with you.

options.text: Stay quiet. It's their money to lose
options.then: They keep adding. Nobody tells them.

options.text: Post one warning in the group, then drop it
options.then: Some read it. Most scroll past, and the app keeps spreading.

options.text: Tell them what you saw, and to report on 1930
options.then: One sulks, one listens. The one who listens files a report.

steps.why: Sharing what you know, without shaming, helps them act.

steps.prompt: You want your money to grow the real way. What do you do?

options.text: Try a second app to win back what friends lost
options.then: It's another app with the same promises.

options.text: Wait for a really good tip from a friend
options.then: The tips keep coming, and none can be checked.

options.text: Put everything in one 'sure' offer
options.then: One offer feels safer. It still promises what nobody can.

options.text: Build an emergency fund and a small regular saving
options.then: It's slow and dull. But the balance only goes up.

steps.why: Real wealth builds slowly, through steady habits.

scenarios.debrief: Guaranteed daily profit is a scam pattern; never risk savings on it. Report it on 1930.
scenarios.relearn: 'Guaranteed daily profit' apps are scams; never risk savings on them.

scenarios.hook: A relative pressures you to take a loan in your name 'just on paper' for his business.

steps.prompt: Your uncle brings forms, saying it's only a formality. What do you do?

options.text: Believe his promise to repay makes it safe
options.then: He pats your shoulder. "Good. Sign whenever you're ready." Nothing is signed yet.

options.text: Tell yourself 'just on paper' means no risk
options.then: He nods. "Exactly, only paper." The forms stay on the table.

options.text: Ask to see his business accounts first
options.then: He changes the subject. The forms are still in front of you.

options.text: Say no, since the debt would be yours
options.then: His face hardens. "It's just paper. Family helps family."

steps.why: A loan in your name is your legal debt, and you can say no.

steps.prompt: The next day he says your aunt and parents are counting on you too. What do you do?

options.text: Believe you'd be letting the family down
options.then: The guilt grows. He notices and presses harder.

options.text: Tell yourself everyone does this for family
options.then: He takes your hesitation as a yes. The pressure returns the next day.

options.text: Believe a smaller loan can't really hurt you
options.then: He nods. A smaller loan would still be your debt to repay.

options.text: Speak to someone you trust before anything is signed
options.then: An older cousin says no is fair, and helps you plan the words.

steps.why: A trusted person can back you up, and saying no is fair.

steps.prompt: A few days later he says the lender only needs your ID scans and an OTP. What do you do?

options.text: Ask him to show the exact loan amount first
options.then: He names a figure and says you'll never need to pay it.

options.text: Ask a friend if giving ID copies is normal
options.then: She isn't sure. "Maybe it is, for family?" You still feel uneasy.

options.text: Refuse. No ID copies and no OTP, ever
options.then: He calls you difficult. You keep your ID and your phone.

options.text: Tell yourself the OTP is just a formality
options.then: He says the same. "Just a formality," he repeats, and holds out his hand for your phone.

steps.why: IDs and OTPs let someone act in your name, so keep them.

steps.prompt: The pressure keeps coming. Who do you reach out to?

options.text: Keep it secret so the family doesn't split
options.then: It stays quiet. The pressure doesn't.

options.text: Ask his friend to reason with him
options.then: He talks to him. The friend takes his side.

options.text: Call 181 or 1091, and tell a trusted person
options.then: The helpline listens without judging and explains your options. You feel less alone.

options.text: Threaten to tell the whole family
options.then: He turns furious. You're now in a fight without support.

steps.why: Help exists, and being pressured like this is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Pressure to borrow in your name is economic abuse, never your fault. Help is at 181 or 1091.
scenarios.relearn: A loan in your name is your debt; you can decline borrowing for others.

scenarios.hook: A festival sale tempts you to clear out your savings for discounted upgrades.

steps.prompt: Every app shows big discounts for three days. What do you do?

options.text: Spend from savings. These deals won't return
options.then: Your cart is full by night. The savings balance has a hole in it.

options.text: Buy on BNPL and pay after the festival
options.then: Nothing leaves your account today. The bills arrive in a cluster later.

options.text: Wait for the last-minute lightning deals
options.then: Lightning deals push quick, unplanned buys. The cart fills faster than planned.

options.text: Set a small fun budget and keep savings intact
options.then: You pick a limit and two items. The savings stay where they are.

steps.why: A fixed fun budget lets you enjoy the sale and keep your cushion.

steps.prompt: A friend shows a bundle offer that saves more if you buy three. What do you do?

options.text: Buy the bundle. You save on every item
options.then: You 'save' on three things and spend more than planned.

options.text: Ask your friends to split the bundle
options.then: Splitting makes it cheaper, and you still leave with things you never planned.

options.text: Browse around for more ideas first
options.then: Browsing turns up four 'must-haves'. The list grows by the hour.

options.text: Stick to what you came to buy
options.then: You pass on the bundle and buy only what you came for.

steps.why: A discount only helps on something you meant to buy anyway.

steps.prompt: After the sale, you look back at your statement. What do you do?

options.text: Cut all spending next month as punishment
options.then: You feel strict for a week, then rebound with a bigger splurge.

options.text: Ignore the statement and move on
options.then: The numbers stay unknown, and the next sale looks the same.

options.text: Take more BNPL to cover the gap
options.then: The gap moves to next month, where it grows.

options.text: List what you spent, and set a limit for next time
options.then: You see where the money went. Next sale, you know your limit.

steps.why: Looking back at what you spent turns the sale into a lesson.

scenarios.debrief: A sale is fine within a small set budget; don't raid savings or stack BNPL for it.
scenarios.relearn: Set a small budget for a sale; don't drain savings or stack BNPL.

scenarios.hook: A caller claiming to be your bank's fraud team asks you to read out the OTP just sent.

steps.prompt: They know your name and bank, and say a payment is in progress. What do you do?

options.text: Read it out since they know your details
options.then: You read six digits. A debit alert arrives a moment later.

options.text: Read half the OTP to check them
options.then: They say it's not enough and ask for the rest. Half was already too much.

options.text: Ask them to prove who they are first
options.then: They read out your address and last transaction. It sounds convincing.

options.text: Hang up, and never read out an OTP
options.then: The line goes dead. No code has left your phone.

steps.why: Knowing your details proves nothing, and an OTP is never shared.

steps.prompt: A caller snaps: "Your account will be frozen in minutes!" What do you do?

options.text: Give the OTP to stop the freezing
options.then: The panic ends. A larger debit follows.

options.text: Ask them to call back in an hour
options.then: They say the freeze happens in minutes. Urgency is their lever.

options.text: Argue with them for a while
options.then: They stay on the line, pressing until you tire.

options.text: Hang up and call the number on your card
options.then: Your bank says there's no problem and logs the attempt.

steps.why: Calling the number on your own card puts you back in control.

steps.prompt: A hostel mate lost money to a call like this. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her it's her own fault
options.then: She goes silent and tells nobody, including her bank.

options.text: Suggest she wait for the money to return
options.then: She waits. The window to act quickly passes.

options.text: Help her report on 1930 and tell her bank
options.then: The bank blocks her card, and she files the report the same day.

options.text: Tell her to keep it quiet to avoid embarrassment
options.then: She stays quiet. The scammer tries the next hostel.

steps.why: Fast reporting helps, and being fooled is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: No genuine bank ever asks for an OTP; hang up and report it on 1930.
scenarios.relearn: No genuine bank asks for your OTP; hang up and report it.

scenarios.hook: Sort each move: builds your safety, or pulls you into a trap?

items.text: Saving a fixed amount every payday
Paying only the card minimum each month
Keeping three months of essentials saved
Borrowing from one app to repay another

scenarios.hook: Sort each offer: probably honest, or a scam?

items.text: "Double your money in a week, guaranteed"
A recurring deposit at a modest, slow return
"Pay a fee now to release your prize"
A salary credited from your employer
"Share your OTP to claim a refund"
A bank's published, ordinary interest rate

A course that grows your earning power

A big unavoidable cost you can repay

items.text: Unused subscriptions you forgot to cancel
Impulse buys you don't remember making

items.text: "Your statement is ready in the app"
"Urgent: share your OTP to stop a block"
"Reset your PIN inside the official app"

scenarios.hook: Spot the two scam lines hiding among the genuine ones.

"Pay a small fee to release your refund"

options: Pick an amount I won't miss

options: Wait a day before tapping buy
Count it as debt, not a discount

options: Friends in it doesn't make it real
I can say no and stay friends
scenarios.affirm: Trusting your own read over the crowd is exactly the instinct that keeps your money safe.
scenarios.relearn: A scheme isn't real just because friends joined; you can opt out.

scenarios.hook: A friend can't stop talking about a money group he has joined.
scenarios.setup: He adds you to a chat before you answer.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Bro, guaranteed returns. Everyone's in. Don't miss out."

options.text: "Fine, sign me up so I don't miss out."
options.then: "Nice! I'll send you the joining details."

options.text: "Maybe later, when I have more money."
options.then: "Later it costs more. Join now."

options.text: "Nobody can guarantee big returns. I'm out."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "You'll regret this." But he reads it again.

options.text: "Let me look at the group first."
options.then: "Sure." The group is full of screenshots and cheering.

steps.why: Nobody can promise big, quick returns, so a guarantee like that is a scam sign.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Deposit by Sunday. Everyone in the group got paid last round."

options.text: "If everyone's paid, I'll put in a small amount."
options.then: "Small? Go bigger, bro." He sends the link anyway.

options.text: "I'll ask the group admin if it's safe."
options.then: The admin says it's completely safe. Of course he does.

options.text: "Fine, you all do it. Just don't ask me."
options.then: He shrugs. "Suit yourself." He keeps adding people.

options.text: "Guaranteed returns are a scam. I'm out. Be careful with yours."
options.then: He scowls. "Even if the whole group got paid?"

steps.why: A guaranteed high return is the scam sign, however many people say they were paid.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "What if this is the real deal? Think how much you could make."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. One small try won't hurt."
options.then: "That's the spirit." He sends the link right away.

options.text: "Ask me again next month."
options.then: "Sure." He asks again in a week, with a deadline.

options.text: "Real wealth is slow. I'll risk missing it."
options.then: He sighs and lets it drop. The chat keeps pinging.

options.text: "Only if you'll repay me if it fails."
options.then: "Promise!" A promise from him protects nothing.

steps.why: Missing a 'sure thing' costs far less than losing your savings.

scenarios.relearn: Decline 'guaranteed high returns' schemes clearly; they're a scam sign.

scenarios.hook: You've just got your first debit card in the post.
scenarios.setup: Your phone rings while you make chai.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "This is your bank. Read me the OTP so we can stop a fraud."

options.text: "Okay, the code is... hold on."
options.then: "Quickly, quickly. We're running out of time."

options.text: "Which branch are you calling from?"
options.then: "Main branch. Now the code, please."

options.text: "Can I read only the first three digits?"
options.then: "Fine. Now the last three."

options.text: "My bank never asks for an OTP. Goodbye."
options.then: The caller sputters. "Wait, wait!" You hang up, and the phone rings again.

steps.why: A real bank never asks for an OTP, so hang up.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "Your account will be blocked in two minutes. I'm helping you."

options.text: "Please don't block it. I'll read the code."
options.then: "Thank you. Go ahead." You hesitate over the digits, and he waits.

options.text: "Let me check my app first. Hold on."
options.then: "Just read the code. It's faster."

options.text: "Send me an email first. Then I'll share."
options.then: "Emails take time. The code now, please."

options.text: "I'll call the bank myself, on my card's number."
options.then: "No need for that!" The line goes dead. Then your phone rings again.

steps.why: Calling the number on your card is the safe way to check.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "We already have your card details. Just one code and it's done."

options.text: "Then you don't need the OTP. Keep talking."
options.then: "Exactly, but we need one code to finish."

options.text: "Tell me my last transaction. Then I'll share."
options.then: He names one. Sounding right proves nothing.

options.text: "Okay, okay. The code is coming."
options.then: "Good. Hurry." The call turns friendly.

options.text: "Banks never ask for it. I'm ending this."
options.then: Silence, then a click. You report the number later.

steps.why: Having your details doesn't prove a caller is your bank.

scenarios.relearn: Refuse to share an OTP, even to a caller claiming to be your bank.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin has a business idea and wants your name in it.
scenarios.setup: Your cousin brings it up again after lunch.

steps.prompt: Your cousin Vikram says: "Take a loan in your name for my shop. I'll pay every instalment."

options.text: "If you promise to repay, it should be fine."
options.then: "Promise! I'll bring the papers." A promise isn't written on the lender's paper.

options.text: "Maybe I'm selfish for even hesitating."
options.then: "A little," he says, smiling. He waits for your yes.

options.text: "Why not ask a bank for a business loan?"
options.then: "They'd refuse me. That's why I need you."

options.text: "A loan in my name is my debt and risk. I can't."
options.then: His smile fades. "It's just paper. Family helps family."

steps.why: A loan in your name is your debt, so you can say no.

steps.prompt: Vikram says: "The family already knows I'm asking you. They expect you to help."

options.text: "Maybe I should just help. Family is family."
options.then: He relaxes. "Good." He starts talking about the papers.

options.text: "Please keep this between us for now."
options.then: He nods. Nobody else hears of it, and the pressure stays hidden.

options.text: "Then I'll tell everyone how pushy you are."
options.then: He snaps. "Go ahead. They'll side with me."

options.text: "Let them expect it. I won't take that loan."
options.then: He glares. "We'll see," he says, and tries another way.

steps.why: A calm, firm no stays a no, even when the pressure rises.

steps.prompt: Later Vikram says: "Just give me your ID and OTP. I'll handle the forms myself."

options.text: "Maybe ID copies are harmless without the OTP."
options.then: "Harmless," he says. "Just send them." He keeps asking for the OTP too.

options.text: "A smaller loan would be safer, right?"
options.then: "Smaller is fine." A smaller loan would still be yours to repay.

options.text: "No. They stay with me. I'll talk to Mummy."
options.then: He backs off, muttering. You think about telling your mother.

options.text: "I'll ask my friend whether it's safe."
options.then: Your friend says it's probably fine if he pays. She isn't sure.

steps.why: Your ID and OTP let someone act in your name, so keep them.

steps.prompt: A few days later your mother asks: "You've seemed quiet lately. What's wrong?"

options.text: "Nothing. Family problems stay in the family."
options.then: She lets it go. The worry stays with you.

options.text: "He wants help, and I feel selfish."
options.then: She says family matters, but doesn't ask more. The guilt stays.

options.text: "Vikram wants a loan in my name, and I don't want it. Can you back me?"
options.then: Your mother puts an arm around you. "You did right. I'll speak to him."

options.text: "Don't tell Papa. I'll handle it."
options.then: She nods, uneasy. You're alone with it again.

steps.why: A trusted person can back you. Help exists at 181 or 1091, and it is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: A loan in your name is your debt; you can decline borrowing for others.

scenarios.hook: A familiar voice in your head has big plans for today.
scenarios.setup: You stand outside a mall, stipend just credited.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice says: "It's payday. You've earned this. Spend it all today."

options.text: "I'll spend now and save next month."
options.then: "Perfect. Next month always comes." It rarely saves more.

options.text: "Savings move aside first. I spend what's left."
options.then: "Hmm. Guilt-free sounds nice. How much goes aside?"

options.text: "I'll treat myself big, then start budgeting."
options.then: "Big treat, then budget. Sounds fun." The budget starts with less.

options.text: "I'll check my balance and see how I feel."
options.then: "Feel rich? Then spend." The feeling wins.

steps.why: Setting savings aside first lets you spend the rest without guilt.

steps.prompt: A few hours later your inner voice asks: "So how much should you save this month? Too much and you'll feel poor."

options.text: "A small fixed amount I won't really miss."
options.then: "Small and fixed. That I can live with."

options.text: "As much as possible. I'll live on nothing."
options.then: "Nothing? That lasts about a week."

options.text: "Whatever feels right on the day."
options.then: "Feelings change." The amount shrinks every payday.

options.text: "Only what's left after every purchase."
options.then: "Leftovers, again." There usually aren't any.

steps.why: A small, fixed amount is easy to keep up every month.

steps.prompt: Your inner voice asks: "And how will you stop yourself touching it?"

options.text: "I'll just remember not to touch it all month."
options.then: "Sure you will." Memory loses to a sale.

options.text: "Keep the cash in my drawer at home for now."
options.then: "The drawer is close. So are friends who ask."

options.text: "Ask my roommate to hold it for me each month."
options.then: She holds it. Now it's her job, not your habit.

options.text: "Move it to a separate account the same day."
options.then: "Out of sight." The balance on your app looks smaller, and calmer.

steps.why: Moving it the same day puts savings out of reach of spending.

scenarios.relearn: Move savings aside first, then spend the rest; don't postpone saving.

scenarios.hook: A want has caught your eye, and the shop has a deal for it.
scenarios.setup: You're at the billing counter.

steps.prompt: The salesperson says: "No-cost EMI. Zero interest. You won't even feel it."

options.text: "EMI is fine for a big purchase like this."
options.then: "Exactly." He prints the forms.

options.text: "It's still debt for a want. I'll save up instead."
options.then: He looks surprised. "You can pay later, but the offer ends."

options.text: "Sure, put it on EMI. It's basically free."
options.then: "Sign here." He slides the pen across, and the forms are ready.

options.text: "I'll take it, but close the EMI early."
options.then: "Sure." Early closing can carry a charge, and the want still sits on credit.

steps.why: A no-cost EMI is still debt, and it's for a want.

steps.prompt: The salesperson adds: "Take the bigger model on the same offer. It ends tonight."

options.text: "Okay. If it ends tonight, I'll take the bigger one."
options.then: He nods and swaps the forms. The EMI now runs longer.

options.text: "Fine, but only the smaller one on EMI."
options.then: "Smaller it is." It's still debt for a want.

options.text: "Let me call my parents and ask."
options.then: "Call, but the offer may end." You're still deciding under pressure.

options.text: "Then I'll miss it. Offers come back."
options.then: He shrugs. "Suit yourself." The pressure eases once you step away.

steps.why: Offers that end tonight are designed to rush you, and they return.

steps.prompt: A friend beside you says: "Everyone uses no-cost EMI. It's no big deal."

options.text: "It's still a loan for something I don't need."
options.then: "Hmm. Fair." She looks at the price tag again.

options.text: "You're right. Everyone does it."
options.then: She grins. The forms are on the counter again.

options.text: "I'll do it just once to see how it goes."
options.then: "Once." The one time is a twelve-month plan.

options.text: "Fine, but split it over fewer months."
options.then: "Shorter is better." It's still an instalment for a want.

steps.why: What everyone does doesn't change what a loan is.

scenarios.relearn: An EMI on a want is still debt; save up rather than borrow for it.

scenarios.hook: A junior is excited about a job offer and wants your opinion.
scenarios.setup: She shows you the offer in the canteen.

steps.prompt: Your junior asks: "They want a registration fee, but the pay is great. Should I pay?"

options.text: "If the pay's that good, the fee's worth it."
options.then: She brightens. "That's what I thought." She opens her payment app, then hesitates.

options.text: "Ask the recruiter if it's refundable."
options.then: "Fully refundable," he says in seconds. He would.

options.text: "A real job pays you. A fee means a scam."
options.then: She pauses. "Really? Even with an offer letter?"

options.text: "Pay a little and see what happens."
options.then: She hesitates. "Maybe a little." Her thumb hovers over the payment app.

steps.why: A real employer pays you, and never charges you to start.

steps.prompt: She says: "They also sent an offer letter with a logo and everything."

options.text: "Then it must be real. Go ahead and pay."
options.then: She nods and pays. The 'joining kit' fee arrives next.

options.text: "Check the company name on a search site."
options.then: She finds a neat page made last month. Looks don't settle it.

options.text: "Ask the recruiter for a video call first."
options.then: He agrees, with a blurred background and a pleasant voice.

options.text: "Letters are easy to fake. Real ones skip fees."
options.then: She reads it again. "There is a fee line. Hmm."

steps.why: A letter can be faked, but a fee for a job never fits a real employer.

steps.prompt: She says: "What do I do now? They keep messaging me."

options.text: "Reply and argue with them till they stop."
options.then: They reply for an hour. Each reply tells them she's reachable.

options.text: "Ignore them. It'll probably fade on its own."
options.then: The messages slow down, but her number is on their list.

options.text: "Post their number in the whole college group."
options.then: It helps some. Then strangers flood the number and things get messy.

options.text: "Block them and report on 1930. Not your fault."
options.then: She blocks the number and files the report. The messages stop.

steps.why: Blocking and reporting protects others too, and being approached is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: A real job never charges an upfront fee; warn against paying to start.

scenarios.hook: Sahil, a close friend, has seemed stressed about money lately.
scenarios.setup: He admits it over late-night chai.

steps.prompt: Your friend Sahil says: "I take from one app to pay the other. It's working, mostly."

options.text: "Whatever keeps you going, I guess. Your call."
options.then: He shrugs, relieved you didn't push. The next top-up is tomorrow.

options.text: "Try a third app with a lower rate."
options.then: "A third? Maybe." Another app means another due date.

options.text: "How did you even get into this mess?"
options.then: He stiffens. "I'm not here to be judged."

options.text: "That's a spiral. Let's map a way out together."
options.then: He exhales. "Yeah. I know. I just didn't want to say it."

steps.why: Naming the spiral, without judging, is the first step out.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "I'm scared to add it all up. What if it's worse than I think?"

options.text: "Then don't add it up. Just pay what's due."
options.then: He nods. Not knowing the total keeps the fear and the debt growing.

options.text: "I'll cover your next due date for you."
options.then: He's hugely relieved. Next month has the same gap.

options.text: "It'll sort itself out once your pay rises."
options.then: "Right, once the pay rises." The apps don't wait.

options.text: "Let's list every loan, amount and due date."
options.then: It takes an hour. The total is a number now, not a fog.

steps.why: A full list turns a scary unknown into a number you can plan around.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "I can't keep going like this. What should I do first?"

options.text: "Take one big new loan to clear them all quickly."
options.then: One large due date now hangs over him, and nobody checked the terms.

options.text: "Just pay the minimums everywhere."
options.then: The balances barely move. The interest doesn't wait.

options.text: "No new loans. Costliest first. Ask a qualified person."
options.then: He writes it down. "Costliest first. And I'll ask someone who knows."

options.text: "Close the smallest ones and ignore the rest."
options.then: Two small loans close. The big ones keep growing.

steps.why: Stop borrowing, tackle the costliest debt, and get qualified advice.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "I'm so embarrassed. I don't want my parents to know."

options.text: "Keep it secret then. They'd only panic."
options.then: He relaxes for now. He's still carrying it alone.

options.text: "Tell them today, whatever happens."
options.then: He panics. He wasn't ready, and stops telling you things.

options.text: "It's your mess. Sort it out alone."
options.then: He goes quiet. You're no longer the person he tells.

options.text: "Many get stuck. Someone you trust can help."
options.then: He thinks. "Maybe my cousin. She won't judge."

steps.why: Debt is common, and help from a trusted person beats carrying it alone.

scenarios.relearn: Borrowing to repay borrowing spirals; name it and plan a way out.

scenarios.hook: A cousin has big money news and wants you in on it.
scenarios.setup: He shows you a message on his phone.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "This tip is sure. Put in your savings and double it by Diwali."

options.text: "Okay, take it all. Sounds like a sure thing."
options.then: He grins. "You won't regret it. I'll send the account details."

options.text: "I'll put in half and keep half."
options.then: "Half works." Half your safety net is still riding on a tip.

options.text: "Who gave you the tip?"
options.then: "A guy in a group. Everyone trusts him." No name, no record.

options.text: "That's my safety net, not gambling money."
options.then: He blinks. "It's an investment, not gambling." He scrolls for proof.

steps.why: Emergency savings are a safety net, so they never go on a tip.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "Here's my screenshot from last week. See how it works."

options.text: "Wow. Maybe I should have started earlier."
options.then: He nods. "Start now, then."

options.text: "Send me the details. I'll think about it."
options.then: He sends them in seconds, with a deadline attached.

options.text: "A screenshot isn't proof. My savings stay put."
options.then: He scowls, then shrugs. "Your loss."

options.text: "I'll join if you cover any loss."
options.then: "Sure, sure." His promise isn't a safety net.

steps.why: A screenshot shows a balance on a screen, never money in your hands.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "Put in all your savings. Big chances bring big money."

options.text: "You're right. Life is about chances."
options.then: "Exactly." The emergency cash starts to look like extra.

options.text: "I'll test with a bit of my savings first."
options.then: "A bit." The bit comes out of your safety net.

options.text: "Maybe I'm just too scared of risk."
options.then: "Then be brave. Fortune favours the bold."

options.text: "Not on a tip. Emergency money stays safe."
options.then: He thinks about it. "Hm. I hadn't thought of it as emergency money."

steps.why: Emergency money is a safety net, and reliable sources beat hot tips.

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "The group says to hurry. Only today."

options.text: "Okay, fast then. I'll send it today."
options.then: He cheers. The money leaves before you can think twice.

options.text: "Let me transfer a little and watch."
options.then: "A little." A little becomes more when the screen shows gains.

options.text: "Let me ask the group if it's safe."
options.then: The group says it's completely safe. The group would say that.

options.text: "A rush is a red flag. I'll ask a qualified person."
options.then: He sighs. "Suit yourself." You close the chat.

steps.why: Reliable sources beat hot tips, and real advice never needs a rush.

scenarios.hook: A friend is drowning in BNPL debt and is too ashamed to ask for help.

steps.prompt: She shows you four BNPL bills due this week and looks away. What do you do?

options.text: Lecture her on how it happened
options.then: She nods at the floor. She goes quiet for a day, then texts you again.

options.text: Quietly pay one bill and say nothing
options.then: She's relieved. The habit stays, and the next bills arrive.

options.text: Tell her to take a fifth plan to cover them
options.then: The fifth plan approves instantly. The total due grows, and more dues are on the way.

options.text: Reassure her, and look at real help together
options.then: She lets out a shaky laugh. "Okay. Could we ask the bank for a plan?"

steps.why: Shame keeps debt hidden. Reassurance and a bank or qualified person open the door.

steps.prompt: A few days later she says more dues are coming this week. What do you suggest?

options.text: Skip them and hope the reminders stop
options.then: The reminders turn into late fees.

options.text: Switch each plan to a loan app for more time
options.then: She gets time, at a higher interest rate.

options.text: List every due date and pay the most urgent first
options.then: The list fits on one page. Two dues get paid, and the rest have a date.

options.text: Pay half of each bill and hope
options.then: Four half payments leave four open bills with fees.

steps.why: A clear list of dates lets her pay in order of urgency.

steps.prompt: She promises never to use BNPL again. What do you say?

options.text: Say great, that settles it
options.then: She feels relieved. The plan is still missing, and so is the limit.

options.text: Suggest she delete every shopping app forever
options.then: She deletes them. A month later she reinstalls one.

options.text: Ask her to tell you before every purchase
options.then: She agrees. You've become her guard, not her friend.

options.text: Say a plan matters more. Set a spending limit
options.then: She writes a monthly limit. The promise now has a number behind it.

steps.why: A plan with a limit holds up better than a promise.

scenarios.debrief: Debt shame keeps people stuck; a no-shame nudge toward real help is what frees them.
scenarios.relearn: Reassure a friend in debt without shame and point them to real help.

scenarios.hook: A caller says your account is blocked and asks for the OTP just sent to you.

steps.prompt: He sounds official and says to hurry. What do you do?

options.text: Share the OTP to unblock it fast
options.then: You read out the six digits. A debit alert lands a minute later.

options.text: Give only half of the OTP
options.then: He says that's enough to start, and asks for the rest.

options.text: Ask for his employee ID first
options.then: He reads out a number. It sounds real and proves nothing.

options.text: Refuse, hang up, call the bank yourself
options.then: The bank says there's no block and notes the attempt.

steps.why: Nobody real needs your OTP, so end the call and call the bank.

steps.prompt: Later that day a message says your account is 'under review' and to call a number. What do you do?

options.text: Call the number in the message
options.then: A polite voice asks for your card number to 'verify'.

options.text: Forward it to friends to ask
options.then: They say it looks real. None of them can check it.

options.text: Ignore it, and call the number on your card
options.then: Your bank says nothing is under review, and logs the message.

options.text: Reply with your name and account number
options.then: Now they know who you are. Calls start the next morning.

steps.why: Only the number printed on your own card is a safe route to the bank.

steps.prompt: A coworker says she gave her OTP to a caller yesterday and is scared to tell anyone. What do you say?

options.text: Say she must have been careless
options.then: She goes silent and tells nobody, including her bank.

options.text: Tell her to wait and see if any money goes
options.then: She waits. The time to act fast slips by.

options.text: Tell her to keep it from her employer and everyone
options.then: She stays quiet. The account stays open to the scammer.

options.text: Say it's not her fault. Call the bank now, then 1930
options.then: She makes the call from the corridor. The bank blocks the card.

steps.why: Acting fast with the bank and 1930 helps, and it is never her fault.

scenarios.debrief: No genuine bank or service ever asks for your OTP; sharing it is handing over the key.
scenarios.relearn: Never share an OTP; hang up and call the bank's official number yourself.

scenarios.hook: A reel promises to double your money in a month, guaranteed, if you join today.

steps.prompt: The reel has thousands of likes and comments saying 'it works'. What do you do?

options.text: Put in 'just a little' to test it
options.then: The app shows a fake bonus on your little deposit. That's the hook.

options.text: Send it to friends to see what they think
options.then: Two friends reply 'wow'. You've helped a scam spread.

options.text: Read the comments to see if it works
options.then: The praise comes from brand-new accounts. It proves nothing.

options.text: Scroll past. Guaranteed doubling can't be real
options.then: You scroll on and your savings stay where they are. The offer turns up again anyway.

steps.why: Too good to be true means a scam, and no one can guarantee doubling.

steps.prompt: A friend messages: 'I doubled mine. Here's my link.' What do you do?

options.text: Click her link just to look
options.then: The page asks for your number and a small 'verification' payment.

options.text: Join through her link so she gets a bonus
options.then: You pay. Her bonus comes from your money going up the chain.

options.text: Decline, and say no one can guarantee doubling
options.then: She goes quiet. "It shows in the app. Withdrawals take time."

options.text: Tell her she's silly and leave it
options.then: She feels attacked and ignores you. She keeps recruiting.

steps.why: A guaranteed doubling is the scam sign, whatever the app shows or pays.

steps.prompt: Weeks later a mate says he lost his savings in a similar offer. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him he should have known better
options.then: He stops talking about it, and doesn't report anything.

options.text: Suggest he try another offer to win it back
options.then: He tries. The second offer takes another round of his money.

options.text: Tell him it's not his fault, and to report on 1930
options.then: He files the report and tells his bank. He looks less alone.

options.text: Tell him to keep quiet about it
options.then: He keeps quiet. The scammer is free to try the next person.

steps.why: Being fooled is never the victim's fault, and reporting helps others.

steps.prompt: You want your own money to grow. What do you do?

options.text: Follow a finfluencer's 'sure' picks this month
options.then: The picks are loud and clear. Their results are neither.

options.text: Spread a little money over everything new
options.then: A little everywhere adds up to a lot of untested bets.

options.text: Build a small saving habit and verify big moves
options.then: Progress is slow, and it is yours.

options.text: Wait for a better guarantee
options.then: Guaranteed doubling offers keep coming. None are real.

steps.why: Real wealth builds slowly, and big decisions deserve a qualified check.

scenarios.debrief: Too good to be true means a scam; real wealth builds slowly, never on a guarantee.
scenarios.relearn: Skip 'guaranteed doubling' offers. They're scams, so report them at 1930.

scenarios.hook: Your partner asks for your PIN 'to manage everything', and for you to close your own account.

steps.prompt: Rishi says it's about trust and keeping things simple. What do you do?

options.text: Think trust means handing over your PIN
options.then: You hesitate. He smiles. "Trust means no secrets." He doesn't offer his own PIN.

options.text: Believe a good partner would close the account
options.then: You say you'll think about it. He smiles, and asks again the next day, and the next.

options.text: Wonder if you're overreacting. It's only a PIN
options.then: You let it go. He asks for the PIN again every day.

options.text: Keep your own account, and talk to someone you trust
options.then: He looks annoyed. You message your friend that night.

steps.why: Your own account and access are yours, however the request is framed.

steps.prompt: Rishi says that if you loved him, you'd have nothing to hide. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you are being selfish
options.then: You start doubting yourself. He senses it and pushes harder.

options.text: Take a friend's word that showing him calms things
options.then: He likes the idea. "Good. Start with your statement."

options.text: Say no calmly, and tell someone you trust
options.then: He goes cold. Your friend says it isn't about love, and stays in touch.

options.text: Tell yourself a login is harmless
options.then: You say it's only a login. He says "Just a quick look" and is already reaching for your phone.

steps.why: Love doesn't need your PIN, and guilt-tripping is a control tactic.

steps.prompt: He now says your salary should go into his account 'for the family'. What do you do?

options.text: Tell yourself families always pool salaries
options.then: You say families pool pay. "Exactly, it's for the family," he says, and asks again that week.

options.text: Believe a man should manage the household money
options.then: You voice the old idea that a man manages the money. "That's how it should be," he says, and asks for your account details.

options.text: Keep your salary in an account you control
options.then: He sulks for a day, then drops it. Your pay stays yours.

options.text: Ask his parents what they think
options.then: They take his side. The pressure doubles.

steps.why: Your salary stays in an account you control, whatever it is called.

steps.prompt: He starts checking your phone and asking who you've paid. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you really are hiding something
options.then: You start second-guessing yourself. He keeps checking.

options.text: Believe he checks because he cares
options.then: He calls it caring. The questions grow, and the checking continues.

options.text: Tell yourself every couple does this
options.then: The doubt fades. The checking doesn't.

options.text: Reach a trusted person, and call 181 or 1091
options.then: The helpline listens without judging and explains your options.

steps.why: Checking and controlling is abuse, and calling 181 or 1091 is always an option.

steps.prompt: A few days later you tell a close friend everything. She asks how she can help. What do you ask for?

options.text: Nothing. You don't want to burden her
options.then: She offers anyway, and you still feel alone.

options.text: Keeping it secret from everyone
options.then: She agrees, worried. Nobody else knows, so nobody else can step in.

options.text: Help making a safety plan, and staying in touch
options.then: She sits with you for an hour and writes it down. You feel steadier.

options.text: Confronting him together
options.then: He turns angry, and the risk to you goes up.

steps.why: A trusted friend and a plan help, and none of this is your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Taking your access or closing your account is financial control, which is abuse and never your fault. Help is at 181 or 1091.
scenarios.relearn: Keep your own account and access. Controlling it is abuse, so reach 181/1091.

scenarios.hook: You're about to sign a big loan you don't fully understand, and the agent says 'just sign'.

steps.prompt: The agent says the offer ends today. What do you do?

options.text: Sign now so you don't lose the offer
options.then: You pick up the pen, and he flips to the last page. "Initials first," he says.

options.text: Skim it yourself and sign if it seems fine
options.then: The small print runs six pages. You miss the fee on page four.

options.text: Pause, and have a qualified person check it
options.then: The agent frowns and taps his pen on the desk.

options.text: Trust the agent. He does this every day
options.then: He smiles. His job is to close the deal, not to explain it.

steps.why: A rushed signature is a red flag, and a pause costs little.

steps.prompt: The agent says everyone signs this without reading. What do you do?

options.text: Assume it's fine, since everyone does
options.then: It feels normal for a minute. You still haven't read a word of it.

options.text: Ask for a short verbal summary instead
options.then: His summary is short and sweet, and leaves out the charges.

options.text: Ask a friend who took a different loan
options.then: Her loan has other terms. Her advice doesn't fit yours.

options.text: Ask for a copy to take home and review
options.then: He hesitates, then hands it over. The terms are clearer at your own table.

steps.why: A copy lets you read at your own pace.

steps.prompt: A cousin who works at a bank glances at the offer and says the interest and fees are high. What do you do?

options.text: Sign anyway, since you've come this far
options.then: The time spent doesn't change the terms.

options.text: Ask the agent for a 'special rate' by phone
options.then: He offers a slightly lower rate, valid only today.

options.text: Borrow from a quick loan app instead
options.then: It's quick. The rate is higher still.

options.text: Compare options and borrow only what you need
options.then: You find a clearer offer, or decide to borrow less.

steps.why: Comparing options and borrowing less keeps the cost down.

steps.prompt: Later, the same agent calls with another great deal. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes. You've already met him before
options.then: Familiarity feels safe. The terms are the same kind of small print.

options.text: Ask for written terms, and check them first
options.then: He sends them. You read them slowly, and with someone who knows.

options.text: Take it if the monthly amount sounds small
options.then: The monthly amount is small. The term is long, and the total isn't.

options.text: Ask him to decide what suits you best
options.then: He picks the loan that pays him best.

steps.why: Every big money offer deserves a written check first.

scenarios.debrief: Big decisions deserve a qualified, neutral check; this is education, not personal advice.
scenarios.relearn: Pause and check big money decisions with a qualified, trusted source first.

scenarios.hook: Your older brother pressures you to take a loan in your name 'for the family'.

steps.prompt: He says the family is counting on you. What do you do?

options.text: Believe he will repay, so it should be fine
options.then: He relaxes. "I'll bring the forms tomorrow." Nothing is signed yet.

options.text: Think a smaller loan can't do much harm
options.then: He agrees at once. A smaller loan would still be yours to repay if he doesn't.

options.text: Ask him to write the promise down
options.then: He writes a note. The lender won't accept a note between you.

options.text: Decline, and get advice before signing
options.then: His jaw tightens. "Everyone else would help."

steps.why: A loan in your name is your debt, so advice comes before any signature.

steps.prompt: The next day he says the family's whole future rests on this loan. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you really are being selfish
options.then: He senses the doubt. "Think about it," he says, and the reminders begin.

options.text: Point out that he already owes others
options.then: A fight starts. You're both shouting and nothing changes.

options.text: Say you care, but can't borrow for others
options.then: He mutters, but the conversation moves on.

options.text: Ask your cousin to convince him for you
options.then: Your cousin tries. He says it's none of her business.

steps.why: You can care about family and still refuse a loan in your name.

steps.prompt: He brings forms with your ID details already filled in. What do you do?

options.text: Think it is already filled in, so it must be official
options.then: He nods and holds out the pen. The forms look official, and he gives you no time.

options.text: Ask a friend if checking the amount is enough
options.then: She says check it and sign. The amount is big, and a checked signature is still a signature.

options.text: Ask him to leave the forms for you to read
options.then: He leaves them. They sit at home with your details on them.

options.text: Refuse, and put your ID somewhere safe
options.then: He stares. You put your documents in your bag and leave.

steps.why: Your ID documents are yours to keep safe, and you can refuse to sign.

steps.prompt: The pressure keeps coming every day. What do you do next?

options.text: Keep quiet so the family stays together
options.then: The house stays quiet. The pressure doesn't.

options.text: Tell him you'll decide after he clears old debts
options.then: He says he's paid them. You can't check.

options.text: Tell yourself it will stop on its own
options.then: The house stays tense. The pressure carries on every day.

options.text: Call 181 or 1091, and tell a trusted person
options.then: The helpline listens without judging and explains your options.

steps.why: Pressure to borrow for someone else is abuse, and help is at 181 or 1091.

scenarios.debrief: Being pressured into debt in your name for someone else is economic abuse, never your fault. Help is at 181 or 1091.
scenarios.relearn: Don't take coerced debt in your name. It's economic abuse, and help is at 181/1091.

scenarios.hook: You have just received your first payslip.

steps.prompt: The credit is thousands lower than your offer letter's number. What do you do?

options.text: Assume you were cheated and stew quietly
options.then: The worry sits all week. Nothing gets explained.

options.text: Ignore the payslip and carry on as usual
options.then: You miss any real error, and what you actually earn.

options.text: Tell everyone in the office HR cheated you
options.then: The gossip spreads. HR hears, and the facts still aren't clear.

options.text: Read the lines, then ask HR about gross and net
options.then: The lines make more sense once HR explains them.

steps.why: Net is gross minus deductions, and HR can explain each line.

steps.prompt: Days later you open the payslip again and see lines for provident fund and tax. What do you do?

options.text: Skip them. They're automatic anyway
options.then: You still don't know what you pay, or why.

options.text: Ask a senior to explain in the canteen
options.then: He gives a quick guess. His deductions differ from yours.

options.text: Ask HR to remove the deductions you dislike
options.then: HR says some are required by rule, and some are your own savings.

options.text: Look up each line and ask HR about unknown ones
options.then: You learn what each one covers. The provident fund line is your own saving.

steps.why: Knowing each line shows what is tax and what is your own saving.

steps.prompt: The numbers turn out to be right, and the take-home is what it is. What do you do?

options.text: Plan your budget from the gross number
options.then: You budget for a bigger number than arrives, every month.

options.text: Feel cheated and plan to quit
options.then: You stew for a week. Nothing has changed except your mood.

options.text: Ask HR to raise your pay to make up the deductions
options.then: HR says deductions aren't underpayment, so there is nothing to raise. The budget still misses.

options.text: Budget from net pay, not gross
options.then: The plan matches what actually arrives. There's no monthly surprise.

steps.why: Net is the money you can plan with.

steps.prompt: A friend gets her first payslip and is upset at the same gap. What do you tell her?

options.text: Tell her deductions are a scam
options.then: She's angry. The facts remain unexplained.

options.text: Tell her to ignore it and move on
options.then: She ignores it. A real error would go unnoticed.

options.text: Tell her to quit and find a better payer
options.then: She doesn't, and she's still confused about her pay.

options.text: Explain net and gross. Tell her to ask HR
options.then: She nods. "So the gap isn't missing money."

steps.why: Sharing what you learned helps her read her payslip too.

scenarios.debrief: Net is gross minus deductions like tax and provident fund; reading the payslip prevents surprises.
scenarios.relearn: Read your payslip. Net is gross minus deductions, so ask HR if it's unclear.
