scenarios.hook: Your wages came into your bank account this morning.
scenarios.setup: Your phone buzzes as you finish your shift.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "Bank security here. Read me the OTP on your phone."

options.text: "Okay, hold on. Let me read it out to you."
options.then: "Quickly, please. The system is timing out."

options.text: "I'm not sure. Maybe I'll give it just this once."
options.then: "Just this once. Go on, read it."

options.text: "Can you send it to me in writing first?"
options.then: "Writing takes time. Read the code instead."

options.text: "I never share OTPs. I'll call the bank myself."
options.then: A pause. "There isn't time for that."

steps.why: An OTP is never shared, so call the bank on its own number.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "Your account locks in five minutes. Do it now."

options.text: "All right. I don't want it locked. Here it comes."
options.then: "Good." He waits while you fumble for the message.

options.text: "Let me ask my supervisor if I should."
options.then: "No need. Supervisors don't handle this."

options.text: "Then lock it. I'll call the bank tomorrow."
options.then: "Don't hang up. Just give me the code." The call drags on.

options.text: "A rush is a scam sign. I'm hanging up."
options.then: The line cuts. You start dialling the number on your card, and he rings back.

steps.why: A rush is the scammer's tool, so slow down and check.

steps.prompt: The caller says: "Before the code, read me your card number. It's for security."

options.text: "It's 4, 5, 6... wait, why do you need it?"
options.then: "For security. Keep going."

options.text: "Only the last four digits, then."
options.then: "That's a start. Now the rest."

options.text: "Okay. If it's for security, here it is."
options.then: "Yes, yes." He now has a door into your account.

options.text: "No. I won't give any details. Goodbye."
options.then: He hangs up. You note the number to report on 1930.

steps.why: A real bank never asks for card details on a call, and you can report on 1930.

scenarios.relearn: Never share an OTP; hang up and call the bank's official number yourself.

scenarios.hook: A friend has a money-making scheme he can't stop talking about.
scenarios.setup: He catches you after class.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "My cousin doubled his money in three weeks. Guaranteed. Join me."

options.text: "Fine, I'll put in a little so you stop asking."
options.then: "Great! Send it to this number now."

options.text: "If you're sure, I guess I'll trust you on it."
options.then: "I'm sure. Everyone's in."

options.text: "Guaranteed doubling is a scam. I'll pass."
options.then: "Come on. You'll miss out." He looks at you, unsure.

options.text: "Tell me more. I'll decide later."
options.then: He sends a link and a deadline.

steps.why: A guaranteed doubling is never real, so pass.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "It's legit. There's a certificate and a support team."

options.text: "A certificate? Then it must be real."
options.then: "Exactly!" He sends you the joining link.

options.text: "Let me test with a very small amount."
options.then: "Small is fine." The small amount leads to a bigger ask.

options.text: "A certificate proves nothing. A guarantee is the scam sign."
options.then: He frowns. "But it's registered!" He has no answer to the guarantee.

options.text: "Fine, I'll join. Just keep my name out of the group."
options.then: "Fine." He adds you anyway.

steps.why: A guarantee is the scam sign, and a certificate doesn't change that.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Send the money tonight. This round closes at midnight."

options.text: "Okay. I'll stop overthinking and send it."
options.then: "That's the spirit." He sends the account number.

options.text: "I'll check later, after I've put some in."
options.then: "Sure." Later, the money is already gone.

options.text: "Checking is how I keep my money safe."
options.then: He sighs. "Fine. Your loss." But he doesn't ask again.

options.text: "Let's ask the group if it's safe."
options.then: The group cheers for it. Of course they do.

steps.why: Checking before acting on money advice keeps your savings safe.

scenarios.relearn: 'Guaranteed doubling' is a scam; pass and verify before you act.

scenarios.hook: Your partner has a plan for how your money should be handled.
scenarios.setup: He raises it while you both cook.

steps.prompt: Your partner Neel says: "Close your account. I'll handle everything. It's simpler."

options.text: "Maybe it really is simpler if you manage it."
options.then: "Exactly." He looks pleased and talks about how simple it would be.

options.text: "My mother says a good partner trusts completely."
options.then: "She's right," he says. He starts talking about next steps.

options.text: "My cousin says I should just let you see everything."
options.then: "I'd rather manage it. Seeing isn't enough."

options.text: "I'm keeping my own account. It's not negotiable."
options.then: His face tightens. "Why are you making this difficult?"

steps.why: Your own account is yours, and it isn't up for negotiation.

steps.prompt: Later Neel says: "I've already got the bank's closure form. You just sign it."

options.text: "Maybe I am being unfair to you."
options.then: He softens at once. "I knew you'd see it." The form stays on the table.

options.text: "I won't sign. My account is my independence."
options.then: He looks away. "Independence from me?" But he puts the form down.

options.text: "A friend says peace matters more than an account."
options.then: He nods. "Your friend gets it." The talk comes back every week.

options.text: "Maybe a good partner puts everything in one place."
options.then: He takes it as agreement. "Good. Let's sort it this week."

steps.why: Your account is about independence, not distrust, and it's yours to keep.

steps.prompt: Neel says: "My parents say couples put everything in one account."

options.text: "Maybe your parents know better than me."
options.then: He smiles, satisfied. "They've seen more of life."

options.text: "Then ask them to explain it to my parents."
options.then: "A family meeting? That would make it worse."

options.text: "Couples can share some money. My own account stays."
options.then: He hesitates. "Your own account." He doesn't agree, but he repeats it.

options.text: "Maybe one account is how real couples show trust."
options.then: He nods. "Exactly. So we agree." The pressure doesn't let up.

steps.why: Couples can share some money, and your own account stays yours.

steps.prompt: That week Neel says: "Close it by Sunday. Don't expect me to stay calm if you don't."

options.text: "Maybe a good partner would just close it."
options.then: He nods, pleased. The threat is still sitting there, unanswered.

options.text: "My friend says if I show you everything, you'll calm down."
options.then: He nods. "Smart friend." He keeps asking about your bag and your phone.

options.text: "Maybe I'm the one making you angry for no reason."
options.then: He says nothing, and the silence grows heavy. He turns colder.

options.text: "I won't decide under pressure. I'm going out for a bit."
options.then: He scoffs, but lets you go. Outside, you text your sister.

steps.why: Stepping away from a threat is safe, and reaching someone you trust helps.

steps.prompt: A few days later your sister asks: "You've seemed tense. What do you need from me?"

options.text: "Nothing. I'll manage."
options.then: She nods, unsure. You're alone with it again.

options.text: "Just don't tell anyone."
options.then: She agrees, worried. No one else knows, so no one else can step in.

options.text: "Tell Neel what I said. He'll listen to you."
options.then: She tries. He turns angry with her, and with you.

options.text: "Help thinking it through, and 181 or 1091."
options.then: She writes the numbers down with you. You feel less alone.

steps.why: Help exists at 181 or 1091, and control over your money is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: Keep your own account; being pushed to close it is a financial-control red flag.

scenarios.hook: Your first take-home pay is lower than you expected.
scenarios.setup: You sit down in the HR manager's office.

steps.prompt: The HR manager says: "You wanted to talk about your payslip?"

options.text: "It's fine. I'm sure it's all correct anyway."
options.then: "Okay, then." She closes the file, but pauses. "You seemed worried when you came in."

options.text: "I think you paid me less than you promised."
options.then: She stiffens. "That's a serious claim. On what basis?"

options.text: "Is everyone's pay this much lower than promised?"
options.then: "Pay differs by person. Let's look at yours."

options.text: "Can you walk me through the deductions?"
options.then: "Of course. Let's start with gross, then net."

steps.why: Asking to be walked through the lines is polite and effective.

steps.prompt: The HR manager turns the payslip towards you: "Here's gross, then tax, provident fund and deductions. Questions?"

options.text: "No, that's clear. Thanks."
options.then: "Great." She doesn't look convinced. "Still, let me explain net pay."

options.text: "Can we lower the provident fund deduction?"
options.then: "It's set by rule. I can't change that."

options.text: "Who else checks these numbers?"
options.then: "Payroll double-checks." It doesn't explain your lines.

options.text: "What does each deduction cover, and is it fixed?"
options.then: "Tax varies. Provident fund is a set share, and it's yours."

steps.why: Knowing what each line covers shows which are taxes and which are savings.

steps.prompt: The HR manager says: "Net is what reaches your account. Does that make sense?"

options.text: "Sort of. I'll figure it out later."
options.then: "Sure." The confusion returns next payday.

options.text: "So the company keeps the difference?"
options.then: "No. It goes to tax and to your provident fund."

options.text: "Yes. So I should budget from net, not gross."
options.then: "Exactly. That's how most people plan."

options.text: "Can you just increase my net pay?"
options.then: "Pay is fixed by your contract. I can't change it."

steps.why: Net pay is the real number to plan your month with.

steps.prompt: The HR manager says: "Anything else before you go?"

options.text: "No, thanks. I don't want to bother you again."
options.then: "It's no bother." You leave without a contact.

options.text: "I'd like a raise, since the net is low."
options.then: "That's a separate conversation, with a different basis."

options.text: "Can I see a colleague's payslip to compare?"
options.then: "Payslips are private. I can't share those."

options.text: "Yes. Can I get a written breakup, and who to ask?"
options.then: "Yes, I'll email it. Ask me anytime."

steps.why: A written breakup and a contact make future questions easy.

scenarios.relearn: Ask HR to explain deductions: net is gross minus tax, provident fund and the rest.

scenarios.hook: You have gone to a loan agent about borrowing money.
scenarios.setup: He slides the papers across his desk.

steps.prompt: The agent says: "Sign right now and the offer is yours. Tomorrow it's gone."

options.text: "Okay, if I might lose the offer, I'll sign now."
options.then: He nods and hands you a pen.

options.text: "You seem trustworthy, so I'll just go ahead."
options.then: He smiles. He doesn't point out the fees.

options.text: "Give me ten minutes to read the main page."
options.then: "Ten is fine." The main page is three lines. The fees are on the rest.

options.text: "I don't sign what I don't understand. I'll check."
options.then: He frowns. "Offers like this don't last." You keep the papers.

steps.why: Never sign what you don't understand, however short the offer.

steps.prompt: The agent says: "Look, nobody reads all that. It's standard, so let's finish up."

options.text: "Standard, okay. Where do I sign?"
options.then: He flips to the last page, and points.

options.text: "Read me the important parts aloud."
options.then: He reads the top lines quickly, skipping the charges.

options.text: "I'll sign the first page now, the rest later."
options.then: "Sure." The first page already holds your signature.

options.text: "Then it won't hurt to let me take a copy."
options.then: He hesitates, then slides a copy over. He doesn't look pleased.

steps.why: A copy lets you read the terms in peace.

steps.prompt: The agent says: "The rate is a bit higher than I said. It may rise again tomorrow."

options.text: "Then I'll sign here. I can't risk it."
options.then: He nods and turns to the last page, ready for your signature.

options.text: "Can you hold today's rate for me?"
options.then: "I can't promise. Rates move."

options.text: "Then a qualified person checks it first."
options.then: "As you like." You gather the papers and leave to get them checked.

options.text: "I'll ask a friend who took a loan last year."
options.then: Her loan was different. She can't read yours.

steps.why: A qualified check beats a rushed rate.

steps.prompt: Your friend, who came along, says: "He seems fine to me. Just take it."

options.text: "Fair. He seems fine, so I'll sign."
options.then: You sign, and feel relief for a minute.

options.text: "You're right. I'm overthinking it."
options.then: She smiles. The papers stay unread.

options.text: "I'll sign only the smaller loan."
options.then: "Smaller is easier." It's still a loan you didn't check.

options.text: "A few days to check is cheap. A bad loan isn't."
options.then: She shrugs. "Fair point." You take the papers home.

steps.why: A few days to check costs little, while a bad loan costs far more.

scenarios.relearn: Don't sign what you don't understand; check big decisions with a qualified person first.

scenarios.hook: A relative has a money favour to ask of you.
scenarios.setup: Your uncle catches you alone in the kitchen.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Take the loan in your name. I'll repay it every month. I promise."

options.text: "Maybe saying no would hurt the family."
options.then: "It would," he says. "So help us." He waits for your answer.

options.text: "If you promise to pay it, it should be fine."
options.then: "Of course. I'll bring the forms." The promise isn't on the lender's paper.

options.text: "A smaller one can't hurt, can it?"
options.then: "Smaller is a start." He nods. It would still be your name on it.

options.text: "I won't take a loan in my name for someone else."
options.then: He sighs. "It's only paper." But he hasn't got an answer.

steps.why: A loan in your name is your debt, so you can say no.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "I'd never let you pay for this. Family looks after family."

options.text: "Family is family. Maybe I'm being too careful."
options.then: "Good." He's already reaching for the forms in his bag.

options.text: "I trust you. Just write it down on paper."
options.then: He scribbles a note. The lender won't read it.

options.text: "Then I'll be the guarantor, not the borrower."
options.then: "Nearly the same." The lender could still come after you.

options.text: "It's not about trust. A lender can chase only me."
options.then: He's quiet for a moment. "Hm. I hadn't thought of it that way."

steps.why: Trust and legal debt are different things, and the lender only sees your name.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "First, one quick signature from you here. Just as a witness."

options.text: "A witness signature is just a formality."
options.then: He smiles. "Exactly." A signature can carry more weight than it looks.

options.text: "Only if you show me the full papers."
options.then: He shows one page. The rest stay in his bag.

options.text: "Everyone in the family has signed something like this."
options.then: "They have," he says quickly. "It's normal." Nobody mentions what it cost them.

options.text: "I'll sign nothing. I'm talking to someone I trust first."
options.then: He mutters, but puts the papers away.

steps.why: Get advice before signing. Pressure to borrow is never your fault, and help is at 181 or 1091.

scenarios.relearn: Coerced debt in your name is economic abuse. Decline and get advice, and reach 181/1091.

scenarios.hook: A friend has been unusually quiet lately, and today she finally talks.
scenarios.setup: She says it quietly, looking at the floor.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I'm buried in debt. I can't even tell my family. I'm so ashamed."

options.text: "How did you even let it get this bad?"
options.then: She flinches. "I knew you'd say that."

options.text: "Just don't tell anyone. It's embarrassing."
options.then: She nods. The secret stays heavy.

options.text: "I'll cover it. Don't worry about it."
options.then: She tears up. "You can't afford that either."

options.text: "No judgement. Let's find the right help together."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "Together. Okay."

steps.why: No shame and a steady offer to help are what she needs first.

steps.prompt: She says: "I don't know where to start. There are so many loans."

options.text: "Let's just not look at the numbers today."
options.then: "That feels good for an hour." The numbers stay the same.

options.text: "Ignore the small ones. They don't matter."
options.then: "Okay." The small ones grow fees of their own.

options.text: "Take a new loan to clear the old ones."
options.then: "A new loan?" It clears two loans and starts a bigger one.

options.text: "Let's list each loan and its due date first."
options.then: She opens a notes app. "Six loans. It's a lot, but it's a list."

steps.why: A written list turns a pile of worry into something you can plan.

steps.prompt: She says: "Who would even help with something like this?"

options.text: "Ask the guy on Instagram who fixes debts."
options.then: "He wants a fee first," she says. "Up front."

options.text: "Nobody. It's better to sort it alone."
options.then: She nods, and feels more alone.

options.text: "Your family will only blame you. Skip them."
options.then: She agrees. The loneliest route is the one she takes.

options.text: "A bank or a qualified, trusted source can help."
options.then: She writes that down. "A qualified, trusted source. Okay."

steps.why: A bank or a qualified, trusted source can give a plan for her case.

steps.prompt: A few weeks later she says: "I keep worrying. What if this happens again?"

options.text: "It won't, now that you've learned."
options.then: She smiles. Without a plan, the same pattern returns.

options.text: "Then stop spending on anything fun."
options.then: "Nothing fun?" It lasts a few weeks.

options.text: "Then call me and I'll fix it."
options.then: "You can't fix my debts." She looks uneasy.

options.text: "Then we'll notice sooner. Let's set a monthly check."
options.then: "A monthly check-in. That I can do." She types a reminder.

steps.why: A small monthly check helps catch trouble early.

scenarios.relearn: Reassure a friend in debt without shame and find the right help together.

scenarios.hook: You've researched the market rate and are about to talk pay with your manager.
scenarios.setup: You sit down with her after your review.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "So, you wanted to talk about your pay?"

options.text: "I don't want to seem greedy. Forget I asked."
options.then: "All right." She starts to move on, then pauses. "You came in for a reason."

options.text: "Whatever you think is fair, I'll take it."
options.then: "Okay." She offers a small increase, then asks, "Is that all you wanted?"

options.text: "My friends earn more than me. It's unfair."
options.then: "I can't compare with your friends. Let's look at your role."

options.text: "Based on the market rate, I'd like to discuss pay."
options.then: She nods. "All right. Go on."

steps.why: Naming the market rate keeps the talk about facts and value.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "If there is a number you want, say it now. What do you have in mind?"

options.text: "Anything you can offer is fine."
options.then: "Okay." The offer is lower than the market rate.

options.text: "Double what I earn now."
options.then: "That's far outside what we can do." The talk stalls.

options.text: "I'd rather you tell me your number first."
options.then: "I'd like to hear yours first." The talk sits still.

options.text: "Near the top of the market range, given my results."
options.then: She writes it down. "That's clear. Let me think."

steps.why: Stating a reasoned number is normal and professional.

steps.prompt: Your manager says: "The budget is tight this year. I can't move much."

options.text: "Okay, never mind then."
options.then: "Thanks for understanding." She closes her notebook.

options.text: "Then I'll start looking for another job."
options.then: "I'd hate for you to go. Let's not jump there yet."

options.text: "I want a written promise of a raise next year."
options.then: "I can't promise figures in writing."

options.text: "I understand. Can we set a review date?"
options.then: "That I can do. Let's say three months." She makes a note.

steps.why: A set review date keeps the door open when the budget is tight.

steps.prompt: As you get up, your manager says: "Leave it with me for now."

options.text: "Okay, whenever. I'm happy either way."
options.then: "Good to know." There is no real deadline now.

options.text: "I need an answer today, though."
options.then: "I can't decide that fast." The room cools.

options.text: "Fine. I'll mention it to the team meanwhile."
options.then: "Please don't. Let's keep it between us."

options.text: "Thanks. I'll email a note of what we said."
options.then: She nods. "Please do. That keeps us both clear."

steps.why: A short written note keeps what you discussed clear and the follow-up moving.

scenarios.relearn: Negotiating from the market rate is normal and smart, not greedy or rude.
